item.title: The 3-Ingredient Pumpkin Soup You'll Fall For
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit Score: 2.46
It’s That Simple is our series about recipes so easy, you can make them with your eyes closed. Think tiny ingredient lists, laid-back techniques, and results so delicious you’ll text home about them. Each fall the first crimson-hued leaf drops to the ground, declaring the start of Pumpkin Season. And suddenly the perennial darling is everywhere. Pumpkin bread, pumpkin spice lattes, babies in pumpkin costumes, the list goes on. This year we’re declaring our favorite: a comforting curry pumpkin soup that comes together with just three ingredients. A three-ingredient soup may sound like a hack job, but think again. Each element—pumpkin purée, curry paste, and coconut milk—brings its own strength, creating a flavor that’s as cozy as a vintage sweater. Start by heating oil in a pot. Any type works, but I like to use unrefined coconut oil for a tropical fruitiness. From there, add a dollop of red curry paste. For a gentle warmth, turn to a jar of Thai Kitchen. To level up the spice, grab a can of Maesri, our Test Kitchen’s go-to brand. Cook the paste until it deepens to a sun-baked terra-cotta hue and is fragrant enough to tickle your nose. This step unleashes the nuances so you can taste every ingredient, like chiles, shallots, and lemongrass—none of which you had to prep yourself. Next, dump in cans of pumpkin purée and coconut milk, add some water, and let it all simmer. Taste and add salt if needed. That’s it. You’ve just made soup in 15 minutes. And a really good one at that! Feel free to gussy it up. I like to reserve a few spoonfuls of coconut milk from the can to swirl on top. (Once a food stylist, always a food stylist.) You could stir in baby spinach or top with cilantro or mint. For a hit of protein, poach a handful of shrimp in the simmering pot. However you serve it, this soup is bound to be an annual favorite, a nourishing bowl you can pull off even on the busiest fall night.

item.title: The Most Remote Places on Earth You Can Actually Visit
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 5.99
Reaching the most remote places on Earth takes more than just a plane ticket—it takes patience, endurance, and often a string of connections that make the arrival feel like an achievement in itself. These are places where airports are rare, ships arrive only a handful of times a year, and the communities you meet are outnumbered by wildlife. What they offer in return is a kind of distance that feels almost impossible in the modern world—skies free of light pollution, landscapes shaped by extremes, and the rare quiet that comes from being far beyond the usual travel circuit. Why do we seek remoteness? Journeys to places like these are rarely simple, but that difficulty is part of the allure. They remind us what travel feels like when the destination is hard-won, when the act of arriving carries its own reward. In the Kerguelen Islands, there are no hotels or tour buses, only wind, sea, and wildlife. In Russia's Oymyakon, for example, just stepping outside is an act of endurance. And on South Georgia, hundreds of thousands of penguins gather on beaches once scarred by whaling. In a world where so much feels accessible, true remoteness has become rare. These are the most remote places on Earth that shift our sense of scale and remind us that there are still corners of this planet where distance is intact. Kerguelen Islands, Southern Indian Ocean Nicknamed the “Desolation Islands,” this French territory sits marooned in the southern Indian Ocean, approximately 1,865 miles from Madagascar. Few places feel so utterly cut off. Volcanic cliffs plunge into storm-lashed seas, while king penguins and elephant seals crowd the beaches in their thousands. Nobody lives here permanently—only rotating teams of scientists, engineers, and unconventional travelers. What surrounds you is a world sculpted by wind, sea, and stone, where humanity has left little mark. How to get there: The French supply vessel Marion Dufresne II sails from Réunion Island several times a year. The voyage takes around six days. Quttinirpaaq National Park, Canada On the northern tip of Ellesmere Island, just shy of 500 miles from the North Pole, Quttinirpaaq lives up to its Inuktitut name: “top of the world.” It is a place of extremes—glaciers stretch for miles, jagged peaks rise from polar deserts, and the summer sun never sets. Muskoxen graze the tundra, Arctic wolves hunt in silence, and traces of ancient Inuit encampments remind you how long people have endured at this latitude. Few visitors make it here, but those who do find a landscape that feels infinite. How to get there: Travel first to Resolute Bay in Nunavut, then connect by charter plane to Tanquary Fiord, open only in the summer months. Ittoqqortoormiit, Greenland Few places capture the human will to survive like Ittoqqortoormiit, a settlement of around 450 people perched at the edge of Scoresby Sound, the world's largest fjord system. Wooden houses painted red, blue, and yellow dot the snowy cliffs, while rhythms of life here still follow the seasons: hunting and fishing sustain families, sled dogs line the streets, and in winter the sea ice seals the town off from the outside world completely. The surrounding waters carry drifting icebergs, and it's not unusual to see polar bears wandering the coast. How to get there: Reachable by helicopter from Nerlerit Inaat Airport, itself connected by small aircraft from Reykjavik, Iceland. Longyearbyen, Norway Longyearbyen, in the Svalbard archipelago, is the northernmost town of its size in the world. Despite its isolation, it's surprisingly lived-in, with cafés, a craft brewery, and even a fine-dining restaurant. Beyond town, reindeer roam freely, glaciers carve the landscape, and the Global Seed Vault safeguards the world's crops in a frozen hillside. Here, summers pass in endless daylight; winters in an unbroken stretch of night. How to get there: Daily flights connect Oslo and Tromsø to Svalbard Airport, making it one of the more accessible remote places. South Georgia, South Atlantic Ocean A remote island once known for whaling, South Georgia is now a sanctuary where wildlife has reclaimed the land. More than half a million king penguins gather on its beaches, while elephant seals occupy the shore in extraordinary numbers. Rusting relics of abandoned whaling stations remain, and the grave of polar explorer Ernest Shackleton—the Anglo-Irish Antarctic explorer who led three British expeditions to the Antarctic—lies at Grytviken, a pilgrimage for history enthusiasts. After decades of ecological strain, including the introduction of reindeer by whalers, conservation projects are now restoring the island’s native habitats and protecting its fragile ecosystem. How to get there: No airports exist—visitors arrive by expedition ship, usually as part of cruises departing from Ushuaia, Argentina. McMurdo Station, Antarctica On Ross Island, McMurdo Station is the largest research base on the continent, supporting around 1,000 people each summer. It has been the launch point for many of Antarctica’s most important expeditions, from early 20th-century journeys led by Scott and Shackleton to modern scientific studies on climate change and glaciology. The surrounding landscape—glaciers, volcanic peaks, and the vast Ross Ice Shelf—has shaped much of what we know about the polar world. Travelers can’t stay at McMurdo, but expedition cruises to the Ross Sea sometimes include landings nearby, offering the rare chance to stand at the centre of Antarctic exploration. How to get there: Expedition cruises to the Ross Sea depart from New Zealand or Australia, with limited charter flights from Christchurch supporting specialist itineraries. Pitcairn Islands, South Pacific Ocean Home to just under 50 people, the Pitcairn Islands are one of the world’s least populated territories. Settled by the HMS Bounty mutineers in 1790, the community is still made up of their descendants. Life moves at a slow rhythm, shaped by the island’s rugged volcanic terrain and the surrounding Pacific waters. For visitors, the appeal lies in the intimacy: hiking to hidden caves, diving into crystalline waters, and being welcomed by almost every resident. How to get there: Fly to Tahiti, then on to Mangareva in French Polynesia. From there, a supply ship makes the 32-hour crossing to Pitcairn several times a year. Changthang, Ladakh, India High on the Tibetan Plateau, Changthang is a high-altitude desert where the air is thin and the landscape seems endless. Nomadic Changpa herders graze yak and goats across sweeping plains, while saltwater lakes like Tso Moriri and Pangong Tso shimmer beneath snow-capped peaks. Black-necked cranes, wild asses, and even snow leopards are spotted here, adding to its sense of undisturbed isolation. How to get there: Flights run from Delhi to Leh, followed by an overland journey across rugged mountain passes into the plateau. This article was originally published in Condé Nast Traveller Middle East.

item.title: Newport, Rhode Island, Is New England’s Gilded Jewel—Here’s Where to Eat, Stay, and Play
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 5.24
Newport, Rhode Island, has certainly been having a moment as of late. You can attribute it to the Gilded Age dramas taking over small screens, the old-money aesthetic taking over TikTok, the Real Housewives of Rhode Island taking over Bravo, or just the fact that it’s beyond beautiful all year long. Either way, it’s undeniable that this compact coastal city has become a mecca of sorts for travelers eager to live out their East Coast fantasies—seafood, seersucker, sailboats, and all. But truth be told, Newport has never been a bad idea. The charming city has been a popular summer destination since the early 19th century, first as a playground for America’s elite, with families like the Vanderbilts and Astors building massive mansions along the water to serve as vacation homes (more on those later). Today, it’s a little less exclusive and a hot spot year-round, with New Englanders and international visitors alike spending sunny days becoming one with the sand at Easton’s Beach, breezy afternoons hiking the Cliff Walk, and chilly nights imbibing their way through Bowen’s Wharf before retreating to shingled cottages and luxurious hotels across town. If all that sounds like your kind of bliss, keep reading for a guide to seeing Newport in all its glory, as compiled by two New Yorkers who have been returning over and over again for the past decade. Here’s where to eat, stay, and play in the City by the Sea. Where to eat We’d argue the food and drink scene in Newport is reason enough to come to town, boasting old favorites and newer hubs that have given the city’s dining scene some fresh energy. Early birds, hit up Cru Cafe for a cozy bistro vibe and elevated comfort dishes like smoked salmon avocado toast. If you’re willing to wait in line, The Nitro Bar is a newer favorite (especially among influencers) with coffee and pastries that just might be worth the hype. Or, head to locally loved Franklin Spa, a legendary diner that hasn't changed its retro greasy-spoon energy in decades, and still serves one of the best lunches in town. Speaking of lunch, if the weather calls for it, take yours alfresco. Use Bowen’s Wharf as your hub: Belly up at 22 Bowen’s outdoor bar-restaurant area, have a casual seafood lunch at The Mooring, or get your clam chowder fix at The Black Pearl, with its lively dockside setting. You'll also find Clarke Cooke House, one of Newport's most popular restaurants, at the wharf. Its ship-like setting is one for the books, and the bistro offers a big menu spanning summer sushi to burgers, native cod, and even steak frites. For something less serious, Wally’s Weiners is another classic, and the kind of place you'll want to work into a day of wandering around Thames Street, known for being the center of the city. For harbor views and a Mediterranean-inspired menu, head to Flora, one of the newer names in town housed within the Gardiner House hotel. White Horse Tavern, on the other hand, offers classic Americana, with upscale farm-to-table dining (and stellar rum drinks) inside a building dating back to 1673. Crossing the bridge into Jamestown? Head to Beech if you want dinner to be the main event, with tasty, seasonal American fare headed up by locals. Where to stay Newport has no shortage of gorgeous hotels scattered from busy Thames Street to breezy Castle Hill Cove. Most guest rooms fall on the smaller side—this is a compact city, after all—but the best properties go big on glamour, offering gobsmacking views, old-world interiors, and exceptional in-house eateries and wellness facilities. Those looking for a taste of the Gilded Age should opt for spots like The Vanderbilt, an Auberge property built by a member of the Vanderbilt family in 1908, or Francis Malbone House, a Georgian-style mansion that dates back to 1760. If you’re all about location, location, location, book The Chanler at Cliff Walk for easy access to the popular waterfront hiking trail, Hammetts Hotel if you want to be steps from some of the city’s best bars and restaurants, or Forty 1º North Hotel Marina Resort to be so close to the water you’re basically swimming. Whether you’re staying there or not, you don't skip a stop inside Castle Hill Inn, a landmark Victorian mansion and one of the most iconic hotels in town. With an incredible location atop rocky bluffs that overlook the sailboat-studded ocean, the property’s Lawn Terrace is where you’ll want to grab a glass of Sauv Blanc and pretend you’re an Astor. Of course, hotels in Newport can be pricey, so if you’re on a budget or traveling with a group, an Airbnb might be a better bet—especially if the sound of a kitchen or common hangout space tickles your fancy. You can find smaller homes and apartments in Newport proper, like this four-bedroom with harbor views right downtown or this minimalist waterfront condo in the Historic District, but many visitors look to Middletown, Rhode Island—a town right outside Newport—for bigger, more affordable rentals. This adorable three-bedroom cottage with a shingled façade, for example, is technically in Middletown, but just five minutes from downtown Newport. Where to play The soul of Newport is rooted in the very concept of play. It’s a family-friendly destination and a romantic coastal escape; a place where sweet boutiques meet cool bars and Gilded Age history meets a working harbor. In the warmer months, chase the sea: Easton’s Beach is the most convenient option near town, Gooseberry Beach is tucked along Ocean Drive, and Second (or Sachuest) Beach offers a long stretch of sand and Atlantic surf. Post up at Second for a lobster roll and fries (sold from a beachside concession stand, the best), then grab an icy, refreshing Del’s Lemonade served from its iconic truck before heading home. Oh, and before you go, buy your next beach read at Commonwealth Books of Newport in the Historic Hill neighborhood. If you time it right, you can hit Newport's renowned Jazz Festival and the Newport Folk Festival, both hosted annually at the end of July (and sometimes running through early August). Plan in advance to secure tickets, as they can go quickly. For a more last-minute excursion that's completely free to the public, walk the Cliff Walk on the southeastern shoreline. The scenic coastal path threads between the Atlantic and the Newport Mansions, which, of course, you'll want to go inside and tour. If you’d rather be on the water than beside it, Sail Newport offers a Try Sailing experience, as well as afternoon-to-sunset sails. For something further from the coast, the International Tennis Hall of Fame is a great rainy day pit stop for exploring the history of the beloved sport and sniffing your way through the gardens surrounding the iconic grass courts. The Preserve in Blackstone Valley offers guided horseback tours, carriage rides, and sunset strolls, while Shephard’s Run Winery is a dreamy estate that gives you an excuse to head inland in South Kingstown for a tasting. As for a great Irish pub, The Fastnet has frosty beers on tap, while O’Brien’s is ever-abuzz and makes a mean house mudslide. If you want to make a night of it, have a drink and bites at Hotel Viking’s French-inspired Pescadou restaurant, then dance to the live DJ at its rooftop bar, Cap Club. Midtown Oyster Bar is perfect for a nightcap.

item.title: These US Airlines Have Mishandled the Most Bags in 2026, According to New Data
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 4.99
Most travelers have experienced that sinking feeling at baggage claim when the carousel stops and their checked luggage is still nowhere to be seen. While lost or delayed bags are sometimes just an unfortunate part of air travel, there are some airlines that statistically mishandle checked bags more often than others. The situation can be extra frustrating in 2026, as most carriers have significantly raised the cost of checking luggage on domestic and short-haul international routes to an average of $45 for the first bag. Despite the elevated fee, US airlines have collectively mishandled 1,120,760 checked bags in the first six months of 2026, according to new data from the Department of Transportation (DOT). That’s an average of about 0.5 bags mishandled per 100 bags enplaned. Although those numbers can seem shocking, they’re similar to mishandled baggage rates for the same stretch in 2025, which saw an average of 0.52 bags mishandled for every 100 loaded into planes’ cargo holds. If you’d like to avoid your carefully packed luggage being on the wrong side of those statistics, it’s a good idea to know which airlines routinely have the highest rates of mishandled bags. The DOT’s monthly air travel consumer reports compare the 13 largest US airlines and how many bags each carrier mishandles per 100 loaded onto planes. A mishandled bag includes baggage that is lost, delayed, damaged, or stolen. In the first half of 2026, American Airlines had the highest rate of mishandled bags, with an average rate of 0.73 mishandled bags per 100 enplaned, the DOT data shows. Closely following is American’s wholly owned regional subsidiary Envoy Air, which mishandled an average of 0.72 bags per 100 enplaned. United Airlines was next, with a mishandled baggage rate of 0.66 bags per 100 enplaned from January to June 2026. On the flip side, low-cost carrier Allegiant Air had the best baggage handling rate, with just 0.12 bags mishandled per 100 enplaned. Travelers who want to keep close tabs on their checked luggage can put devices like Apple Air Tags into their bags and track them during each stage of the flight. Many airlines now integrate Air Tag data into their baggage tracking process, allowing travelers to share the device location with customer service representatives through their mobile apps. Here’s a look at the DOT’s full US airline rankings for the most mishandled bags per 100 enplaned for the first half of 2026: - American Airlines: 0.73 bags - Envoy Air: 0.72 bags - United Airlines: 0.66 bags - Skywest: 0.55 bags - Republic Airways: 0.53 bags - Alaska Airlines/Hawaiian Airlines: 0.53 bags - Frontier Airlines: 0.51 bags - Spirit Airlines: 0.47 bags - PSA Airlines: 0.44 bags - Delta Air Lines: 0.38 bags - Southwest Airlines: 0.32 bags - JetBlue Airways: 0.31 bags - Allegiant Air: 0.12 bags

item.title: The Best Beaches in Italy, From Sicily to Puglia
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 4.89
You’d be hard-pressed to find a more quintessential Italian pastime than spending a summer day at the beach—and the best beaches in Italy lend themselves to precisely that kind of leisurely indulgence. The country has nearly 5,000 miles of coastline, so you can bet there’s a piece of waterfront for everyone. Some are long, wide strips of sand dotted by neat rows of lounge chairs and umbrellas, while others are rocky inlets or hidden coves reachable only by boat or hike. The list below culls our picks for the best beaches all along the peninsula and on the islands, from Liguria in the north to Sicily in the south, along with tips on where to stay near each. Some are accessible by train or public ferry, while others require a car (road trip, anyone?). Keep in mind that summer (especially July and August) is the high season, so expect beaches to be more crowded than at other times of the year. For fewer crowds, consider shoulder season months like May, early June, and September. Tips for visiting the best beaches in Italy For some expert advice on planning a beach-oriented itinerary in Italy, we tapped Georgia Yuill, a Condé Nast Traveler Top Travel Specialist and Butterfield & Robinson’s region director for Italy. Though the best time to visit Italy can vary depending on the type of trip you want to have, a beach vacation warrants some summer vibes—and strategy. “The best time to go to the beaches of Italy are on the weekdays of June, early July, and September,” Yuill says. “Waterfronts in Sardinia and Sicily are particularly lovely in September with the water warmed up over the previous months and visitor numbers low, leaving you with a tranquil and gorgeous setting.” Yuill says the beaches can get crowded on the weekends in June, July, and August, when you’re competing not only with fellow tourists for spots on the sand but also with Italians who are on their own vacations as well. “That said, experiencing the coastline or islands such as Sardinia by gulet or catamaran is an excellent solution to finding quiet inlets and harder-to-reach beaches,” says Yuill. This list features beaches that are free to access, but if you can swing it, private strips of sand at beach clubs are a great option as well. “Not only are they perfect for people-watching, but they provide all the things travelers may not have packed, like umbrellas and lounge chairs,” Yuill says. Plus, families traveling to Italy with kids will especially appreciate the lifeguards on duty. And who can say no to the convenience of showers, changing areas, and eateries? Finally, Yuill suggests choosing an area designated as a Blue Flag Beach, which indicates that it is clean and well cared for from an environmental perspective. This gallery has been updated with new information since its original publish date. Additional reporting by Kris Fordham and Caitlin Morton.

item.title: When Is Prime Big Deal Days? Here's Everything Travelers Need to Know About the Fall Sale
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 4.01
Another Amazon Prime Day is just around the corner, and I already have a shopping cart full of wish-listed items I'm hoping to save on. I usually wait for Prime Big Deal Days to stock up on my favorite home and beauty essentials—and this year, I might even try to get a head start on some holiday gifts before all the chaos of Black Friday and Cyber Monday. After all, Amazon tends to offer its steepest discounts during its twice-a-year mega sale. In years past, I've scored on trending shoes, hard-shell luggage, and electronics for up to 50% off. And since Amazon just announced the dates for this year's highly anticipated Prime Day, let this be your sign to start thinking about what you need to restock and which big-ticket items it might be time to buy (hello, Ōura Ring 5). Prime members are guaranteed to find deals across all major categories, including clothing and shoes, luggage, tech, premium beauty and skincare, outdoor gear, and home goods. Below, I'm breaking down everything there is to know so far about Prime Big Deal Days 2026. Plus, I've listed out some deals running on Amazon right now, so you can start shopping—and saving—early. What is Prime Day? In case you're not familiar with Amazon's best sale of the year, let's get you up to speed: Prime Day is an annual savings event where thousands of products are marked down for a limited time. Prime members will have the chance to save up to 60% off best-selling gear, trending apparel, and so much more. Historically, Prime Day runs in July—but for the past few years, Amazon has been offering a similar sale in October, giving eager shoppers yet another chance to save big. Electronics and home goods tend to be the most popular—and most heavily discounted—items during these Prime Day events, but we typically also see great deals on clothing and shoes, luggage, beauty products, outdoor gear, and travel essentials. When is Prime Day? Amazon finally announced the dates for its fall sale. This year, Prime Big Deal Days will run from Tuesday, October 6, through Wednesday, October 7, 2026. This makes right now a great time to start thinking about which items you hope to see on sale and start building your wish list. Do I have to be an Amazon Prime member to shop the sales? Yes, to take advantage of the limited-time mega sale, you must be a Prime member. Not only do members get access to Prime Day deals, but they also earn free two-day shipping all year long. A Prime membership costs $139 annually or $15 per month. If you're on the fence about joining, sign up for a free 30-day trial. What did our readers buy most last Prime Day? Need some inspo on what to add to your shopping cart ahead of Prime Day 2026? Say no more—check below to see what CN Traveler readers bought most during Amazon's July sale. First and foremost, Away luggage was very popular—and for good reason. The brand's lightweight suitcases are some of our editors' all-time favorite carry-ons and checked bags to travel with. Our readers also picked up a bunch of in-flight essentials, from comfy eye masks to neck pillows (these must-haves can make even the longest flights in economy a little bit more bearable!). In addition, comfortable sneakers, trendy jelly flats, Levi's jeans, portable steamers, and the viral Ōura Ring were big hits among our readers. What early sales can I shop now? We're still a few weeks away from Prime Big Deal Days, but Amazon has plenty of great deals running right now worth checking out. From Bagsmart's top-selling toiletry bag to noise-canceling headphones from Beats, there are already plenty of discounted travel essentials marked down. Also on sale: expandable carry-ons and luggage sets from Samsonite, as well as some travel backpacks and duffel bags. Discounted sneakers, Chelsea boots, and workout sets are all up for grabs too. This article has been updated with new information since its original publish date.

item.title: 9 Standout Galapagos Cruises for Sailing the Bucket-List Wildlife Destination
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 3.64
An extraordinary archipelago 600 miles off the coast of Ecuador, the Galapagos promise a once-in-a-lifetime travel experience—and many agree there's no better way to visit, than by ship. Unlike the typical island-hopping cruise itinerary you'll find elsewhere, Galapagos Island cruises invite travelers to experience some of the most unspoiled environments on earth. The vessels here are small, too—sometimes accommodating as few as 16 passengers. There are no water parks, Broadway-style shows, or casinos on board. Instead, pristine surroundings, uninhabited islands, and rare wildlife are the featured attractions. These cruise itineraries offer the chance to get up close to giant tortoises and playful sea lions, to snorkel among coral and stingrays, and look for rare birds like the blue-footed booby, a species only found in parts of the Pacific Ocean. Leave the logistics to your captain, and let yourself enjoy an incredible adventure of hiking through untouched natural environments or kayaking, paddleboarding, or snorkeling through one of the most interesting parts of the Pacific Ocean. After all, in the Galapagos, animals outnumber people and some of the most interesting scenes are found on the water. Cruises to this remote region usually span about a week and visit multiple islands. And while it is generally an expensive destination, given the hard-to-reach nature of the islands, there are some more affordable ways to cross off this bucket-list trip. Below, we cover nine of the best Galapagos cruises—with options for every type of traveler. The best Galapagos cruise for luxury travelers Ecoventura offers one of the most luxurious—and family-friendly—cruises in the Galapagos. The company operates three expedition yachts, Origin, Theory, and Evolve, each of which can accommodate 20 guests across 10 staterooms. Children six and up are welcome on board, and some staterooms can be connected to create spacious family suites. The crew is the shining star of these yachts, ensuring personalized service, pleasant surprises—like a pirate-themed send-off party to end the trip—and a menu to suit every palate. There’s a breakfast buffet every morning featuring Ecuadorian specialties and international favorites, and a multicourse dinner every night, with plenty of options for vegetarians. Onboard Ecoventura’s yachts, kayaks, stand-up paddleboards, snorkeling gear, and zodiacs are on offer. There’s also a hot tub, fitness center, and plenty of outdoor nooks for taking in the unforgettable views. Off the ship, experienced naturalists lead daily excursions to lava fields, scenic viewpoints, idyllic snorkeling spots, and secluded beaches. Even if you're new to watersports like snorkeling, the ship’s patient guides will teach you how to get comfortable in the water so you can enjoy swimming among turtles, fish, and stingrays. The best Galapagos cruise for solo travelers Join a small group of future friends on the Reina Silvia Voyager, G Adventures’ newest catamaran that’s custom-built for sailing the Galapagos. Two of its 10 cabins feature single beds and are reserved for solo travelers. All come with a private bathroom, desk, and a large picture window to frame the pristine Galapagos views beyond. A 10-day itinerary starts and ends in Quito, taking guests on a journey through the Central and East Islands to look for sea lions, iguanas, and a seemingly endless variety of birds. Go kayaking, snorkeling, scuba diving, or paddleboarding—or kick back and relax on the spacious sundeck while enjoying some of the most unspoiled views in the world. There’s a chef on board to ensure you never go hungry, a hot tub to soothe any sore muscles, lots of spaces for socializing when you want to, and a bar that’s perfect for sunset cocktails—with or without your shipmates. The best Galapagos cruise for travelers craving personal space The Celebrity Flora is one of the largest ships sailing the Galapagos Islands, but don’t expect it to be packed with crowds. While it's about twice the size of the Celebrity Xploration, which also sails to the Galapagos, the Flora carries the same number of people—about 100. The size difference gives the ship a more spacious feel and roomier suites that start at around 224 square feet. Some cabins have floor-to-ceiling windows that open up to make your suite feel like it has a balcony. Others have actual balconies, some as large as 321 square feet. These eco-conscious ships are designed to navigate the most remote parts of the Galapagos Islands. There’s also a retractable marina onboard to make it easier for travelers with mobility issues to get in and out of the vessels ferrying them from ship to shore. The best Galapagos catamaran cruise Avalon Waterways may be better known for its European river cruises, but it also sails the Galapagos Islands, with a chartered luxury catamaran, the Treasure of the Galapagos. The boat can accommodate a maximum of 16 guests and offers a rare amenity in the Galapagos: private balconies. The largest suite comes in at 430 square feet and features not one but two private outdoor spaces. Guests feast on dishes from creative, locally inspired menus featuring seasonal ingredients. There’s also a hot tub and a naturalist on board, and fares include wine with dinner as well as coffee, tea, and water. The best Galapagos cruise for foodies There may be few better places to eat in the Galapagos than The Grill, one of two restaurants on board the Silver Origin, a 100-passenger ship operated by the luxury cruise line Silversea. The Grill serves up premium cuts of meat cooked tableside atop fiery lava stones. Indulge in locally sourced lobster, Andean quinoa, and fresh Galapagos-caught fish. Meals at The Grill are served alfresco, and it’s hard to find a better view for dinner than these natural landscapes. Elsewhere onboard, guests can learn the art of ceviche-making from the ship’s chef and sample Ecuadorian cheese that has been aged in lava tubes. The smallest suites on board are 325 square feet, and many come with balconies. Even the showers offer ocean views, and there’s butler service onboard for anything you might need. While the Silver Origin is another one of the largest ships sailing the Galapagos Islands, these voyages tend to sell out—book early. The best Galapagos cruise for adventure seekers Sailings on board the La Pinta, operated by Uncruise, are designed for adventurous spirits who also appreciate time to unwind. This isn’t the newest or most luxurious ship sailing the Galapagos, but it’s comfortable, unpretentious, and recently refurbished. Onboard this 48-passenger yacht, you’ll find plenty of gear: kayaks, paddleboards, snorkeling equipment, scuba equipment, and a glass-bottom boat included. The itinerary includes visits to seven islands and islets as well as a visit to the Charles Darwin Research Station. Hike Dragon Hill on Isla Santa Cruz while looking for iguanas and flamingos, paddleboard alongside sea lions at Isla Floreana, or enjoy a stroll along a secluded white-sand beach. If you think cruising isn’t your thing, Uncruise might just change your mind. The best Galapagos cruise for science lovers If ever you’ve wondered what life would be like as a scientist, HX Expeditions has the Galapagos cruise for you. The company operates a Citizen Science Program on board the MS Santa Cruz II, enlisting guests to help with completing research projects. Guests can join onboard researchers in collecting samples, learn to make field observations, and visit the onboard science lab to analyze materials and work with experts to process data. Between following in the footsteps of Charles Darwin, visiting his namesake research station, and working with onboard researchers, this is a vacation where learning is accessible—and prioritized. The best affordable Galapagos cruise For travelers craving the wild majesty of the Galapagos at a more affordable price, Nature Galapagos & Ecuador delivers an authentic, expertly curated experience that doesn’t compromise on adventure nor break the budget. Specializing in small-ship and land-based tours, their budget-class cruises—aboard intimate, 8 to 10-person yachts like the New Flamingo and Merak—offer access to remote islands, expert bilingual naturalist guides, and daily excursions that bring you face-to-face with marine iguanas and Galapagos tortoises. Accommodations are simple but comfortable, with snorkeling gear, meals, and interisland logistics seamlessly included. Expect to spend around $3,000 for a four‑ to five‑night cruise, compared to about $7,600 for a seven-night sailing on G Adventures. The best Galapagos cruise for kids Inspire your kids to learn about science and exploration by hopping on board the National Geographic Gemini, a ship that sails the Galapagos as part of a partnership between Lindblad Expeditions and National Geographic. These journeys, led by National Geographic experts, give kids the chance to become National Geographic Explorers-In-Training. The exclusive, hands-on program is designed to teach kids about geographical exploration and scientific research. The National Geographic Gemini can accommodate up to 48 passengers in 27 suites. More than a dozen suites come with private balconies, and one of those balconies is large enough to accommodate a private hot tub. But don’t fret if that suite is already booked; there’s a whirlpool hot tub on the sundeck that’s open to all guests. There’s also a library, well-stocked bar, and meals made with locally sourced ingredients on board. FAQ: How early should I book a Galapagos cruise? For the widest selection of vessels and sailing dates, aim to book your cruise four to nine months ahead of your intended sailing. More spontaneous travelers may find last-minute deals booking two to eight weeks ahead of their intended departure, though some itineraries will be sold out by then. Where do I embark on a Galapagos cruise? Getting to the Galapagos requires some logistical planning. After flying into Quito or Guayaquil, passengers typically spend a night in one of these mainland destinations before flying to the islands to board their ships. Your cruise line will tell you where to be on the islands for your departure, and in some cases, flights from the mainland will be included (or booked for an additional fee). When is the best time to cruise the Galapagos Islands? With a consistently mild climate year-round, the Galapagos can be visited at any time, although certain seasons offer exceptional wildlife viewing. December is when the giant tortoises hatch, and July marks the mating season for blue-footed boobies and short-eared owls. In April and May, marine iguanas typically hatch, while sea turtles begin laying their eggs at the start of the year. Given the diverse wildlife and year-round natural phenomena, there's never a "wrong" time to visit the islands. Are Galapagos cruises expensive? The Galapagos Islands aren’t a bargain destination. Expect to pay somewhere between $5,000 and $12,000 per traveler, depending on the ship, itinerary, and length of the voyage, though there are options starting in the $3,000s. What kind of wildlife can I expect to see on a Galapagos cruise? The Galapagos Islands are renowned for their unique wildlife, including giant tortoises, marine iguanas, blue-footed boobies, and sea lions. The islands’ ecosystems are so diverse that you can see a variety of species in different environments, from volcanic shores to lush highlands. This article has been updated with new information since its original publish date. Additional reporting by Paris Wilson.

item.title: How I Travel: Shania Twain Brings Spinach To Her Hotel Rooms
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 2.94
Most people’s carry-on bags hold items like a sweater, book, tablet, chargers, snacks, maybe hand sanitizer, and an eye mask. Pop music icon Shania Twain is bringing a mini recording studio everywhere she goes. “In my carry-on for many, many years is my Pro Tools set-up for recording,” says Twain. “I do a lot of writing and recording in my hotel rooms, so I bring an Apollo [audio-processing hardware], my microphone, the laptop, all of that.” Her latest album, Little Miss Twain, features songs that she wrote and produced years ago, with themes stretching back to her teen romances. The best-selling country-pop artist of all time, Twain got nostalgic with Condé Nast Traveler about her first business-class flight, which she took after signing her record deal, as well as more recent travel—like her 12-night stint performing with Harry Styles in London at Wembley Stadium this past summer—and shared future trips, like the one she’s plotting to India this winter. Plus, other quirky items on her packing list. Her favorite mode of transportation: If we're speaking about touring, bus is my favorite way to travel. I just love moving into it and then not having to unpack every day. I don't love living out of a suitcase. I like to settle in; that's my thing. I like sleeping in small spaces. Her first flight in business class: It was from Toronto to Nashville, after I signed to my record label. They bought me a business-class ticket. People were still smoking on planes then, and I’m so sensitive to cigarette smoke. I thought ‘gee, if you’re moving up in the world, do you have the right to say, Do you mind?’ I was so perplexed that people could smoke in business class, but that was the way it was. And I remember the food was better. Her packing approach: I'm a good packer, a really good packer. I would say I'm a thoughtful packer, in the sense that I've got a good routine down. I pack in categories: I’ll do the shoes, then jewelry, then pajamas, then underwear and socks. Quite organized. How she passed the time in London between shows this summer: I love London. I love to walk, and London has a lot of really quaint, walkable areas with pubs and cafes and shopping. I love Hyde Park. I've ridden horses and gone to concerts there, and it's all walkable from the hotels. And there's the theaters! This summer, I took advantage of seeing Paddington, which was extraordinary. It was just adorable. The cast is really exceptional. I mean, the story is great—we all know the story—but I just thought the theater was ideal for the intimacy of it. Her favorite places to stop through on tour: Quebec City is a great place for a day off on tour. It’s very Paris-like, this little time capsule—like a little bit of Paris was brought over to Canada. It's so quaint and beautiful, and on the water. Very walkable as well. The part of Canada she wants more tourists to see: I would recommend people visiting Canada see more of where I'm from [in northeastern Ontario], because nature is the most extraordinary. We've got areas where you can go moose watching, for example. You're not in a zoo. You see all these wild animals and it's really beautiful. Her priorities when planning a vacation: Food definitely motivates me when I'm traveling. I need to make sure that I'm going to enjoy the food because, as a vegetarian especially, it can be quite limiting. One of my favorite places to visit and eat as a vacation trip is Egypt, because it gives me everything I need. I like to walk everywhere and see the architecture. That's a big thing for me—to see history on every block. I love ancient history particularly, and the cities and villages that are museums in themselves. And then, like I said, the food. The Lebanese food [in Egypt] is extraordinary for vegetarians. So that's a part of the world that I really love. Why she chose to have a home in Switzerland: I had a language base of French growing up in a bilingual town in Ontario and I wanted to maintain that, which I get to do in Switzerland, living on the French side. Plus, the benefit of being in Switzerland is you have the valley and the lakes below, but then you can just drive up for 20 minutes and be on a glacier. I'll never give up my four seasons—and being Canadian, I love winter. The items she needs in her hotel room: One thing I miss the most when I'm traveling in hotels is not being able to cook. I love to cook so I always make sure that there is a really good blender, and that I have things like raw spinach, avocados, tomatoes, and bread—things that I can put olive oil and salt and pepper on and make my own snack without calling room service. The place she’s never been that she’d like to see next: Even though I’ve been very lucky to travel in my career, there's a lot of places I haven't been. I've never been to India. I've got a trip planned this January to Hyderabad, because I have friends from there. I've heard so much about [the country], and I know so many people that have gone, but this will be my first experience. And don't forget, India has the best vegetarian food!

item.title: 9 Hotels With Indoor Water Parks Worth Planning a Trip Around
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 2.62
Hotels with indoor water parks have saved more than a few family vacations from the tyranny of the weather forecast. When the main attraction is tucked under a roof, a rainy Saturday or surprise cold snap suddenly matters a lot less. And for anyone traveling with kids, there’s something deeply appealing about checking into a hotel where the day’s biggest activity requires little more planning than putting on a swimsuit and taking the elevator downstairs. I’ve spent years writing about hotels and family travel, and the resorts that stick with me tend to be the ones that make life easier without making the trip feel generic. A great indoor water park does exactly that. Kids get the big-ticket fun of slides, wave pools, and lazy rivers, while parents get a vacation that requires considerably less logistical gymnastics. The best properties go further, pairing all that chlorine-fueled chaos with skiing, horseback riding, mountain adventures, good restaurants, or even a little grown-up downtime. The resorts below are places where the water park can justify the trip, but it doesn’t have to consume it. Read on for the best hotels with indoor water parks in the US. FAQ: What's the best indoor water park resort in the US? For a trip where you want the water park to be the main focus, I'd pick Kalahari Resorts & Conventions in Wisconsin Dells. The town itself is built around water parks, and Kalahari's is 125,000 square feet right now and set to grow another 75,000 when the expansion opens in late October 2026. There's also enough else on the property—restaurants, a spa, shops, an adventure park—that you don't need to leave the premises for a long weekend. If, however, you want mountain time to be part of the trip too, Camelback, Jay Peak, and Boyne Mountain are all solid choices. Which hotel has the biggest indoor water park? Kalahari Resorts & Conventions in Round Rock, Texas, currently boasts America's largest indoor water park resort, at 223,000 square feet. Among the nine listed here, Kalahari Wisconsin Dells and Camelback's Aquatopia are tied at 125,000 square feet. However, Kalahari Wisconsin Dells will pull ahead once its expansion opens in late October 2026. Why pick an indoor water park over an outdoor one? It's simple: It removes the weather variable. A climate-controlled park stays warm through winter, through a rainy spring break, and through a cold fall weekend, so you can book the trip without checking a forecast first. This matters even more at mountain resorts, where a day might start with snow and ski boots and end with a lazy river. Several of these resorts also have outdoor pools that open seasonally, so you're not locked into one or the other. How we choose the best hotels with indoor water parks Every hotel review on this list has been written by a Condé Nast Traveler journalist who knows the destination and has visited that property. When choosing hotels, our editors consider properties across price points that offer an authentic and insider experience of a destination, keeping design, location, service, and sustainability credentials top of mind.

item.title: 23 Best Airbnbs in Vancouver for Proximity to Nature, Culture, and Delicious Cuisine
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 2.53
A born-and-raised Vancouverite, I’ve spent a lifetime exploring my city’s distinct neighborhoods, and many of my favorite places are found well beyond the downtown core where most of Vancouver’s top hotels are located. Settling into one of the city’s distinct neighborhoods puts the area’s best attractions right outside your door, offering a chance to connect with the surrounding nature, exceptional food scene, and immersive cultural experiences you might otherwise miss. To truly get a taste of all this city has to offer (and experience it like a local), consider booking an Airbnb. A short-term rental gives you options, whether you want to be steps from sandy Kits Beach, close to the eclectic shops and cafés of Commercial Drive, or tucked away on a leafy residential street in Shaughnessy. For those exploring without a car, many of Vancouver’s neighborhoods are well connected by public transit, too. From a cozy houseboat in the harbor to a light-filled log home on the beach, these are the spots I’d choose for a truly unforgettable stay in the city. Read on for the best Airbnbs in Vancouver to bookmark for your next trip. We've vetted these listings based on Superhost and Guest Favorite status, ratings, amenities, location, previous guest reviews, and decor. Our top picks: - Best for families: Trendy townhouse near Mount Pleasant - Best for couples: Beachfront living in West Point Grey - Best for a unique stay: Floating home in Lonsdale Quay - Best for large groups: Voguish villa for 10 FAQ: What are the best neighborhoods to stay in Vancouver? While there are plenty of neighborhoods in Vancouver to choose from, each suits different interests and budgets—there are no wrong choices. Downtown Vancouver is bustling, dynamic, and offers easy access to iconic landmarks like sprawling Stanley Park and vibrant Granville Island. Meanwhile, Yaletown, located within the city's core, is chic and replete with upscale restaurants, trendy boutiques, and vibrant nightlife. Giving a glimpse into Vancouver's storied past, Gastown welcomes visitors with cobblestone streets, gas lamps, and the iconic Steam Clock. What’s the best way to get around Vancouver? If you’re staying in the heart of the city, it’s easy to explore Vancouver’s best sites by foot, bike, bus, or boat. Rideshare options are also available and easily accessible. If you plan to stay downtown, the Vancouver Skytrain serves areas between downtown and Metro Vancouver's larger suburbs. To experience the greater Vancouver area, especially if you plan to venture to Vancouver Island, driving is the way to go—just be sure to book your car rental in advance. How long should you visit Vancouver for? You'll want to spend at least three days in Vancouver to experience the best of both nature and city. Enjoy a day exploring the stylish boutiques, world-class museums and galleries, and diverse cuisine. Then spend time outdoors, cycling the Stanley Park Seawall, sunbathing on the sandy beaches, paddling the coastline, or hiking the forested trails. If you have extra time, venture beyond the city proper. Head to the North Shore for an action-packed day of hiking, skiing, or wildlife spotting at Grouse Mountain, or teeter across the Capilano Suspension Bridge—a must-try for first-time visitors to Vancouver. This gallery has been updated with new information since its original publish date. Additional reporting by Megan Honan.

item.title: Say Goodbye to the Bulky Travel Sneaker—This Trending Shoe Is Taking Over the Terminal
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 2.50
I have a theory about travel shoes: The ones you pack with the most optimism are not often the ones you want to be wearing by day three. The chic flat starts rubbing and the chunky sneaker suddenly feels too casual for a sundress. And somewhere between takeoff and dinner, you might find yourself wishing for a shoe that can do it all. Enter the Mary Jane sneaker, fashion’s latest—and surprisingly convincing—attempt to make a practical shoe a little more fun. I became infatuated with the fad via Puma's Speedcat ballet sneakers. I couldn't believe how a shoe so stylish could be so comfortable—and actually travel-friendly. It's so easy to slip these on for just about anything—they look stellar with denim, skirts, dresses, you name it. I love them so much that I bought them in another color. The Mary Jane sneaker's formula is wonderfully simple: Give it the low-slung shape of a ballet flat with the sole support of your favorite sneaker. The common denominator? That little Mary Jane strap that somehow makes a sneaker feel instantly more dressed up. At first glance, some versions of the Mary Jane sneaker are barely distinguishable from a classic flat; others come in a technical mesh with a chunky tread or cushiony insoles. The Mary Jane, of course, has been doing its own sort of shape-shifting for more than a century. The name traces back to Mary Jane, a fictional character in Richard Felton Outcault’s Buster Brown comic strip which debuted in 1902, who often appeared wearing the now iconic shoe style. It evolved into a practical, strap-secured shoe for children and eventually became a fashion staple for women everywhere, cycling through patent leather, ballet flats, platforms, and beyond. Now it has found its way onto a sneaker—and the timing is just right. Fashion has spent the last few years making sneakers progressively less athletic-looking. Slim retro trainers and terrace shoes brought them closer to everyday fashion; ballet sneakers softened the silhouettes. Even sporty-forward brands like Salomon and Merrell have experimented with shapes that lean more street shoes, rather than those you wear to the gym. The Mary Jane sneaker makes this movement even more appealing for the traveler: It offers you sneaker-level practicality without making your outfit look like it was built solely around comfort. The best Mary Jane sneakers are also splendidly packable. The low-profile styles can easily disappear into a spare corner of your suitcase, rather than eating up the space that a bulky sneaker demands. Wear them on the flight and they can become your primary walking shoe; or pack them just in case for those outfits that need a little more oomph without risking any blisters. Below, I’ve rounded up 12 stylish Mary Jane sneakers I’m eyeing this season. From Puma’s cheetah-print ballet flats to Dolce Vita’s suede sneakers, these styles just might be your hardest-working travel shoe this fall.

item.title: 11 National Parks That Are Even More Beautiful in the Fall
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 2.42
I’ve traveled far and wide through America’s national parks, and if there’s one thing I’ve learned, it’s that some landscapes are simply better with a little fall color. Come September and October, sweeping valleys turn gold, forests flare in riots of red and pops of orange, and high country trails welcome that crisp, exhilarating drop in temperature that makes you want to keep trekking a little farther. Even parks we know and love in summer feel completely transformed: the sunsets shine differently, wildlife activity changes, and the seasonal crowds begin to give way to a quieter, more immersive experience. Thanks to the breadth of terrain across the US national parks, there’s no single version of how to experience fall. You might be leaf-peeping beneath the peaks of the Tetons, winding through Acadia’s brilliant coastal forests, hiking Yosemite in the cooler weather, or watching the aspens flicker across the Rockies. And when the sun goes down, the day doesn’t have to end: there are campfires to linger around, stars to seek out, and hot springs to slip into. Below, I’ve rounded up 11 national parks that are particularly spectacular in autumn. Take note: Fall may be shoulder season, but don’t assume that means easy availability—lodges, campgrounds, permits, and popular activities can still book up, so check current park conditions and reservation requirements before you go. —Jessica Chapel This gallery has been updated with new information since its original publish date.

item.title: Calling All Women Who Travel Solo—Add These US Destinations to Your Bucket List
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 2.18
There’s something wonderfully freeing about traveling alone as a woman. You get to make every decision—where to stay, what to order, whether to spend the afternoon in a museum or outside, and when to call it a night—and there’s a particular pleasure in discovering a place at your own pace. The best destinations for solo women travelers make that freedom feel easy, too: welcoming enough to settle in, interesting enough to keep you curious, and full of reasons to leave the hotel and see what happens. Across the US, that might mean wandering Savannah’s moss-draped squares, pedaling along Nantucket’s bike lanes, lingering over Palm Springs’s colorful midcentury architecture, or heading to mountain towns in Wyoming or Montana. It could be a long weekend of galleries and good food in Kingston, a guided hike through Joshua Tree, or a cocktail at the bar in Carlsbad. The appeal is really as varied as us girls. If you're looking for a little inspiration to get out and go, our Condé Nast Traveler editors and trusted contributors have shared destinations below that deliver on both the fun and the practicalities of hitting the road solo, adding ideas for where to stay, eat, and explore along the way. Consider this your excuse to book the room for one, order exactly what you want, and go somewhere simply because you want to see it. Read on for the places we recommend most for women to travel solo in the US, in alphabetical order. Big Sky, Montana I became a little infatuated with solo travel after heading to Big Sky, Montana, on my own for Cowgirl Up Week, an annual gathering at the iconic Lone Mountain Ranch. The celebration takes place each September at the tail end of the summer season and draws women from around the world itching for a taste of the quintessential American West. Our days were filled with horseback rides led by head wranglers, a guided trip to Yellowstone, an end-of-season rodeo, and lessons in everything from trotting to communicating with your horse. What stuck with me most was how many women had come alone—some finally making a bucket-list trip happen, others simply giving the dude ranch life a shot. You could ride off on your own or join a group, so making friends with the other gals was remarkably easy. My group even has a group chat called “Cowgirls Forever,” filled with new mothers, local ranch-owning women, and travelers from Florida to Connecticut. More and more dude ranches are creating women-focused weeks and general programming, so it's easier than ever to saddle up solo in this New Age, women-led, John Wayne world. —J.C. Where to stay in Big Sky: - Best for a stay right on the ranch for Cowgirl Up Week: Lone Mountain Ranch - Best for a convenient base for treating yourself: Montage Big Sky - Best for a more affordable base right in town: The Lodge at Big Sky Boston, Massachusetts I went to Boston two falls ago to visit a friend, and it was one of the most comfortable solo travel experiences I’ve had. I loved that I could reach most areas of interest in Cambridge and Charlestown on foot, and it’s sure hard to beat a crisp autumn in New England, especially in a city with such deep-set roots. I stayed at a houseboat Airbnb docked in the Charlestown marina, which was as serene as it was unique. It was fantastic being able to spend long nights on the deck, looking out to Boston city proper after spending the days romping through town. While this isn’t the part of the country that usually takes the cake for hospitality, I found that everyone local was incredibly friendly, helpful, and eager to share recommendations on where to head next. If you think you’re tired of hearing AI-this, new buzzy techword-that, still pay a visit to the MIT Museum, where the cutting edge feels hands-on, interactive, and actually exciting. —Kat Chen Where to stay in Boston: - Best for an iconic houseboat rental: A spacious yacht Airbnb - Best for a music-inspired hotel: The Verb Hotel - Best for a five-star waterfront hotel: Boston Harbor Hotel Carlsbad, California Often overshadowed by its flashier southern neighbor San Diego, Carlsbad has a more laid-back, surfy charm perfect for solo female travelers. I stayed at Beach Terrace, a family-owned hotel built directly on the sand about 50 feet from the water, when I visited. Sunday morning started with oceanfront yoga, where I connected with fellow travelers before exploring on foot (no car needed). Carlsbad Village is incredibly walkable and safe, even at night, with everything from antique shops to boutique clothing stores and Michelin-starred dining within reach. I joined a Carlsbad Food Tour to sample the town’s best eateries—such as the Strawberry Shack and Señor Grubby's—with a small, friendly group. For a solo dinner that doesn’t feel lonely, grab a seat at the bar at Campfire, where wood-fired dishes and communal energy make it easy to strike up a conversation with locals. —Kaila Yu, contributor Where to stay in Carlsbad: - Best for surf charm: Beach Terrace - Best for proximity to Carlsbad State Beach: The Green Room - Best for affordability but great service: Cape Rey Carlsbad Beach, a Hilton Resort and Spa Cody, Wyoming One of my favorite trips was a solo journey deep into Wyoming for a week on a ranch. Having traveled all the way from London, I took a couple of days to relax beforehand in Cody—the town I flew into—before continuing onward. Founded by none other than Buffalo Bill, this small town proved to be the sweetest spot for a few days of travel all alone. Everything worth visiting is within comfortable walking distance, with most restaurants, shops, and attractions no more than a 10-minute stroll away—a welcome relief if you feel hesitant about relying on rideshares in unfamiliar places. There is a fantastic range of museums—head to the Buffalo Bill Center of the West, which is so vast that entry tickets are valid for two consecutive days. I loved the historical Old Town Trail, which was altogether too absorbing for me to ever feel lonely. I frequently struck up conversations with locals in restaurants, so dining solo also never felt awkward. In truth? I hardly felt alone at all. Another highlight is Cody’s proximity to Yellowstone: I booked an excursion with CoveredGround Adventures, who picked me up directly from my hotel and had us deep among the pines within a 40-minute drive. By the time we returned that evening, my guide, a Cody local, and I had gotten on so well that she offered to drive me around the next day if I needed a ride anywhere. With welcoming faces, stunning landscapes, cowboys, and some of the finest cinnamon buns I have ever tasted (courtesy of Cody Coffee Bar), I would repeat the experience on my own in a heartbeat. —Charley Ward Where to stay in Cody: - Best for a historical hotel: Buffalo Bill's Irma Hotel - Best for a charming small town experience near Yellowstone: Chamberlin Inn - Best for a park-friendly, amenity-forward base: The Cody Johns Island, South Carolina On rugged Johns Island, 40 minutes outside of Charleston, Auberge’s debut of The Dunlin deftly centers the coastal charm of the South Carolina sea islands—the second most bioactive habitat in the world, after only the Amazon Rainforest. Aptly named for a ploving shore bird, the 72 cottage-style guest rooms and suites offer transformative wildlife immersion over the 2,000 acres, from dolphin and seabird safaris amid the towering piles of massive oysters that make up the meandering coastline (and will be fresh on your plate come dinner time), to an on-site farm and 20 miles of waterfront hiking trails to work up a sweat on before sinking into a bedroom soaking tub overlooking the marsh. Guests are chic Southerners (expect plenty of chatty Texans who will strike up a conversation at the stylish bar) and transplants here for the relaxing natural setting, spa treatments, and wine-paired food in between hikes and river cruises. The setting is intimate and the visitors friendly, from babymooning couples at the pool to girls trip groups in Lily Pulitzer shift dresses by the birdcage-themed bar. —Shannon McMahon Where to stay on Johns Island: - Best for a lush nature escape in solitude: The Dunlin, Auberge Collection - Best for a waterfront rental in the trees: Private elevated tree house Airbnb - Best for a riverfront porch with coastal views: The Oystercatcher bungalow Airbnb Key West, Florida Key West is no stranger to group travel—walk down Duval St. at night, and you’ll encounter crowds of bachelorette parties, cruise-goers, and rowdy spring breakers. But the quirky Conch Republic is also home to a thriving artistic community that opens its arms to solo travelers without hesitation. Stop by Andy’s Cabana on open mic nights, the Key West Yoga Sanctuary for community classes or creative writing workshops, and Fort Zachary Beach to camp out under the palms. By doing just this, I have befriended fishing guides, van-lifers, painters, musicians, and writers who welcomed me into their creative circle. My favorite part about traveling solo is that it forces you to meet new people and try new things, and the Keys have long embodied the essence of this independence and freedom. Just don’t be surprised if you get invited out on a sailboat (or two) on your first day. —Hannah Towey Where to stay in Key West: - Best for an oasis of calm: Pier House Resort and Spa - Best for sunsets: Ocean Key Resort and Spa - Best for those drawn to the historic side of Key West: Ella's Cottages Kingston, New York I recently took a solo trip to Kingston, New York, and it was exactly what I needed. Just a quick jet up north via Amtrak, the town is easy to explore on foot and has a calm, welcoming vibe. I started my day with breakfast at Hotel Kinsley—home to good coffee, a quiet atmosphere, and vintage records by each window. Then I spent time reading with a cappuccino at Rough Draft Bar and Books. From there, I wandered through Italian provisions at Salamone’s, picked up playful stickers at quirky bookstore Everywhere Shop, and browsed the home goods at Kingston Social. What stood out most was how safe and queer-friendly it felt. The rainbow crosswalk near the main street felt like a warm welcome, and every shop I visited felt easy to be in. —Laura Delarato, contributor Where to stay in Kingston: - Best for vintage vibes and fresh air: Hotel Kinsley - Best for a tucked-away cabin retreat: Hutton Brickyards - Best for woodsy wellness nearby: Woodstock Way Hotel Litchfield, Connecticut Anytime I mention Litchfield to my colleagues, there’s invariably one person giggling or rolling their eyes. Not because they don’t think it’s a deserving mention, but because of how much love I have for this tiny region in Connecticut’s northwest corner. First, a short geography lesson: While Litchfield is a town, it is also a county—but think of it as a daisy chain of little towns and villages. Base yourself in the main town for a long weekend and drive around for easy access, passing through bucolic landscapes along the way. This is the kind of place that feels especially rewarding solo: You can spend your days following your own curiosity—from architecture and antiques to nature walks—while still finding a sense of community along the way. I usually stay at Belden House and Mews (from the owners of the Hudson Valley estate hotel Troutbeck); go for drinks and dinner at The Abner, refashioned from the town’s old courthouse; get coffee and crumb cake at Krafted Brew Lab; shop at chic home-goods store Milton Market; take a pottery lesson with Charlie at Dumais Made; and browse Jeffrey Tillou’s inventory of 18th- and 19th-century furniture and fine arts.—Arati Menon Where to stay in Litchfield: - Best for good style and tasty bites: The Abner - Best for splendid wellness and design: Belden House and Mews - Best for some peace and quiet: The Litchfield Inn Miami, Florida A little over a year ago, I flew from Denver to Miami for my January birthday, as I wanted to be somewhere warm, near the water, and full of vibrant food. I chose to stay at The Standard—it’s a solid hotel with easy-to-access water, plus it's removed enough from the hubbub of South Beach (but also just close enough, if that's what you're looking for). There are a handful of restaurants within a short walking distance, and even more restaurants a quick rideshare away, making it easy to move around at night alone as well. Pop over to Little Havana for exceptional Cuban food via a food tour (an opportunity to make new friends) or just by exploring on your own. The Brickell area has a cozy little wine bar called Niu Wine, and I can't recommend SuViche enough for casual, fresh Peruvian ceviche after a sunny walk or lazy beach day. —Amanda Villarosa, photographer Where to stay in Miami: - Best for a conveniently located and reliable hotel: The Standard Spa - Best for splurging on a maximalist-designed oasis: Faena Hotel Miami Beach - Best for an affordable stay in South Beach: Hotel Greystone Nantucket, Massachusetts Last October, I took a trip to Nantucket in the off-season to enjoy a “readaway”—that is, a vacation where the main objective was to get some fresh air and read my book. I stayed in this gorgeous loft above a bookstore, and felt so safe in the heart of town. I had a marvelous time visiting the Whaling Museum and counting how many lightship baskets I could find at antique shops—with not one single person rushing me along. Perhaps the highlight of my trip was the sunset hike I took along the Bluff Walk, where I peeked into quiet, gray-shingled cottages, spotted some seals, and marveled at the towering Sankaty Lighthouse. The scariest part of the trip was the plane ride over the Atlantic on a nine-passenger Cape Air propeller, but even then, I've never experienced a softer landing than with my two female pilots. —Jessica Sulima Where to stay on Nantucket: - Best for a true literary oasis: Traveler-recommended readaway rental - Best for one of the few year-round stays: The Nantucket Hotel and Resort - Best for a central 20-room boutique: Greydon House Nashville, Tennessee The Tennessee capital is a quintessential bachelorette town in every sense of the phrase, but works just as well for a solo trip. There’s no need to get glammed up unless you absolutely wish to: If you’re feeling lonely, your next best friends might be just a honky tonk dance floor away. And while the world’s your oyster here, that also includes kicking back and enjoying the city’s slower offerings, like a day filled with art at the Frist Art Museum, or balmy outdoor reading at Centennial Park. You can’t go wrong with a show at the Opry, which turned 100 last year, and where—famously—there is no such thing as a bad seat. Nashville is kitsch, it’s booming, and between the hot chicken and barbecue, you won’t miss out on heartwarming food. I grew up visiting every year when I was a kid, and I still feel a childlike sense of adventure when I visit now. Dare I say it may be even more fun all grown up. —K.C. Where to stay in Nashville: - Best for a colorful and lively stay: The Graduate Nashville - Best for wow-factor: The Russell - Best for easy access to the hubbub: Drift Hotel Nashville North Fork, New York There's something about a solo getaway that isn't far away, or wildly different from where you live, that purely exists to give you permission to carve out a type of me time you can't get at home. One of those places, for me, is the North Fork at the very end of Long Island. It's a waterfront getaway—within three hours of my apartment in Brooklyn—where the pace is slow, the towns are small, the beaches are quiet, my main mode of transportation is a bicycle (available at most hotels), and I can spend my days eating farm-to-table (or sea-to-table) with no sense of urgency. There are lovely places to stay, like the Silver Sands Motel or Hotel Moraine, and cheffy restaurants, like Nookie's and the North Fork Table and Inn, but you can also rent an Airbnb and grab your own seafood at Little Creek Oyster Farm and the Southold Fish Market. Every morning, I go for a run, end it with a swim in the sound, then plan my days around reading between meal times—all to rinse and repeat. I suggest taking two or three days off mid-week (my hack for a solo trip without the FOMO), and keeping a small cooler and oyster knife in your car for whenever you pass honor-system fresh seafood stalls on the side of the road (like Peconic Gold). —Megan Spurrell Where to stay on the North Fork: - Best for a foodie-forward stay: Silver Sands Motel - Best for a chic farm stay in Southold: North Fork Table and Inn - Best for a splashy, seaside resort in Greenport: Hotel Moraine Palm Springs, California On a solo trip to Palm Springs for a group design tour with Palm Springs Mod Squad, I experienced a showcase of several pristinely preserved architectural gems built in the prevailing Desert Modern style. I spent an afternoon indulging in the city’s incredible vintage shops along the strip before popping into Superbloom, an innovative paint studio, where a childlike sense of play emerged as I splattered paint on a new passport holder and luggage tag. For pampering, do as I did and make your way to the Agua Caliente Band of Cahuilla Indians's Spa at Séc-he and indulge in a hot stone massage with cold lavender-scented towels. Then sip on a phenomenal prickly pear lemonade before relaxing in the hot spring–fed thermal pool. Don't skip the designated Dark Sky Park that is Joshua Tree—knowing I’d eventually lose cell phone reception, I downloaded an offline map to navigate the park alone in the dark—an anxiety-inducing experience that felt like driving into an endless void, yet one I’d recommend to women looking to step out of their comfort zones and build confidence in an unforgiving desert landscape. My disappointment about not having enough time to see the Mojave Desert’s famous succulent in the daylight quickly dissipated during my stargazing tour with Joshua Tree Astronomy Adventures. Sharing a canopy of stars with just a few strangers, I contemplated the magnitude of the universe and felt humbled by my own existence. —Katherine Gallardo, contributor Where to stay in Palm Springs: - Best for a tucked-away boutique hotel: Villa Royale - Best for a full-service hotel in the middle of town: Kimpton Rowan Palm Springs Hotel - Best for a design-forward, restorative oasis: Korakia Pensione Savannah, Georgia I took a February trip to Savannah two winters ago—a long weekend based at Hotel Bardo—during which I planned to walk lazily through sunny parks, indulge in great food, and soak up the small city’s history. I traveled with my partner, but when a work thing came up on his end, I had a day to myself and found the city to be perfect for a party of one. At Mrs. Wilkes Dining Room, an institution of a soul-food kitchen (they still have the chair Obama sat in when he visited on display), you’re seated around a big, family-style table with whoever else walks in when you do—ideal for a solo traveler looking for company. The gorgeous Common Thread, where fluke crudos and roasted sunchokes sit side by side, also has seats at the bar if you don’t have a reservation (bar seats are most often the perfect choice as a solo traveler). Because this was a city where I actually wanted to do a tour, I easily slid into a mixed group being guided through the Owens-Thomas House and Slave Quarters. It was a highlight of the trip: Home tours of opulent 1800s-built properties are popular in the city, and the team at Owens-Thomas does a particularly great job of acknowledging everyone who lived in the home, including the enslaved people who kept it running. It was yet another reminder of how much there is to learn in this city—and how it is evolving constantly. —M.S. Where to stay in Savannah: - Best for the seasoned and curious traveler: Hotel Bardo - Best for a sweet and aesthetic stay: The Drayton Hotel - Best for a central boutique hotel: The Douglas This article has been updated with new information since its original publish date.
