item.title: 12 best islands in Thailand to visit 2026 for honeymooners, families and solo travellers
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 6.34
The best islands in Thailand evoke images of pristine white sands, rustic-chic beach shacks, and gently swaying hammocks offering views of the turquoise sea and famed rock formations. But with a total of 1,430 islands spread across the Gulf of Thailand and Andaman Sea, not all are born equal. The largest, Phuket, is one of the busiest in terms of travellers, with its own international airport and some of the best hotels in Thailand. Then there are the tiny, off-the-beaten-track gems like Koh Lipe, small enough to explore by foot and only accessible by speedboat or ferry from the Thai mainland. With so many to choose from, one of the best approaches is to base your itinerary on the time of year. Islands off the West Coast such as Phuket, Koh Lanta and Koh Lipe are at their best in December to April, while Koh Samui and Koh Tao off the east coast are ideal for visiting from February to September. There's no need to choose just one island either, with day trips by boat readily available to take you from plush resort to remote islet and back again. Lauren Burvill For inspiration, we round up the best islands in Thai including what they offer and where to stay. Editor's picks of the best islands in Thailand - For families: Koh Samui - For couples: Koh Lipe - For solo travel: Koh Pha Ngan and Koh Phi Phi - For divers and snorkelers: Koh Phi Phi How to travel between islands in Thailand? It depends on what islands you'll be travelling to during your holiday. It is best to take the ferry between islands in Southern Thailands. For example, Phuket (a great starting point) has a daily ferry to Ko Phi Phi that takes anywhere between 45 minutes to an hour plus. There are also some islands like Phuket, Krabi and Koh Samui that can easily be accessed via airplanes too.

item.title: Where was 'The Dog Stars' filmed? The surprising mountainous hideout that stood in for Canada's peaks
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 4.91
On Location peels back the curtain on some of your favourite films, television shows, and more. This time, we ask: where was The Dog Stars filmed? The year is 2035. Along a mountain range on the south side of Denver, survivors are navigating an unprecedented, post-pandemic world. A deadly flu outbreak has wiped out a vast majority of the human population, and many who have survived remain with a debilitating blood disease. This is the premise of Ridley Scott’s latest blockbuster, starring Jacob Elordi as young pilot Hig, Margaret Qualley as Cima and Josh Brolin as Bangley. While Bangley has no intentions of leaving the efficient homestead he and Hig have settled into, Hig is determined to track down other survivors, frequently embarking on tracking missions alongside his trusty dog, Jasper. As these stories unfold in a post-apocalyptic world far from crumbling metropolises, the natural world plays a major role in Scott’s latest movie. While set in Canada, filming took place in Italy between April and June 2025. “The size and scale of the production footprint in Italy was ideal for what we needed,” says The Dog Stars production designer Chris Seager. “We found a combination of quality locations that could convincingly represent Colorado, while also being relatively close together. This allowed us to work much more efficiently from a production point of view.” “We also considered Canada,” says Chris. “But ultimately Italy offered the best combination of location quality, scale and practical logistics. Being able to concentrate so many of the locations within a manageable area was a huge advantage for the production, helping us maximise our time and resources.” So where exactly did the team set up camp during the epic-scale production? Here, we uncover some of the key locations to keep an eye out for. Cinecittà Studios, Rome While much of The Dog Stars’ cinematography took place beside forests and mountain peaks, Rome’s Cinecittà Studios played a crucial role in the scenes set at Grand Junction Airport. “Cinecittà was amazing,” says Chris. “It quickly became evident that, to achieve the scale and complexity of the effects that Ridley wanted, we needed to work on a soundstage where we could have complete control over the environment.” Chris recalls how the set within Europe’s largest film studio was built in just four weeks. On the studio filming, cinematographer Erik Messerschmidt said, “[Cinecittà Studios] houses Italy’s most modern sound stages. It’s the centre of studio production and is familiar to all local crew. It was the best and most obvious option.” Abruzzo Much filming also took place in Italy’s Abruzzo region. One such apocalyptic scene honed in on the city of Avezzano. Chris says: “One of the biggest and most challenging locations was the petrol station [in Avezzano] where we filmed the city landing sequence – we actually landed the plane in the street! We transformed the location entirely: we trashed the petrol station and the surrounding area to create the sense of a world that had been abandoned and reclaimed by nature. The greens department and the layered set dressing played a huge role in this. “To represent the cycle of life, we created a swimming pool and diving board, which we filled with dead bodies and overgrown vegetation, crocuses growing through the remains. It was a very strong visual expression of the post-apocalyptic, graphic world, but it also presented considerable logistical challenges in terms of access and working within the location.” EUR, Rome The Roman business and residential district of EUR (Esposizione Universale Roma), known for its cultural happenings and Fascist-era architecture, saw the production team set up more post-apocalyptic scenes. “The Roman neighbourhood of EUR stood in for the Denver city hall triage centre where Hig goes to retrieve supplies. It was a challenging place to shoot, as it’s normally a busy city, but the Roman authorities were very helpful in making it happen for us, and it was ultimately one of the most successful sections of the film,” says Erik. Bordano Bordano was an empty field that is used for hang-gliding, so we had to transform the entire site from scratch,” says Chris. “We built nine airplane hangars, Bangley’s house and tower, as well as a number of smaller sheds and a trailer home. We also dressed large quantities of grass and other greenery to make the location feel abandoned and overgrown.” “The whole process took approximately five weeks, which was a very tight turnaround given the scale of the build. The major benefit of working on location was the sheer amount of space and the ability to create the environment at the scale required, rather than being constrained by a studio. It also allowed the buildings, runway and surrounding environment to exist together as one cohesive world, giving the finished locations a greater sense of authenticity and scale.” The Dog Stars is in UK cinemas now

item.title: The world's most connected airport has been revealed – and it's no longer London Heathrow
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 4.48
Each year, the OAG Megahubs Index reveals the best-connected airports around the world, revealing the sleek aviation hubs are best for getting us on our merry way – whether that’s on a fly-and-flop resort stay or somewhere altogether more niche and intrepid. Airport connectivity is assessed across various categories: Top 50 Most Connected Airports; Top 25 Most Connected Low-Cost Carrier (LCC) Airports; Top 25 Most Connected US Airports; Top 10 Most Connected Airports (International) by region. Ascertaining the world’s most connected airports is a mammoth task. To do so, flight data specialists at OAG analyse data from the 100 largest international airports over a 12-month period and calculate the number of possible connections between inbound and outbound flights within a six-hour window. In 2025, London Heathrow (LHR) retained its title as the world’s most connected airport for the third consecutive year, with more than 59,000 connections to 226 destinations on the busiest day of operations. Istanbul Airport (IST) saw one of the greatest increases from eighth position in 2024 to second in 2025, while Kuala Lumpur (KUL) was the best-connected Asian airport, in joint fourth place globally with Frankfurt (FRA). However, geopolitical tensions and airports’ determination to attract new travellers, among other factors, have led to significant movement in 2026’s rankings. London Heathrow has officially been overtaken by Istanbul, which has become the most connected airport in the world for the first time. As a result of connections to 337 global destinations – many serviced by Turkish Airlines, the world’s best-connected airline – the eighth-busiest airport globally acts as a gateway to much of the world. London Heathrow only slips by one place to second, with potential connections on the busiest day of operations between September 2025 and August 2026 falling by six per cent compared to the year before. Middle East schedules have undoubtedly affected Heathrow’s position, with Istanbul often serving as an alternative to hubs that experienced flight cancellations and delays as the conflict persisted. Amsterdam Schiphol (AMS) has seen both capacity and destinations grow, claiming third position, while Kuala Lumpur retains fourth position – despite potential connections falling slightly since last year, destinations served have increased from 151 to 154.

item.title: Where was 'Widow’s Bay' filmed? The New England towns that provided the supernatural backdrop
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 4.43
On Location peels back the curtain on some of your favourite films, television shows, and more. This time, we ask: where was Widow's Bay filmed? Last night saw comedy-horror series Widow's Bay making history at the Emmys, taking home 14 awards – a first for the genre. The Apple TV series is set in the fictional New England town of Widow’s Bay, which is reportedly the focus of a centuries-old curse that causes all kinds of supernatural occurrences. Starring Matthew Rhys as the local mayor determined to transform his town into the new Martha’s Vineyard, the show premiered in April and has quickly gained a cult following, with a second season currently in the works. Creator, showrunner and executive producer Katie Dippold has deliberately kept the location of the fictional island a mystery and explained that she was inspired by the eeriness of Stephen King novels. “It’s a long ferry ride; you don’t know exactly if the ferry comes from Massachusetts or Maine,” she said. “But I purposely wanted to keep that a little vague.” Although fictional, various coastal towns in New England served as the backdrop for the series. “You immediately have this kind of mythical mysticism surrounding it,” Rhys told The Boston Globe in April 2026. “That New England history so perfectly lent to this piece. Once we shot there, it just enriched it tenfold.” These are the real-life places you can visit to retrace the footsteps of Mayor Tom et al. Rockport A lot of the action takes place in the picturesque town of Rockport. Specifically, Old Harbour Road served as the town centre, while the restaurant, The Salty Whale, is on the site of the former Dark Star Philosophia at 14 Old Harbour Road. Even the blink-and-you’ll-miss-it retro-looking ice cream shop, simply called The Ice Cream Store, is a real place: you can visit it at 14 Bearskin Neck. Other spots that fans can visit include the picnic bench where Patricia – the Mayor’s eccentric assistant, played by British actress Kate O’Flynn – reads her mysterious book (located at White Wharf). “Places like Gloucester and Rockport, for me, just gave you that essence for free,” Rhys told The Boston Globe. “You don't have to suspend any imagination. It’s all in front of you.” Berlin Town Hall Berlin Town Hall stands in for the Widow’s Bay Town Hall, where Tom and Patricia work. Originally built in 1870, the Berlin Town Hall’s historic exterior has the perfect, slightly eerie feel for the show. Berlin (pronounced BUR-lin, to differentiate it from the German capital) has a population of just over 3,000, and has been a town since 1665, with a rich agricultural background specialising in growing asparagus. It was also used as a location in the 2023 film The Holdovers. Gloucester Several locations in the picturesque town of Gloucester were used as stand-ins for Widow’s Bay. Lanes Cove, the port, was used as the Harbour Master’s Office where people catch ferries to and from the mainland. Half Moon Beach is where Tom swims as part of Widow’s Bay’s ‘inaugural swim’ of the summer, while the Eastern Point Lighthouse at Cape Ann serves as the show’s lighthouse. The latter featured heavily in a scene between Tom and the lighthouse keeper Garrett. Lorenzo Maynard House In episode two, Tom stays in a haunted inn, with Lorenzo Baynard House in Maynard filling in for the building’s spooky exteriors. Built in the 19th century, it features a distinctive mansard roof, something which was reportedly typical of wealthy post-Civil War industrialists like Lorenzo Maynard (himself the son of a mill operator and prominent local figure). It is actually used as an apartment building, and there have been no reported supernatural goings-on there, so if you did want to visit, you’d be safe to do so. Martha-Mary Chapel This beautiful chapel in Sudbury was used for a rather gruesome storyline (spoiler alert), one which involved the Reverend being found dead behind a door. The non-denominational church was built by industrialist Henry Ford in 1940 and was named after his mother, Mary and his mother-in-law, Martha. It was made from trees that had fallen in a hurricane two years earlier. Fun fact: there’s a schoolroom on the grounds that Ford had transplanted here, and which he believed had been the original inspiration for the nursery rhyme ‘Mary Had A Little Lamb’.

item.title: Flying long haul but can't swing business class? These 16 premium economy seats are the next best thing
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 4.26
There’s a happy medium between the ultra-luxe business class cabin and the cramped claustrophobia of coach class: premium economy. With record-high airfares, splashing out on business class isn’t possible for every flight. Premium economy is designed for travellers who want a bit more pampering but on a tighter budget. The cabin usually offers comfier seats, more personal space, enhanced amenities, and upgraded meal and beverage selections compared to standard economy class. But not all premium economy products are worth the more expensive airfare. The best premium economy cabins are usually found on long-haul aircraft that operate lengthy international routes. These fare classes offer an elevated experience both on the ground and in the sky, with well-designed seats located in a separate, comparatively spacious cabin. During the booking process, it can be difficult to discern all the perks – or lack thereof – included in a premium economy fare. So we’ve rounded up a list of our favourite premium economy products from airlines across the globe. If you spend your precious airline miles or hard-earned cash on an upgrade to any of these seats, you’ll arrive at your destination well rested and ready to go. This story has been updated with new information since its original publish date. Emirates One of the most popular premium economy cabins in the sky, Emirates debuted its version of the offering in 2021. The seats have continued to roll out to more aircraft, specifically on Emirates' double-decker Airbus A380 planes and on select retrofitted Boeing 777 aircraft. The cabin is at the front of the first deck. The seats are now available on more than 30 routes to and from Dubai, including US cities like New York, Los Angeles, Boston, Chicago, Miami, Dallas, San Francisco, Seattle, and Houston. For premium economy travellers, the perks start in the airport, with a separate check-in desk, larger carry-on bag allowance, and free seat selection. Inside the cabin, Emirates uses the same design elements as its iconic business-class cabin, such as cream leather with stitching details and wood accents. Passengers also get a large throw pillow, six-way adjustable headrest, calf-and-foot rests, and an in-flight entertainment screen measuring 13.3 inches wide, as well as a dining table with a side cocktail table and charging ports. As for in-flight dining, expect three-course dinners served on Royal Doulton china tableware with stainless steel cutlery. Emirates always includes a dish from the flight's destination on the premium economy menu – such as Thai pepper beef with jasmine rice and pak choi. Top it all off with a complimentary glass of wine or something sparkly like the vintage 2012 Chandon – one of the array of drink selections from the business-class wine list not available in regular economy. Qantas Australian carrier Qantas's premium economy cabin – available on the airline's Boeing 787 Dreamliners and Airbus A380s – is completely separate from regular economy with 32 to 40 seats in a two-three-two layout. Seats are wider and offer more legroom than coach seats, but they also feature wider armrests with storage compartments, two USB outlets, an ergonomic headrest, and a footrest. One of the most thoughtful aspects is the seat’s “unique recline motion,” designed to “provide a class-leading level of comfort,” Qantas says on its website. Instead of simply reclining backwards, the seat moves forward and up, so your legs and back are slightly elevated in a more comfortable position. Premium passengers are greeted with a complimentary sparkling wine or water upon boarding. Meals are served on custom-designed tableware by David Caan. Other in-flight amenities include noise-cancelling headphones, a large pillow, a 100 per cent wool blanket, and an amenity kit. Passengers in the cabin also have access to a dedicated check-in counter and priority boarding. The cabin class is available out of at least 13 airports, including US hubs like Dallas-Fort Worth, New York JFK, Honolulu, Los Angeles, and San Francisco. All Nippon Airways Premium economy on Japanese carrier ANA is truly a premium experience, starting in the terminal. On international flights, premium economy passengers are afforded access to the airline’s lounges at its major hubs, including Tokyo Haneda, Tokyo Narita, Osaka's Kansai airport, and Honolulu airport. ANA is also launching new premium economy seats on its fleet of fresh Boeing 787-9 aircraft, the first of which will be received in November 2026, that operate long-haul international flights. The overhauled seats offer 40 inches of pitch and nine inches of recline, an improvement of two additional inches for both dimensions. When it’s time to relax, a leg rest pops up that supports the entire calf. A 15.6-inch entertainment screen comes with Bluetooth connectivity and USB-C charging ports. Once in the air, premium economy fliers are treated to refreshments from ANA’s business-class drink menu, which includes curated selections of Champagne, sake, red and white wine, Umeshu plum wine, and shochu. Mealtime offers a selection of Asian-Western fusion cuisine, including the carrier’s homemade bread served in business class. Throughout the flight, premium economy passengers have access to substantial snacks, such as petit fours or cup-style noodles, usually reserved for business class. Upon landing, priority baggage handling means you won’t have to wring your hands at baggage claim, wondering if your checked luggage arrived safely. Virgin Atlantic On board Virgin Atlantic's sleekly designed planes, there's a lot to celebrate – like the revamped Upper Class cabin on the airline's Airbus A350S, featuring The Loft lounge. Not least among them is Virgin's premium economy cabin, simply called Premium, which is available on the carrier's A330-220 and A330-300 planes, its A350-1000s, and Boeing 787-9 Dreamliners. Seats in Premium are roomy: They're up to 21 inches wide (four inches wider than economy), have seven to eight inches of recline, and up to 38 inches of pitch. Each one also has a footrest. Premium fliers get a dedicated check-in and bag drop line, plus priority boarding. Once aboard, passengers are handed a complimentary welcome glass of bubbly. Dinner includes a starter and main course served on china and paired with white or red wine. Select flights also include Virgin's signature afternoon tea service, featuring sandwiches, tea cakes, and warm scones with jam and clotted cream. Singapore Airlines Singapore, known for its over-the-top first-class suites, also offers a solid premium economy product on its A350, A380, and Boeing 777 aircraft. Seats are spacious, with up to 19.5 inches of width, an eight-inch recline, and calf and footrests. Each spot also has two USB ports and a 13.3-inch screen that comes with noise-cancelling headphones. There are also individual stowage areas specially designed for a water bottle, laptop, and headphones. While most of the seats are in a two-four-two layout, the airline's A350-900ULR planes have six single seats available, which would give the experience more of a business class feel. Premium economy passengers have access to additional meal and beverage choices, including Singapore's famous “book the cook” service, available on premium economy flights from 27 cities. This service allows customers to choose from in-flight meals created by the airline's International Culinary Panel and reserve them up to 24 hours in advance. Customers also receive priority check-in, boarding, and baggage handling. Cathay Pacific When it debuted a trio of overhauled cabins in 2025, Hong Kong-based carrier Cathay Pacific received numerous accolades for its new Aria business class suites. But its refreshed premium economy concept also offers a strong dose of luxury. The dedicated cabin has a total of 48 seats in a 2-4-2 layout. It’s easy to get cosy on Cathay’s long-haul routes, thanks to the generous dimensions of the premium economy seats. Expect a roomy 39-inch pitch, a seat width of 19.5 inches, and eight inches of recline, plus a calf rest and a footrest. The 15.6-inch entertainment screen has Bluetooth audio pairing, plus USB-A and USB-C ports, and fliers are provided with noise-cancelling headphones. Upon boarding, premium economy passengers are offered a welcome drink, as well as a menu of gourmet Cantonese cuisine and other international dishes. The cabin also has its own premium economy lavatory with touchless features. On the ground, fliers receive perks like priority boarding, dedicated check-in at select airports, and two free checked bags. Air France In the fall of 2024, Air France renamed its premium economy cabin to simply “Premium” and began installing larger seats in the cabin across its fleet. The new seats recline to a generous 124 degrees, offer 37 to 38 inches of legroom pitch and an adjustable footrest, and have been “widened for extra comfort,” the airline says. As an additional upgrade, Air France redesigned the seat foam and topped it with herringbone fabric for a softer, more cosy finish. The new seat is available on select Boeing 777 planes and Airbus A350 jets, and by the end of 2025, Air France expects them to be installed on 80 per cent of its fleet. Aside from the seat specifications, the Premium cabin offers a priority check-in counter and baggage drop at the airport, as well as priority boarding. Extra in-flight perks include 13.3-inch entertainment screens with Bluetooth connectivity, USB charging ports, noise-cancelling headphones, and an amenity kit designed specifically for the cabin class. And, as France’s national flag carrier, mealtime is its own momentous event. Premium passengers can expect to receive a glass of Champagne upon arrival, followed by a “full ‘French-style’ meal service, comprising snacks, a starter, a choice of two hot dishes, cheese and dessert, served in eco-designed tableware with stainless steel cutlery,” according to the airline’s site. Expect to top it all off with impressive French patisserie, like Paris-Brest and chocolate fondant. Lufthansa In Lufthansa’s new Allegris cabin concept, each seat in the cabin features a hard-shell backing that will allow fliers to recline without encroaching on the passenger behind them. Each seat has 39 inches of pitch, and, on average, Lufthansa’s premium economy seats offer 50 per cent more space than regular economy. The cabin’s 24 seats are laid out in a 2-3-2 configuration and also come with a 15.6-inch 4K monitor, wireless charging stations, leg rests, noise-cancelling headphones, a separate cocktail table, a personal reading light, a coat hook, and a water bottle holder. You’ll also get two free checked bags and, once on board, a welcome drink to sip as you settle in. The new Allegris cabin class is now available on nine of Lufthansa’s Airbus A350-900s, which are flying between Munich and San Francisco, Shanghai, Bengaluru, Mumbai, Chicago, Beijing, and New York-JFK. British Airways When flying in a premium economy seat on British Airways – called World Traveller Plus by the carrier – you’ll find a separate cabin with seats laid out in a two-four-two arrangement, for a total of about 40 seats on most transatlantic-operating aircraft. In terms of dimensions, seats offer 38 inches of pitch and eight inches of recline, and a footrest (but no leg support). The airline also notes that the seats are wider than in regular economy. Once you complete your priority boarding, you’ll be offered a welcome drink of sparkling wine or juice in real glassware. Meals are also served on ceramic tableware. Other amenities include over-ear headphones for your in-flight entertainment, plus a plusher blanket, pillow, and toiletry kit than those offered in coach. Two free checked bags round out the benefits in this comfortable fare class. Japan Airlines Although Japan Airlines has long offered a stellar premium economy product, the newest version of the cabin that’s rolling out on the carrier’s Airbus A350-1000 planes is on a different level. The 24 seats arranged in a 2-4-2 layout have hardshell seat backs so reclining passengers don’t steal away your elbow room. There are also divider walls between seats for extra privacy, and business-class features like motorised recline and leg rest functions that operate at the push of a button. The seat specifications are impressive, too: Leg rests rise to a comfy 90 degrees, and when that feature isn’t in use, a pitch of 42 inches means there’s plenty of room to stretch out. You’ll also find a massive, 16-inch 4K monitor for in-flight entertainment, an AC power outlet, USB type A and C charging ports. At the airport, premium economy passengers can expect priority check-in at a dedicated cabin counter, priority baggage handling, and access to the airline’s Sakura lounges in Japan. As of spring 2025, the airline was flying nine of the 13 total A350-1000 planes it had ordered. The nine planes currently operate on the airline’s routes between Tokyo Haneda and New York JFK, Dallas-Fort Worth (DFW), London Heathrow (LHR), and Paris Charles de Gaulle (CDG). In summer 2025, JAL will begin operating the new aircraft between Los Angeles (LAX) and Tokyo, as well. Air New Zealand Passengers on all of Air New Zealand’s long-haul routes operated by its Boeing 787-9 Dreamliners and 777 jets have the option of upgrading to its premium economy cabin. You’ll breeze through the airport with premium check-in and a luggage allowance of two checked bags. Inside the separate premium economy cabin, where 28 seats are arranged in a two-three-two layout, expect seat features like a legrest, extendable footrest, and 50 per cent more recline than regular economy for a total of nine inches. Seat pitch measures a roomy 41 inches. Come mealtime, you’ll have an upgraded menu to choose from, with dishes like slow-roasted lamb or New Zealand hāpuka fish, accompanied by a selection of award-winning New Zealand wines. What’s more: the airline unveiled the first of its redesigned 787-9 Dreamliners in May 2025, featuring an upgraded premium economy product with more storage options, side wings for added privacy, and fixed outer shells so reclining passengers don’t encroach on your personal space. That initial aircraft – tail number ZK-NZH – will operate flights between San Francisco (SFO) and Auckland (AKL). Seven of the new aircraft variant are expected to be in service by the end of 2025. EVA Air The airline that invented premium economy back in the 90s is still bringing new innovations to the fare class decades later. The Taiwan-based carrier has launched a completely reimagined version of its premium economy cabin on its new Boeing 787-9 Dreamliner jets, and it’s well worth the splurge. For starters, the refreshed concept offers an industry-leading 42-inch pitch at every seat, making the seat’s specifications alone worth the price of an upgrade. Passengers can stretch out and use the seat’s ingenious recline function, which has hard-shell backing and offers a cradling motion that slides the seat forward and up for eight inches of recline without disturbing the flier behind. Footrests and privacy panels add even more comfort, and a 15.6-inch entertainment screen and personal device holder will hold your attention for the long-haul journey. The carrier is continually rolling out more of the 787-9 planes with its latest premium economy cabin and plans to deploy a total of nine of the widebody planes by 2029. Delta’s version of international premium economy – Delta Premium Select – underwent an extensive overhaul in 2022. The result: an even plusher cabin with more comfortable seats, cosier bedding, and food and beverage perks. The latter point may be what charms passengers most. After take-off, Premium Select fliers are now offered a “bubbles and bites” service with complimentary sparkling wine or sparkling water and savoury snacks such as mixed nuts. Other business-class-level touches, like printed menus and an oshibori towel, make meal service an event worth savouring. Seats offer 38 inches of pitch with a leg and footrest, 19 inches of width, and seven inches of recline – each dimension several inches larger than in regular economy. Other upgrades include two free checked bags, priority check-in and boarding, noise-cancelling headphones, and a plush memory foam pillow. Swiss Air If you’re flying to Zurich or Geneva from the US, consider upgrading from coach to Swiss Air’s new “Swiss Senses” premium economy cabin. The separate premium economy cabin features 38 seats in a two-three-two layout, offering an exclusive environment. Each seat is 19 inches wide with 39 inches of pitch, with thoughtful features like a hard shell for easy reclining without disturbing surrounding fliers and privacy dividers attached to the headrest. You’ll also find a leg and calf rest and a 15.6-inch entertainment screen with Bluetooth capability, so you can stretch out and watch a new movie. There’s even a wireless charging pad in the armrest (along with USB-A and USB-C ports) to keep your devices juiced up. Premium economy passengers are allowed two free checked bags, and upon boarding, they get a taste of Switzerland’s famous apéro culture with a welcome aperitif and a Sbrinz cheese snack, along with Swiss wines to complement their in-flight meal. Finnair For a sense of Nordic style in the skies, look no further than Finnair’s premium economy product. The Helsinki-based carrier’s upgraded cabin can be found on long-haul flights aboard its Airbus A350 and A330 aircraft and features collaborations with Finnish designers, including Marimekko amenity kits and Iittala tableware, which is used to serve three-course meals. Aside from its focus on style, the cabin offers substance, too, including spacious seats with 38 inches of pitch and a leg rest that cradles the entire leg. Each spot is also outfitted with a 13-inch entertainment screen, power outlets, and USB-A ports. When it’s time to rest, passengers will notice that the separate cabin, with just 26 seats in a two-four-two layout, fosters a quiet, calm atmosphere conducive to relaxation. ITA Airways Book a seat in ITA Airways’ premium economy class and bring a bit of “la dolce vita” lifestyle to your next flight without busting your budget. The dedicated cabin is outfitted with 24 seats in a spacious two-three-two layout. Every seat is upholstered in stylish beige and cream-colored textiles and offers seven inches of recline, 40 inches of pitch, and 19 inches of width. A leg and footrest, plus privacy wings on the headrest, make falling asleep easy, while perks like a 15.6-inch entertainment screen, noise-cancelling headphones, and USB-A and USB-C ports ensure quality in-flight entertainment. Each seat even has a separate cocktail table that can hold passengers’ welcome drink of prosecco, or maybe a glass of Italian wine, limoncello, or a freshly made espresso from Illy coffee. Meal time means Italian dishes served on porcelain tableware. The benefits extend to the airport experience, too: premium economy fliers are granted priority check-in, boarding, and baggage claim, as well as two free checked bags.

item.title: 10 best ultra-light suitcases that will save you from airline weight fees for 2026
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 3.83
Every traveller knows the sinking feeling of heaving their case onto an airport luggage scale, only to watch the numbers tick perilously close to the limit before you’ve even packed a souvenir. Whether you’re attempting to breeze through security with a single cabin bag or hauling a fortnight’s worth of gear across multiple long-haul legs, every extra gram built into your suitcase is one stolen from your overall packing allowance. Put simply: lightweight luggage is the way to go, especially if you’re a known over-packer. Fortunately, our favourite luggage brands prove that trimming total weight down does not mean sacrificing structural integrity or clever interior organisation. Our constantly-travelling editors have tested nearly 100 suitcases over the years, and the below solidly rank most highly on the weight front, leaving plenty of room for heavy winter knits, extra boots – or a selection of buys from your latest travels. We’ve selected only carry-on cases under 3kg, and checked suitcases under 5kg to earn an esteemed spot as one of our best lightweight suitcases. For the complete edit of the top luggage to know about in 2026, see our full guide, or our guide to the best suitcase sets. Below, the best lightweight suitcases for 2026, thoroughly tested by our editors on real-world trips to ensure they survive the rigours of the baggage carousel without dragging you down. The best lightweight luggage at-a-glance The best lightweight carry-on suitcases The best lightweight check-in suitcases How we test lightweight suitcases Every suitcase in this guide undergoes initial hands-on evaluation in our office by commerce writers Charley Ward and Lauren Burvill, before being trialled on real-world trips by our broader editorial team. Across dozens of flights and rail journeys, we rigorously test shell durability, 360-degree spinner wheel smoothness, lock security, internal organisation – including zip dividers and laptop sleeves – and general value for money. Key metrics like empty weight, exterior dimensions, ease of handling, and overall aesthetics are also weighed during our process. Airline hand luggage weight and size limits - British Airways: 1 personal item (40 x 30 x 15 cm, up to 23 kg) + 1 cabin bag (56 x 45 x 25 cm, up to 23 kg). - EasyJet: 1 under-seat bag (45 x 36 x 20 cm, up to 15 kg). Large cabin bag (56 x 45 x 25 cm) available for an additional fee. - Emirates: 1 personal item + 1 cabin bag (55 x 38 x 20 cm, up to 7 kg combined). - Etihad: 1 personal item + 1 cabin bag (56 x 36 x 23 cm, up to 7 kg combined). - Ryanair: 1 small personal bag (40 x 20 x 25 cm). Large cabin bag (55 x 40 x 20 cm, up to 10 kg) available with Priority booking. - Singapore Airlines: 1 personal item + 1 cabin bag (max combined dimensions of 115 cm, up to 7 kg). - Virgin Atlantic: 1 personal item + 1 cabin bag (56 x 36 x 23 cm, up to 10 kg). What dimensions should a cabin suitcase be? While exact carry-on restrictions vary by carrier, most standard cabin bags measure around 55 x 35 x 25 cm, which comfortably fits into the overhead bins of most major airlines. Most carriers also permit a secondary personal item to stash beneath the seat in front of you – ideal for quick-access items like passports, tech gadgets, and water bottles. If you pack efficiently, a well-structured personal item can even eliminate the need for an overhead trolley bag on quick weekend getaways. What is the maximum weight allowance for hand luggage? Carry-on weight allowances generally range between 7kg and 15kg depending on the airline, with the global average sitting around 8 kg. EasyJet remains one of the most generous carriers with a 15 kg allowance, whereas budget lines often enforce stricter 7kg or 10kg caps. To avoid unpleasant surprises or excess baggage charges at the gate, we recommend investing in a portable luggage scale and double-checking your specific airline's baggage policy prior to departure.

item.title: 21 best hotels in Mykonos to book for a slick and stylish stay
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 3.03
Though you wouldn’t know it now, it wasn’t until the 1980s that Mykonos opened its first luxury hotel on the island’s south coast – and thus began the influx of the best hotels on the island. While this hotel, Myconian Ambassador, still stands, Mykonos today has become synonymous with luxury: hotels, restaurants, beach bars and beyond. It's best known as a place to party, but there’s a lot more to this Greek island, with beats-until-dawn bars mainly confined to the (actually fairly small) area of Mykonos Town. More than ever before, visitors are starting to notice everything Mykonos has to offer away from the late-night dining and dancing scene and are choosing to explore the island’s wild, less-crowded coastlines instead. Where tourists wander, hoteliers follow: over the last few years, there’s been a boom in openings along the island’s south-east coast, from Kalafati beach, where you’ll find Cali Mykonos, to Elia beach, where Four Seasons Mykonos is set to open, the second Greek property from the brand, following its 2019 Athens Riviera launch. See our edit of what to pack for three nights in Mykonos here. Editor's picks of the best hotels in Mykonos - Best for luxury: Four Seasons Mykonos - Best for honeymoons: Amyth of Mykonos - Best beach location: Myconian Sunrise Relais & Chateaux Hotel - Best for a girls' trip: Fouquet's Mykonos - Best boutique hotel: Deos Mykonos - Best for families: Santa Marina, a Luxury Collection Resort What are the best areas in Mykonos to stay in? For all of its hype, Mykonos is relatively small. The island is only 10 kilometres, so wherever you stay, you're pretty close to the action and beaches. Some of the hotels on this list are found along the popular Ornos Beach on the island's southwest. If you want to be based around some hubbub, this option has plenty of shops, restaurants and bars nearby. To be in the thick of the party scene, look to hotels like Mykonos Theoxenia and Bohème, located right in Mykonos town. If you'd prefer to be far removed from it all, Cali Mykonos is hidden away in the reclusive (and exclusive) coastal village Kalafati. When to go to Mykonos The height of the season is July and August, but things are already hotting up in early summer when the fresh produce is better and there are less crowds. If you favour a slightly slower pace, with more comfortable temperatures and less crowds, book a trip to Mykonos in either of the shoulder season months: May or September. How to get to Mykonos Flights from London: Mykonos has an airport serviced by domestic flights from Athens and direct flights from the UK. EasyJet flies directly from the UK to Mykonos; Olympic Air and Aegean Airlines fly to Mykonos via Athens. By ferry from within Greece: Mykonos is easy to reach from Athens' two ports (Piraeus and Rafina) by boat, especially in summer when ferry companies add to their scheduled journeys. Car ferries tend to be comfortable but slow, taking approximately seven hours to get to the island, while modern high-speed catamarans and Sea Jets are more than twice as fast, but not as steady in rough seas. You can also reach Mykonos via other Greek islands if you want to island-hop. How we choose the best hotels in Mykonos Every hotel on this list has been selected independently by our editors and written by a Condé Nast Traveller journalist who knows the destination and has stayed at that property. When choosing hotels, our editors consider both luxury properties and boutique and lesser-known boltholes that offer an authentic and insider experience of a destination. We’re always looking for beautiful design, a great location and warm service – as well as serious sustainability credentials. We update this list regularly as new hotels open and existing ones evolve. Find out more about our editorial standards and how we review hotels.

item.title: 17 national parks so beautiful they look like another planet
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 2.52
Some places are beautiful for one specific reason: a beach at sunset, a mountain perfectly reflected in a lake, a rainforest humming with wildlife. But national parks offer something broader. By definition, they protect entire landscapes and ecosystems – drawing a line around expanses we’ve collectively decided are too precious to lose. For travellers, having a list of designated wonders is also an easy way to know exactly where (and how) to see some of the world’s most incredible natural wonders. That could mean rafting under waterfalls in Argentina, ballooning over fairy chimneys in Turkey, ice caving in Iceland, or hiking for three days to reach a wildflower-filled valley in India. There are many thousands of national parks around the world, so the trickiest part is narrowing down the list – but these 17, spanning six continents and encompassing an extraordinary range of scenery, are a good place to start. Lençóis Maranhenses National Park, Brazil At first glance, Lençóis Maranhenses looks like an enormous white desert – but this vast expanse contains multitudes. The park’s sand dunes are striped with turquoise and emerald lagoons (which accumulate during the rainy season), creating the effect of infinitely repeating oases. Book a five-hour bus ride from São Luís for a surreal swim break. Iguazú National Park, Argentina This park protects the Argentine side of the enormous Iguazú Falls (Iguaçu National Park is a hop over the border in Brazil), a system of some 275 roaring cascades deep in the rainforest. The bombastically – but fittingly – named Devil’s Throat is the standout waterfall here. Admire it from one of the walkways, or ride a speedboat right into the spray. Cabo Pulmo National Park, Mexico Who says national parks have to be in the mountains – or even on land at all? Located on the tip of Mexico’s Baja California Sur peninsula, Cabo Pulmo is a coastal wonderland of quiet beaches and rock formations – but its true appeal lies under the surface. Just offshore, the brilliant Pacific waters protect a vast coral reef system teeming with sea turtles and swirling schools of zooming jacks. Yellowstone National Park, United States Choosing just one US park is a near-impossible task, but Yellowstone takes the narrow lead. Not only was it the first designated national park in the country (and, by most accounts, the entire world), but its geological diversity can’t be beat – within its 2.2 million acres, you’ll find mountains, canyons, geysers, rainbow-gradient hot springs, and more. Banff National Park, Canada This one’s no surprise. Banff National Park is one of Canada’s shining stars, beloved for its staggering views of the Rockies and glacial, almost impossibly blue lakes. Lake Louise, Moraine Lake, and Lake Minnewanka are all standouts, equally lovely when reflecting sunshine in summer and frozen over in winter. Namib-Naukluft National Park, Namibia Namib-Naukluft is the Namibia you came for: burnt-orange sand dunes, blindingly white salt pans, and the eerie skeleton trees of Deadvlei. It’s a little bit Mars, a little bit Fury Road, but an absolute original that has no peer. Tsingy de Bemaraha National Park, Madagascar Madagascar is one of the world’s hardest-to-reach countries, which makes its landscapes feel even more immaculate. Case in point: the Tsingy de Bemaraha National Park. Famous for its forest of limestone needles jutting into the sky, the park is almost terrifying in its beauty – though lightened by the fact that the Malagasy word “tsingy” roughly translates to “where one cannot walk barefoot.” Noted! Serengeti National Park, Tanzania The Serengeti occupies an almost mythical space in our collective mind. The Great Migration, in which millions of wildebeest move across the plains, is one of Earth’s greatest natural shows. But even in stillness, the region is magnificent – golden grasslands rolling beneath the open sky, with acacia trees punctuating the otherwise endless horizon. Vatnajökull National Park, Iceland Iceland is known as the land of fire and ice, and no place better encapsulates that dramatic epithet than Vatnajökull National Park. Its eponymous glacier and accompanying ice caves dominate the scene, but active volcanoes simmer beneath the freeze, and rivers of meltwater cut through the terrain. It’s a true study in contrasts, both elemental and chromatic – brilliant blue ice, inky black rocks. Las Salinas de Torrevieja National Park, Spain Yes, it really is that pink. Torrevieja’s salt lagoon gets its hue from microorganisms that release red pigments in saline conditions – an imperceptible process that yields magnificent results. It’s an Instagram darling, sure, but it’s also a place to appreciate nature’s inner workings and see the world through bubblegum-coloured glasses. Plitvice Lakes National Park, Croatia Plitvice Lakes National Park may not be hidden, but it sure is a gem. Sixteen interconnected lakes cascade through the forest, linked by a series of waterfalls and natural travertine barriers, and ranging in hue from brilliant turquoise to deep blue and green. Make your way through the selfie-snapping crowds, find an empty spot on one of the wooden walkways, and just stand in awe. Valley of Flowers National Park, India The name pretty much says it all: During the summer blooming season, Uttarakhand’s Valley of Flowers transforms into a huge natural garden, with wildflowers blanketing the Alpine meadows in a riot of colour. Getting here requires a lengthy trek (we’re talking several days) through the Himalayas, but the effort just makes the visual payoff that much sweeter. Göreme National Park, Türkiye Göreme is defined by Cappadocia’s fairy chimneys, which are about as magical as they sound. The mushroom-shaped rock structures, carved over millennia by volcanic activity and erosion, are best viewed from above – namely in the basket of a hot-air balloon. Set your alarm and time your ride to sunrise, so you can be the first to watch the landscapes awaken for the day. Kelimutu National Park, Indonesia Three lakes, three wildly different colours. Kelimutu National Park’s bodies of water shift at the whims of the minerals and gases beneath the craters, so you never know exactly what shade you’ll see when you arrive – red, blue, green, or black. It’s as if Mother Nature is wearing a trio of mood rings. Zhangjiajie National Forest Park, China Located in China’s Wulingyuan Scenic Area, Zhangjiajie boasts thousands of jagged sandstone peaks that rise dramatically over lush treetops – and when mist shrouds the valley below, they almost seem to float above the clouds. (Look familiar? The park famously inspired the Hallelujah Mountains in Avatar.) Fiordland National Park, New Zealand Fiordland National Park showcases some of New Zealand’s most striking features, all in one space: mountains, rainforests, waterfalls, and deep glacial fjords. Many visitors zero in on Milford Sound, the undeniable star attraction; but there truly are no bad views here. Uluṟu-Kata Tjuṯa National Park, Australia Few landmarks are as recognisable as Uluṟu, a sandstone monolith rising from an otherwise flat and open desert. The rockface changes colour depending on the sun’s position – ochre during the day, blazing orange and pink at sunset, and purple at twilight.

item.title: The best Airbnbs in Naples to book in 2026
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 2.52
Naples is finally having its moment, and the spike in foreign tourism has also helped revitalise the city’s hospitality scene. The best way to experience this relatively unsung spot for a few nights? By living like a local in one of the best Airbnbs in Naples. This gem of the Mediterranean has always been an inspiration and a second home for artists, so much so that prominent literary figures like Goethe, Shelley and Dumas spent years living in this eclectic and gorgeously complicated city. With visitors of that calibre, the hotel scene was already well developed, but Airbnbs are now catching up, with some so well-curated that they could easily compete with the best hotels in Naples. This southern urban destination has many faces, and choosing your base could really transform the way you experience it. From the buzzing chaos of the Rione Sanità and the chic shopping streets of Chiaia to the affluent Posillipo neighbourhood, we have selected some of the best Airbnbs in Naples to enjoy it all on your terms. For an adventure in the wilderness, it’s hard to resist the lure of bonnie Scotland and it's charming Airbnbs.
