item.title: 10 of the best pubs in Bath for West Country buzz, low-slung beams and crisp cider pints
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 2.32
There’s something about a cold pint in one of the best pubs in Bath that is instantly happy-making. “There ain’t nothin’ like good cider for to make your smile grow wider, and there’s still more cider way down west!” sing The Wurzels. And it’s true: the West Country buzz, the low-slung beams and the beer gardens spilling out alongside the River Avon – it all truly makes you smile. Then there’s the old-world lure of Bath’s drinking holes in a city so drenched in history that the oldest is the Saracens Head at the bottom of Broad Street, built in 1713 and visited by Charles Dickens. If you spend your teenage years sliding in and out of Bath’s pubs as I did, there’s a risk that cider is ruined forever. But time, it turns out, is a healer when it comes to scrumpy overconsumption. And returning to live in the West Country as an adult, there are cooler taphouses and a heady influx of craft beer to discover, as well as the nostalgic old haunts to sink into until last orders. On Saturdays during the summer, Dick Willows cider farm in the pretty village of Claverton Down, just outside of town, opens its doors for live music. And towards Bradford-on-Avon is the Iford Cider Taphouse with its megawatt sunset and sourdough pizzas. In a city where it’s tempting to ferociously frog-march yourself around the sights, here’s our pick of pubs to proudly skive off to, where a swift half happily turns into a whole afternoon at the bar. The Marlborough Tavern It’s hard to trump the location of this 200-year-old pub just minutes from John Wood the Younger’s show-stopping Royal Crescent: the perfect refuge once you’ve ticked off the sights. Wind up here for a run of inventive small plates (think Asian-style king prawn salad), before saddling up for a Marlborough Tavern burger, towering with pickles and smoked cheddar. The head chef’s Bloody Mary is the perfect warm-up for its Sunday roast, and when the sun shines there’s a shady walled garden to spill out into. Address: The Marlborough Tavern, 35 Marlborough Buildings, Bath BA1 2LY Website: marlborough-tavern.com Hop Pole Inn When this 16th-century inn, less than four miles outside of Bath, shut its doors in 2018 and property developers loomed, the villagers launched the Save the Hop Pole Inn campaign with fervour. Fast forward to the beginning of 2025 and the doors were open, interiors stripped back (muted greens and scrubbed wooden tables) and the menu cleverly curated by chef Charlie Rawlings, with meat sourced from his family farm less than a mile away. Locals can once again descend for a pint of ale and the hearty sandwiches (think Coronation chicken piled high in a milk bun from Pipit bakery in nearby Bradford-on-Avon) make it a non-negotiable pitstop for hungry cyclists navigating the towpath along the Kennet and Avon Canal. Address: Hop Pole Inn, Woods Hill, Limpley Stoke, Bath BA2 7FS Website: hoppoleinn.uk The Talbot Inn With a 15th-century church tucked behind it (complete with a statue by Sir Alfred Munnings), the Mells River meandering nearby and the best of Somerset’s rolling countryside as the backdrop, The Talbot Inn is farcically bucolic. This is one of the Beckford Group’s West Country pubs and another masterclass in what a pub should be: candles lit, regulars lining the bar, local ales and tired dogs at heel. Step under the carriage archway into a cobbled courtyard and settle in for a pint of Talbot ale on a wrought iron table or decamp inside for plates of chalk stream trout pate and salted fennel perhaps, or the hearty ploughman’s with Wiltshire ham, Vale of Camelot cheddar and pickles – all well worth the 20-minute trip from Bath. Address: The Talbot Inn, Mells, Somerset BA11 3PN Website: talbotinn.com Electric Bear Brewing Taproom In an industrial corner of town to the west of the city, a cool crowd descends on the taproom at the Electric Bear brewery each weekend. Queues snake for pints of craft beer and the long trestle tables fill with plates piled high from the street food vans (cheese toasties, Greek gyros, slow-cooked beef tacos…) with an eclectic line-up of live music as the soundtrack – plus the chance to recover from the night before with Sunday morning yoga sessions. Address: Electric Bear Brewing Taproom, Unit 12, The Maltings, Brassmill Lane, Bath BA1 3JL Website: electricbearbrewing.com The Bell Inn If arty Walcot Street is proudly rebellious in a city that can feel a little strait-laced with its Georgian grandeur, then the 300-year-old The Bell Inn might be its flag bearer. In 2013, Glastonbury’s Michael Eavis was among the 500-plus-strong customer buyout, which promised to keep this a place that showcased live music, celebrated real ale and cider, artisan produce and analogue sounds and championed Bath’s artistic community. Inside it is happily bohemian, with fairy lights, hops hanging over the bar and live music ringing out. Address: The Bell Inn, 103 Walcot Street, Bath BA1 5BW Website: thebellinnbath.co.uk The Grapes Once a townhouse for the affluent taking the waters in the city, by the late 18th century this pub had its name ‘The Grapes’, and over 200 years later it’s still a place to let off steam. Drinkers spill out onto Westgate Street armed with pints of cider from nearby Iford Manor, or gin from the Bath Distillery, all to the sound of jazz and traditional folk sessions as well as DJ sets. Upstairs in the Jacobean living room (which features an early 17th-century ornate lime plaster ceiling), the pace is altogether calmer, with a roster of events from life drawing classes to its ‘People, Planet, Pint’ meet-ups where locals gather to put sustainability in the spotlight. Address: The Grapes, 14 Westgate Street, Bath BA1 1EQ Website: thegrapesbath.co.uk The Raven Tucked on the cobbled Queen Street in the centre of town, here is a Bath boozer to settle into until last orders. On Bath rugby match days West Country patriotism is alive, but on any weekend it’s as noisy as a good pub should be (it has form as a watering hole: during the Second World War it was a favourite with pilots stationed at a nearby airfield and in the 1980s it was said to be a go-to for the city’s goths and bikers.) You can bag a hearty pie to fill up on (try the ‘deer stalker’ with venison, bacon, lentils and red wine), but it’s the ale that you’re here for. Pull up a stool for its exclusive brews, the Raven Ale and Raven’s Gold, as well as a pick of craft beers including its own hazy IPA brewed by Arbor in Bristol. Address: The Raven, 6-7 Queen Street, Bath, BA1 1HE Website: theravenofbath.co.uk The Chequers In the smartest corner of town, tucked on Rivers Street between The Circus and the Royal Crescent is The Chequers, where head chef Sam Stone has masterminded a menu at odds with any notion of simple pub grub. There’s burrata with crispy garlic chilli oil while you wait, then coppa from nearby Somer Valley Farms perhaps, rarebit made with Westcombe cheddar from Bruton and rib of beef (also local) with brown butter jus. But that doesn’t mean it’s a pub that’s morphed into a hushed restaurant: the bar is reassuringly noisy with locals armed with an ale and after-work drinkers spilling onto the pavement benches outside. Address: 50 Rivers St, Bath, BA1 2QA Website: chequersbath.net The Welly A buzzing taproom rather than a cosy pub, The Welly on pretty Green Street was opened last year by the team behind Somer Valley Farms and Somer Valley Brewing. Here, the best of the West Country’s bounty is up in lights: there’s gin from the Bath Distillery, bread from Landrace Bakery, cider from Iford and beef from its own farm. A perfectly placed pitstop in the middle of town to refuel with nose-to-tail, zero-waste small plates (don’t leave without trying the Somer Valley scotch egg) and a pint of pilsner. Address: The Welly, 9 Green Street, Bath, BA1 2JY Website: somervalleyfarms.com The Wheatsheaf Combe Hay Drive less than 15 minutes south out of town and you’ll end up in rolling Somerset countryside and the village of Combe Hay with its Bath stone cottages. The beer garden in the 16th century The Wheatsheaf, run by the Barton family for over 20 years, is the best kind of post-walk sanctuary. After navigating the impossibly steep footpaths up towards South Stoke or the tiny hamlet of Twinhoe, settle in for a pint of ale or a scoop of Purbeck ice cream. Or succumb to a well-earned long lunch: whole Brixham plaice with samphire, garden beans and café de Paris butter perhaps, with a steaming sticky toffee pudding to refuel you. Address: The Wheatsheaf, Combe Hay Ln, Combe Hay, Bath BA2 7EG Website: wheatsheafcombehay.com

item.title: Inside the secret Yorkshire art walk that’s harder to get into than Glastonbury
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 2.32
I love walking. As a Cotswolds countryside resident, my once-concrete jaunts across east London have been swapped for crunchy grass stomps through cow-laden fields or floating across rolling hills just out my front door. I also love art. Exhibitions and retrospectives are often what dictate my travels. A recent dash on the Eurostar brought me to a speedy 48-hour whip around the late David Hockney exhibition at the Louis Vuitton Museum in Paris, in between long bistro meals and a snoop around the city’s latest new hotel opening. So when a few art-obsessed friends returned from what they called the most incredible walk of their lives up in the North York Moors, but said that they couldn't really tell me why, I was immediately intrigued. I began researching and uncovered an outdoor art walk where tickets to gain access to were as hard as heading to Glastonbury. The walk is, rather intriguingly, called Hanging Stones. I'd heard about artist Andy Goldsworthy from my mother. The contemporary English land artist has been shaping, morphing and discerningly using his hands to form large scale works using natural materials we might often overlook in everyday life: stones, snow, rock, leaves, iron, twigs, mud and more. One of his most talked-about pieces involved transporting 13 one-tonne snowballs from Scotland and placing them on the streets of London during a hot summer's day. He challenges and inspires conversation about our world and its precious land, and for his ongoing project up in Yorkshire – commissioned by the David Ross Foundation – he shifts the focus to the raw beauty of the Moors. To get tickets, eager hikers need to set reminders to check the website. Slots open at hangingstones.org – it’s currently booked out for the rest of the year, but new releases come out regularly. It costs £10 per adult; under-18s and students go free. There’s a maximum of four groups of six allowed each day. On the day, collect your laminated map and keys from Sevenford House B&B, then head to the Milburn Arms in Rosedale Abbey where the circular walk begins and ends. Allow five to six hours... you’ll need it, and wear proper boots (once you have your slot, I’d advise against trying to change it, so prepare for all weather conditions) and bring your own food and water – there are no facilities en route. My husband and I set off up north for a six-mile hike through farmers' fields and dormant heather hills to to pick up an instruction guide and a set of dangling keys… Here's everything we found along the way. To Goldsworthy, the whole walk is an artwork in itself. There are ten stone outbuildings, some rebuilt from ruin, all immaculately beautiful and each with its own installation inside. The tenth, titled Heygate Thorns, is currently in the works, but there’s a tiny window Goldsworthy left for you to have a special glimpse. My favourite stretch was the uphill push to the furthest point you reach before looping back, which is surrounded by hazy gorse and heather. There’s magic in unlocking giant padlocks and not knowing what’s inside. The signposts felt straight out of Lord of the Rings; little slits of eyes hammered into stone are your earmarks to keep you on your way. Don’t forget to look up. The light can change everything. Goldsworthy makes the mundane something joyful to look at. Perhaps the perfect picnic spot, or keep on pushing to the highest point of the walk for a chapel- like shelter on a particularly blustering day.

item.title: 7 best bakeries in Bath for brioche buns, sourdough loaves and sticky cinnamon treats
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 2.27
The best bakeries in Bath mean different things to different people. When my late great aunt came on what felt like a state visit from Scotland to stay with us in Bath each year, for example, she’d insist on tea at the 18th-century Pump Rooms. There was the chandelier opulence that she liked, the harpist, and the starched white tablecloths. But mainly it was her annual Bath bun fix that she was after: soft, round and topped with oversized sugar crystals. Bath has form when it comes to bakeries. There were the brioche-like Sally Lunn buns, first touted around the abbey in the late 17th-century, and then came the sugar-loaded Bath buns during Bath’s glittering Regency years. But fast-forward nearly 350 years, and there’s been a flurry of new bakeries in Bath over the past decade or so, where the stacks of sourdough and trays of sticky cinnamon buns alone justify a trip to this corner of the West Country. The frontrunner is Landrace Bakery on Walcot Street, opened in 2019 and the kind of place I unashamedly plan a trip into town around (getting in early enough to time it right for a cardamom bun for breakfast and holding off a sad piece of toast at home beforehand so that I can savour every bite). But a bun for breakfast is just the start. In a city that’s all walkable with hills at every turn, the need for pick-me-ups is plentiful. So here is our guide to the best bakeries in Bath for coffee and a sugar hit when you start to flag. Landrace Bakery Best for: a cardamom bun The grand dame of Bath bakeries, Landrace was opened by Andrew Lowkes on artsy Walcot Street with sourdough made using speciality grains milled at Westcombe Dairy in Bruton. Get there early for a warm, straight-from-the-oven cardamom or cinnamon bun, with a smooth Roundhill Roastery flat white collected through a hatch on the street. Or grab a table in the ground-floor Caff, where the shelves are lined with loaves, and you can settle in for a pastry armed with your book (croissants filled with Somerset-grown apricot jam perhaps, or a Danish packed with lovage and Lamyatt cheese from Westcombe Dairy). And when you haven’t managed to bag a table upstairs in the restaurant for dinner, from 5pm (Tuesday-Saturday) the Caff serves up 18” pizzas loaded with local ingredients. Address: 59 Walcot Street, Bath, BA1 5BN Website: landrace.co.uk Morso Bakery Best for: savoury pastries In one of the smartest corners of town, a two-minute hop from The Circus, Matt Puchowski and Georgia Barton have opened Morso, years after dreaming of doing just that. The bakes are all vegan (but the pair are low-key about this; you’d be hard-pressed to guess), with coffee from Wiltshire roaster Colours Coffee, a sunny courtyard and benches out the front spilling over with coffee drinkers. You won’t miss it – the front is a cheering apricot colour – and if you can hold out until lunchtime, the savoury pastries are deliciously inventive (try the Danish flavoured with gochujang, maple and confit garlic). Address: 4 Saville Row Bath BA1 2QP Website: instagram.com/_morso_bakery/ Green Street Best for: sandwiches Next to the neon sign glowing in the window at Green Street are hunks of local, grass-fed meat and strings of garlic, with in-the-know locals dashing to get their hands on a rotisserie chicken roll with caramelised shallots for lunch. This is a place that’s big on provenance: the bread is all made at their prep kitchen in Bath before being delivered at the crack of dawn, and the sandwiches are filled with meat cooked from the butcher counter. If you’re passing in the morning, pick up a coffee (Triple Co, roasted in Bristol) and one of their in-house baked croissants, cruffins or, best of all, brown butter cookies. Address: 10-11 Green Street, Bath, BA1 2JZ Website: greenstreetsandwiches.com Society Café Best for: carrot cake At the end of The Corridor, Bath’s 19th-century shopping arcade, you’ll find some of the best coffee in Bath at Society Café (it has another outlet on Kingsmead Square if you’re in that part of town), with beans from Origin Coffee Roasters in Cornwall and deliciously full-fat milk from Bruton Dairy. Stools line the bars at the windows with locals and tourists eking out their flat white with one of the café’s pastries (delivered from The Newt in Somerset), traybakes from the Wild Flour Cake Co in nearby Timsbury, cookies from Bakervee in Bath or its showpiece carrot cake made by Alice Cakes (a recipe they’re most often asked for but can’t divulge…) Address: 19 High Street, The Corridor, Bath, BA1 5AJ and 5 Kingsmead Square, Bath BA1 2AB Website: society-cafe.com Brume Bakery Best for: old school buns This autumn, in a Grade-II building on the cobbled Kingsmead Street, Brume Bakery will open, the brainchild of Bath locals Joe and Tori Hill, who between them have worked for go-to Bath dinner spot the Beckford Canteen, Soho Farmhouse and The Newt in Somerset. Where once there was a fish and chip shop, there will now be the couple’s long-held vision of a Parisian bistro-meets-bakery. Expect sourdough, baguettes and focaccia made using stoneground British flour, as well as croissants, cheesecake, tiramisu and nostalgic-making stacks of iced buns. Address: 38 Kingsmead Street, Bath, Somerset BA1 2AA Website: instagram.com/brumebakery Colonna & Small’s Best for: coffee When husband-and-wife Maxwell and Lesley Colonna-Dashwood opened Colonna & Small in 2009 it was a coup for Bath’s coffee-connoisseurs. The couple had discovered the third wave coffee movement – treating coffee as a craft rather than a basic commodity – in Melbourne the year before and brought this vision to the West Country. Nearly 20 years later coffee is treated just as seriously here (Maxwell is a UK Barista Champion). But that doesn’t mean it’s an intimidating place to get your caffeine fix, with chattering huddles of friends around pared back tables and laptop-wielding workers at the bar. Grab the spot in the window to watch Bath life trundle past, charged with one of their billowing croissants from Hobbs House Bakery to refuel you. Address: 6 Chapel Row, Bath, BA1 1HT, Website: colonnacoffee.com BRaC Best for: focaccia sandwiches On those trips to Bath when you ditch the to-do list and timings go out the window, wandering just out of the centre of town along the River Avon to BRaC is worth the step count. Founded by chef Sam Wylde, the bakery bakes all its focaccia in-house each morning, alongside its baps and a changing line-up of treats (expect Basque cheesecake, chocolate torte and lemon meringue). Milk is from Frome-based Ivy House, eggs from Fenton Farm near Taunton, meat from Ruby and White butchers in Bristol, and blooms from Bath-based Flowers by Passion. Opt for the towering Pollo Caesar Focaccia sandwich for lunch, and when the sun is shining, get it to go and stroll the 10 minutes back up to the Royal Crescent to scoff it with a view. Address: Pegasus Leat, Nelson Villas, Nelson Place West, Bath, BA1 2BD Website: instagram.com/brac

item.title: 21 best UK autumn holidays to book this year
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 2.16
Autumn in the UK is a pretty special time. The last of the summer sun is lingering and the world outside is filled with a kaleidoscope of colour as leaves burn bright, while indoors, crackling fires fill rooms with a warm glow and blankets are laid out for curling up under. Choosing to holiday closer to home means no crowded airports, and no tickets or boarding passes to deal with. The weather is taken as it comes – get lucky and you might arrive at your destination to bright blue skies and sunshine, but it could easily transform into threatening clouds and drizzle in the blink of an eye. Spend days exploring the blustery landscapes spread across the UK or traipsing round cities and quaint villages, but be sure to end each excursion with a gut-busting roast dinner with all the trimmings. Here are our editors' favourite places to go for autumn in the UK, from picturesque villages in the Cotswolds to rugged coastal scapes in Cornwall. For more inspiration, see our guide to where to go in Europe in autumn.

item.title: Grog almighty – the rise and rise of navy-strength gin
item.description:
Source: Food & Drink Score: 4.72
Grog almighty – the rise and rise of navy-strength gin Roula Khalaf, Editor of the FT, selects her favourite stories in this weekly newsletter. Old Raj gin looks like the kind of thing you’d find at the back of your grandfather’s drinks cabinet; its mercantile font and black-and-white portrait of a colonial officer are from another age. Launched in 1972 by Scotland’s oldest independent whisky bottlers, Cadenhead’s, the saffron-laced gin spent decades being resolutely uncool. So I was astonished to find, on a recent trip to New York, that it’s now a cult Martini pour. William Elliott, bar director of Brooklyn’s Maison Premiere, was an early adopter of Old Raj. “We were hunting down obscure, overproof [high abv] gins for a tableside Martini and were struck by its quiet intensity,” he says. “The luxurious application of saffron gives it a tonal and textural quality that was a clear upgrade from the brutishness of most London Dry-style gins.” Old Raj is bottled at two strengths: 46 per cent (Red Label, £30) and a bracing 55 per cent (Blue Label, £34). “The 55 per cent abv version is the must-have,” says Nima Ansari, spirits buyer at Manhattan’s Astor Wines. The fact Old Raj is owned by the company that distils the Campbeltown single malt Springbank is also, he says, a plus for spirits connoisseurs. Blue Label is what they use for Martinis at Maison Premiere and Le Veau d’Or on Manhattan’s Upper East Side. You’ll also see it on the list at Gallaghers Steakhouse, Death & Co and Frenchette, where it’s served in a Martini twist with vermouth and tomato water. “I first came across Old Raj while working at Small Victory in Austin, Texas,” says Jojo Colonna, bar director at Four Horsemen’s buzzing Italian I Cavallini in Brooklyn. If a customer requested Blue Label, he says, “it was a sign of an intentional Martini drinker”. Old-style, high-strength gins have been making a comeback among Martini connoisseurs. “At the higher abv, the spirit holds on to more of those botanical oils and aromas,” says James Stevenson, founder of new Martini bar Brutes of Mayfair, where the house gin is Plymouth Navy Strength (£42), a 57 per cent abv homage to the high-proof gins once drunk by officers in the Royal Navy. “You still get a very dry, clean Martini, but with a much more oily texture, from the gin.” If you’re mixing Martinis with a high-strength gin, “stir with ice for longer than usual to allow for adequate dilution”, advises Kevin Beary, beverage director of Chicago’s Kitty’s Cosmopolitan Club. Erik Delanoy of Elder in NYC also recommends using Old Raj Blue Label for a wet Martini with equal parts gin and vermouth. At Three Sheets in Soho, they favour The Botanist’s 50 per cent abv Distiller’s Strength (£42). “It’s still very soft and mellow,” says co-owner Max Venning. “Because it’s higher-proof, you can stir it down for longer and get the Martini really cold, without losing the lovely wild, floral botanicals.” Forget old-school stiffener – it’s now all about soft power. Comments

item.title: Affordable Alternatives to Japan's Most Crowded Destinations
item.description:
Source: GoBackpacking Score: 8.00
Japan welcomed more visitors in 2025 than ever before, and most walked the same ten streets. The crowding is real but concentrated: a few temples, villages, and viewpoints absorb most of it, while places offering the same experience sit half empty a valley away. Budget travelers hear a tempting promise: quieter must mean cheaper. Sometimes it does. Sometimes the quiet option adds a shinkansen leg or a rural bus that erases every yen saved on admission. The only way to know is to do the math, so this article does it for four popular swaps using prices checked in August 2026 from official sources. That timing matters: JR East raised fares on March 14, 2026, and Kyoto doubled its accommodation tax two weeks earlier, so numbers from older guides are quietly wrong. The pairings come from the Crowd-Free Japan Index, which matches 40 of Japan's most-visited places with curated quieter alternatives. Kanazawa Instead of Kyoto: The Savings Are on the Ground, Not the Rails Kanazawa is often called "little Kyoto," which annoys both cities, but the comparison holds where it counts. The Higashi Chaya geisha district is a smaller, calmer Gion where the teahouses actually let you in: Ochaya Shima charges ¥500 to walk through a working 1820s interior. In contrast, most Gion teahouses remain entirely closed to casual visitors. Omicho Market delivers the seafood-breakfast experience of Tokyo's Tsukiji Outer Market, with locals still doing their shopping there, and entry to Kenroku-en, one of Japan's three great gardens, costs ¥320, compared with ¥500 for Kinkaku-ji or ¥500 for Kiyomizu-dera, each ticketed separately. The biggest savings come from where you sleep. Kyoto's average hotel rate hit a record ¥20,195 per night in 2024. Since March 1, 2026, the city has charged a ¥1,000 per-person-per-night accommodation tax on rooms priced at ¥20,000-49,999, double the previous rate. Kanazawa's tax on the same room is ¥500. | Cost item (August 2026) | Kyoto | Kanazawa | | Shinkansen from Tokyo, one way | ¥14,170 | ¥14,600 | | City bus, single ride | ¥230 | ¥220 | | Transit day pass | ¥1,100 | ¥800 | | Headline garden or temple | ¥500 | ¥320 | | Accommodation tax, per person | ¥1,000 p.p. per night | ¥500 p.p. per night | Note the first row: The train from Tokyo to Kanazawa costs slightly more than the train to Kyoto. The swap pays off in everything after you arrive and compounds with every night you stay. Shima Onsen Instead of Ginzan Onsen: The Clearest Budget Win in Japan Ginzan Onsen's gaslit street has become so popular that the town now meters its own visitors. In winter, day visitors park two kilometers out and ride a shuttle; evening entry requires a paid reservation (¥1,150 in the first season, capped at 100 people per hour), and after 8 pm the street closes to everyone but overnight guests. Those overnight stays start at roughly ¥25,000 per person with meals, and reaching the town from Tokyo costs about ¥13,000 by the Yamagata Shinkansen, plus a ¥1,000 bus that takes cash only. Shima Onsen, tucked in a Gunma river gorge, offers the same Taisho-era wooden-ryokan romance with none of the metering. Sekizenkan's main building dates to 1691, making it Japan's oldest hot-spring inn building, and it is often said to have inspired the bathhouse in Spirited Away; its budget rooms start at ¥10,450 per person. The riverside cave bath Kawara-no-yu is open to day visitors from 9:00 to 15:00 without charge. Best of all, a direct highway bus runs from Tokyo Station for ¥3,500 one way and ¥6,300 round trip, about three and a half hours. | Cost item (August 2026) | Ginzan Onsen | Shima Onsen | | Transport from Tokyo, one way | ~¥14,000 (shinkansen + bus) | ¥3,500 (direct bus) | | Night in a heritage ryokan | From ~¥25,000 p.p. with meals | From ¥10,450 p.p. at Sekizenkan | | Soaking without staying | Winter evenings ticketed | Free cave bath, 9:00–15:00 | One honest caveat: the bus runs once daily each way and must be reserved by 4 pm the day before. If you miss it, the rail route via Nakanojo costs more and takes longer. Book the seat, then relax. Ainokura Instead of Shirakawa-go: Let Your Routing Decide Shirakawa-go itself is not the budget problem; walking the village is free, the Wada House costs ¥400, and the viewpoint shuttle costs ¥300. The problem is that everyone arrives on the same reservation-only buses (¥2,800 one way from either Kanazawa or Takayama) and shares the lanes with them. Ainokura, a village of twenty thatched gassho-zukuri farmhouses on a mountainside in neighboring Gokayama, is listed as a World Heritage site with a fraction of the foot traffic. It is also free to enter on foot, and the World Heritage Bus from Takaoka or Shin-Takaoka costs ¥1,100, less than half the Shirakawa-go fare. Whether that saves you money depends entirely on your routing. Traveling the Hokuriku Shinkansen anyway? Step off at Shin-Takaoka and Ainokura is the cheaper, quieter choice. Based in Kanazawa or Takayama with no plans northward? The extra rail leg to Takaoka eats the difference, so the direct ¥2,800 bus to Shirakawa-go wins. The best-value option for seeing both: the ¥4,000 two-day unlimited pass covers Ainokura, Suganuma, and Shirakawa-go on one ticket, and costs less than buying a single round trip separately. Related: Travelers looking beyond Tokyo and Kyoto can find more ideas in Go Backpacking's guide to Japan's Chubu region. Naoshima and Teshima Instead of teamLab: When Quieter Costs More Honesty requires one counterexample, because quiet does not automatically mean cheap. Tokyo's teamLab Planets charges from ¥3,600, with date-based pricing. The contemplative alternatives are Naoshima and Teshima, neighboring art islands in the Seto Inland Sea: the Chichu Art Museum costs ¥2,500-3,000 with timed reservations that cap visitors. The Teshima Art Museum costs ¥1,800-2,000. The direct ferry from Uno Port to Naoshima costs ¥370, while the ferry to Teshima costs ¥780. Per ticket, the islands undercut teamLab. Per trip, they usually don't: Uno Port is a Shinkansen ride and two local connections from Tokyo, and that transport dwarfs the admission savings. The swap only makes financial sense when Setouchi is already on your route, say between Osaka and Hiroshima. If it is, take it without hesitation; if not, this is the case where the crowded option is genuinely the affordable one. The Cheapest Alternative: Don't Leave the City You're In The most expensive way to escape a crowd is to cross half of Honshu. A same-day dash from Tokyo to Kyoto for Fushimi Inari's torii gates costs over ¥28,000 in return shinkansen fares before you have eaten anything. Meanwhile, Nezu Shrine, one of Tokyo's oldest, has its own tunnel of vermilion torii at the Otome Inari sub-shrine, costs nothing to enter, and sits a ¥180 metro ride from central Tokyo. The same logic covers bamboo. Kamakura's Hokoku-ji temple has a grove where you can sit with matcha for ¥400 admission plus ¥600 for the tea. The Great Buddha at Kotoku-in across town charges ¥300, and the train from Tokyo costs ¥1,040. That makes a full bamboo-and-Buddha day out possible for under ¥5,000, compared with visiting Arashiyama's grove at the far end of a ¥28,000 round trip. Even garden-hopping scales down: Kiyosumi Garden charges ¥150 for stone-hopping across carp ponds that Shinjuku Gyoen crowds pay ¥500 for. Altitude works the same way. Shibuya Sky's rooftop charges ¥2,700 online for daytime entry and ¥3,400 for sunset slots, and shares the deck with everyone else who booked the same golden hour. Sunshine 60's Tenbou-Park observatory in Ikebukuro shows a comparable skyline for ¥700 on weekdays, and the free 26th-floor observation lobby of Carrot Tower in Sangenjaya, a few minutes from Shibuya on the Den-en-toshi line, faces Mount Fuji at sunset and charges nothing at all. Four Rules Before You Swap - Price the final leg first. Rural alternatives live or die by the last bus or ferry: its fare and, above all, its schedule. One missed daily departure can force a taxi that costs more than the whole day. - Admission is rarely the problem. Japanese entry fees are modest: ¥150-800 covers most of the attractions in this article. Accommodation and intercity trains decide your budget, so compare hotel rates and lodging taxes before temple tickets. For a broader breakdown of travel costs, read Go Backpacking's guide to backpacking Japan on a budget. - Some crowded icons are free. Fushimi Inari charges nothing; Shirakawa-go's lanes charge nothing. Swapping away from them buys you a better experience, not a cheaper one. Know which reward you're paying for. - Recheck prices from 2026 onward. The March 2026 JR East fare rise and Kyoto's doubled accommodation tax made many older budget guides inaccurate. The official links above reflect August 2026 prices. Quiet and cheap usually travel together in Japan, but not always, and never automatically. Run the numbers for your own route, and you'll often find the lesser-known option costs less and gives more. When it doesn't, at least you'll know before the bus timetable tells you.

item.title: Kilimanjaro Routes Compared: Which Should You Choose?
item.description:
Source: GoBackpacking Score: 6.58
Seven official routes lead up Kilimanjaro, and most people narrow their choice to two or three within an hour of reading about them. Machame is the popular one, Lemosho the scenic one, Marangu the one where you sleep in huts instead of tents. Those labels are accurate but don't affect whether you reach the summit. Kilimanjaro is 5,895 m (19,341 ft) high. Its standard trekking routes do not require technical climbing equipment (ropes, an ice axe), but the extreme altitude makes acclimatization essential. The number of days on the mountain matters. Five-day itineraries leave less time for acclimatization, while some operators report summit success rates around 95% on eight-day climbs. These are operator-reported figures, not mountain-wide averages. The takeaway is simple: allow your body more time to adapt before summit night. How the Routes Actually Work Seven official ascent routes exist, but they don't stay separate all the way up. Every climb has three phases, and the route you choose changes each of them differently. The approach (the first four to six days) is where the routes differ. Lemosho starts in quiet rainforest on the western flank. Rongai comes from the dry northern side near the Kenyan border. Machame and Marangu climb from the busy south. For four to six days, you circle toward Kibo, the main volcanic cone, gaining altitude through rainforest, moorland, and alpine desert. This is where you acclimatize, so the number of days here matters most. Summit night. The approaches converge toward Kibo, with most standard itineraries using one of two main summit routes. If you came via Machame, Lemosho, Shira, or Umbwe, you leave Barafu Camp around midnight, climb to Stella Point, then walk the crater rim to Uhuru Peak. Marangu and Rongai climbers leave Kibo Hut, and their route to Gilman's Point takes longer because much of it runs over loose volcanic scree. Either way, you gain about 1,200 meters in the dark. The Western Breach is another summit route, but rockfall and unstable ice make it risky. For that reason, careful operators avoid it. The descent. The park separates uphill and downhill traffic. Routes that summit from Barafu come down the Mweka corridor, a trail used only for going down. Marangu and Rongai climbers walk back down the Marangu trail, sharing it with groups heading up. The Routes, Side by Side | Route | Days | Start from | Sleeping | Traffic | Pick it if | | Machame ("Whiskey") | 7 (or 6) | South | Tents | High | You want the classic climb-high-sleep-low profile and the Barranco Wall, and crowds don't bother you. | | Lemosho | 8 (or 7) | West | Tents | Low early, medium later | It's your first high-altitude climb, and you can spare the extra day. | | Marangu ("Coca-Cola") | 6 (or 5) | Southeast | Wooden huts | High | Sleeping in a tent is not an option for you. | | Rongai | 6 | North | Tents | Low | You want quiet, or you're climbing during the short rains. | | Northern Circuit | 8–9 | West, then north | Tents | Very low | You prioritize extra acclimatization time and a quieter approach. | | Umbwe | 6 | South | Tents | Very low | You're already acclimatized and want a steep, direct route. | | Londorossi (Shira) | 6–8 | West, by vehicle to the plateau | Tents | Very low | You want open views from day one and understand the altitude trade-off. | Route by Route Machame: the "Whiskey Route" (7 days) Machame is the most popular route on the mountain, and the nickname compares it to Marangu, the "Coca-Cola Route." The key differences are that Machame is tougher and steeper, and you sleep in tents. In seven days, you pass through every climate zone Kilimanjaro has, from wet rainforest at 1,800 meters to the frozen crater rim. The third day takes you up to Lava Tower at 4,600 meters and then down to Barranco Camp at 3,900 meters to sleep. That is the "climb high, sleep low" principle built into the route, which is why Machame acclimatizes people so well despite its pace. The next morning you scramble the Barranco Wall, a near-vertical face that needs hands for balance but no rope. The downside is traffic. Machame and Marangu take the lion's share of expeditions, and you will share camps with hundreds of other climbers. The Barranco Wall gives the climb real mountaineering character, and the scenery earns the route its reputation. Still, anyone choosing Machame has to be willing to move in a stream of other groups and share the intermediate camps. The other decision on Machame is between six and seven days. The difference is a single night at Karanga Camp after the Barranco Wall. Drop it, and you go straight from the wall to Barafu and into summit night on the same push, when accumulated fatigue shows up. For example, ALPO runs the Machame Route on the seven-day schedule and keeps that Karanga night for this reason; the company reports 95-97% of its climbers reaching the summit on that version. Its guidance on the six-day option is that the success rate is lower. Lemosho (8 days) Lemosho starts on the remote western flank at Londorossi Gate, about three hours' drive from Moshi. The first two days run through rainforest that the southern routes never touch, and you may not see another group. This is where you are most likely to see colobus monkeys. The route then crosses the Shira Plateau from west to east, one of the highest plateaus on Earth, and on the eight-day version you spend two nights up there, at Shira 1 (3,500 m) and Shira 2 (3,840 m). That slow gain is the whole point. From the plateau, Lemosho joins the Machame trail, so the Lava Tower day, the Barranco Wall, and the summit night are the same. The main decision on Lemosho is whether to do seven or eight days. Dropping to seven means crossing Shira in one long stage and losing a night of adaptation, which helps most. Lemosho also costs more than Machame, partly because of the long drive to a remote trailhead and partly because the extra day adds food and crew wages. For someone whose first real altitude climb is this one, the eight-day Lemosho remains the most balanced option; the gain comes slowly enough that your body has time to catch up. Marangu: the "Coca-Cola Route" (6 days) Marangu is the only route where you sleep in permanent wooden huts instead of tents. The huts are dorm-style, with anywhere from 4 to 20 people per room and shared bathrooms. It is also the historic original route and the one with the gentlest approach gradient, which is how it got its reputation as the easy one. That reputation can be misleading: a gentler trail does not remove altitude challenges. If you prefer hut accommodation, compare daily sleeping altitudes and acclimatization opportunities carefully, and favor the six-day itinerary over the five-day version. Summit night climbs from Kibo Hut toward Gilman's Point, and the route uses the same trail for ascent and descent, so you meet descending groups on your way up. The sensible rule is to choose Marangu in exactly one case, when a tent is physically or psychologically not an option for you, and then to take six days, never five. Rongai (6 days) Rongai approaches from the north, close to the Kenyan border, after a long drive to the trailhead. The northern flank is drier, making Rongai the sensible pick if climbing during the short rains in November. It is also the quietest standard route, with a real chance of larger wildlife on the lower section. The early terrain is less dramatic than on the western routes, and summit night from Kibo Hut is long and monotonous. It is probably the most undervalued route on the mountain: introverted, wild, and worth the trade for silence. Editor's note: For a firsthand perspective, read this account of climbing Kilimanjaro via the Rongai Route, from life at camp to the midnight summit push. Northern Circuit (8-9 days) The Northern Circuit is one of the longest itinerary options, giving you more time to acclimatize. As a result, it has one of the higher summit rates. It starts on the western side, like Lemosho, then swings around the northern face of Kibo on a nearly empty traverse before rejoining the main trails for the summit push. The extra days provide more time to adapt, although individual responses to altitude vary. It is generally among the more expensive options because you are paying for a longer expedition, and it requires solid multi-day trekking endurance. If reliably reaching Uhuru Peak is the goal and time is not the constraint, this is the route. Umbwe and Londorossi (Shira) Umbwe is the steepest line on the mountain and the most direct, climbing a narrow forest ridge that almost no one else uses. Its rapid ascent leaves little time to acclimatize, making it a better option for trekkers who are already acclimatized. Previous altitude experience alone is not a substitute. Londorossi, sometimes called the Shira Route, approaches from the west but begins with a vehicle transfer straight onto the Shira Plateau at 3,400 meters. The views open from day one. You give up the gradual gain that every other route builds in, which is worth considering before you book. What To Weigh Before You Book Days on the mountain. When comparing itineraries, prioritize acclimatization time. Look beyond total trip length to daily sleeping altitudes and acclimatization opportunities. Extra time helps, but fitness and previous altitude experience do not guarantee protection from altitude illness. Follow your guide's safety advice and be prepared to turn around. That is not a guidebook opinion. Yevgen Staroselskiy, co-founder of ALPO Guided Expeditions, is a Master of Sport in Mountaineering and holder of the "Snow Leopard" title (#376), with more than 130 major climbs behind him, including Everest (8,848 m, 29,029 ft) and K2 (8,611 m, 28,251 ft), and 25+ groups guided to the top of Kilimanjaro. His view of the time question is blunt: I've climbed Everest and K2, and I can tell you that no route on Kilimanjaro needs that kind of preparation. What it does need is that you take the altitude seriously. Give your body the days, walk slowly, and almost any physically active person will reach Uhuru Peak. Where I see people fail is when they try to save a day. - Yevgen Staroselskiy, Master of Sport in Mountaineering, co-founder of ALPO Guided Expeditions Everything else on this list is secondary to that number. Tent or hut. A binary question, and it settles Marangu yes-or-no before anything else. Crowds. Machame and Marangu are busy. Rongai and the Northern Circuit are not. Lemosho is quiet for two days and then joins the Machame stream. Summit night profile. From Barafu, the climb to Stella Point is steeper, but you are mostly on firm ground. From Kibo Hut, you spend more hours on scree before you reach Gilman's Point. Season. Compare expected rainfall and trail conditions for your travel dates with your operator. Wetter periods mean muddy trails and reduced visibility; the northern approach is generally drier. Conditions vary, so avoid treating any seasonal window as a guarantee of dry weather. The dry windows are June to early October and mid-December to early April. During the short rains in November, the northern side stays drier, which is a point in Rongai's favor. In April and May, the trails wash out, and clouds hide the views, so no route is worth doing then. A Quick Decision Guide - First high-altitude climb and you can spare eight days: Lemosho. - Seven days, and sharing camp with other groups does not bother you: Machame, on the seven-day schedule rather than six. - You will not sleep in a tent: Marangu, six days, no shorter. - Climbing in November, or you want the mountain mostly to yourself: Rongai. - More time for acclimatization and a quieter approach: Northern Circuit. Whichever route you choose, prioritize an itinerary that allows time to acclimatize rather than booking the shortest option. This article was published in partnership with ALPO Guided Expeditions.
