item.title: “Bison Belong on This Landscape.” Judge Blocks Federal Order to Remove 1,000 Animals in Montana
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine Score: 5.53
Bison grazing on American Prairie (Photo: Courtesy American Prairie) Nearly 1,000 bison that faced removal from federal land in Montana will be able to continue grazing for now after a judge blocked a Bureau of Land Management (BLM) order seeking to kick the animals out. The lawsuit stems from a BLM order this May that sought to remove the bison from public portions of American Prairie. The nonprofit preserve covers more than 600,000 acres of private land and public grazing leases on Montana’s shortgrass prairie, all of it open to the public, and features camping, wildlife-watching, and hiking. The BLM granted the permits for the animals to graze in 2005. Its new order is rooted in a reinterpretation of the Taylor Grazing Act, which allows the department to issue livestock permits for public grazing. The rewrite seeks to reclassify livestock as “production-oriented.” U.S. District Court Judge Brian Morris objected. “No statutory language or judicial precedent exists that requires a livestock operation to focus exclusively on production and entirely ignore conservation, range improvement, preservation, or other values,” he stated in the decision. “Congress recognized livestock grazing and livestock management often includes and considers preservation, improvement, and thoughtful development, hand-in-hand with other uses.” The bison will now remain on American Prairie’s leases while the lawsuit proceeds. The decision will delay the BLM’s original removal order, scheduled for September 30. If that order had taken effect, the preserve would have needed to either cull or remove hundreds of bison from the land, as Beth Saboe, American Prairie’s director of public relations, told Backpacker in May 2026 shortly after the BLM announced the changes. “Worst-case scenario, we potentially would have to get rid of hundreds of animals. We don’t want to see that happen,” Saboe said at the time, adding that the organization planned to appeal any adverse final decision. Besides incurring major costs to American Prairie, Saboe said removing the bison from the public range would have stripped a restorative species of its native habitat. The uncertainty around the herd also led American Prairie to cancel its public bison harvest for 2026. While the permit revocation had support from the Montana Stockgrowers Association and many local ranchers, American Prairie’s tribal partners pushed back. In a January 2026 letter to the Secretary of the Interior, J. Garret Renville, chairman of the Coalition of Large Tribes and Sisseton-Wahpeton Oyate of the Lake Traverse Reservation, wrote that American Prairie had provided animals to and worked with a number of tribes attempting to grow their own herds, and that the organization’s methods of raising bison were “largely indistinguishable from the practices and techniques employed by tribal herd managers.” In his ruling, Morris wrote that he “struggle[d] to see” how the BLM’s choice to impose the new regulation while ignoring American Prairie’s evidence could be consistent with the law. With its redefinition, the BLM sought to limit grazing to animals “used as part of an operation to provide output for various purposes, such as meat, milk, fiber, or other products and any animals when they are being used to assist with management of other animals in connection with such operations (e.g. horses that are used to assist with cattle management).” The BLM itself concluded in 2022 that bison grazing would improve rangeland productivity and riparian health on the same lands it now seeks to remove the animals from. If American Prairie ultimately loses the right to graze bison on its leases, it could choose to replace them with cattle. There’s evidence that could compromise the land: Cattle herds often heavily graze one small area before moving on. Bison, on the other hand, tend to graze more gradually while constantly moving over the landscape, covering up to 2-3 miles per day. Studies have shown this can increase biodiversity and even drought tolerance on native grasslands. “These are the ungulates that evolved with the prairie landscape,” Saboe said in May. “They’re one of the main keystone species here, and that’s because of how their presence on the landscape improves the rangeland.” The court’s preliminary injunction covers the three federal allotments where American Prairie bison are currently grazing. It did not grant the organization’s request to protect three other tracts where bison do not already graze. “Bison belong on this landscape, and today’s ruling gives them a chance to stay,” said Alison Fox, CEO of American Prairie. “For more than 20 years, our bison have grazed these lands under federal authorization and without grazing violations. The court recognized the concrete harm that removing them would cause, not just to our work, but to our Tribal partners and the broader effort to return bison to their native home.”

item.title: He Fell 500 Feet Down Mount Shasta. To Survive, He Took Off His Boots and Crawled Through the Night.
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine Score: 5.38
The climber took off his mountaineering boots and walked through the night to a remote wilderness cabin to await rescue (Photo: Courtesy of Shasta-Trinity Forest Service) On September 10, a mountaineer from San Jose, California, summited Mount Shasta around 7:30 P.M. According to a rescue report from the Shasta-Trinity National Forest Service (STFS), that was the least eventful part of his climb. After his summit, the climber attempted to glissade down Avalanche Gulch, the most popular route to the top. Glissading involves sliding down a steep snowpack and is a technique some use to descend a mountain quickly. But he lost control and slid about 500 vertical feet down the slope. During the fall, his feet were severely injured. So, he took off his mountaineering boots and walked through the night to a remote wilderness cabin to await rescue. “However, he ran into trouble shortly thereafter,” the Forest Service wrote. “His cellphone died after summiting, and the climber’s friends became concerned when they were unable to contact him the following day.” Authorities have not released the climber’s name, age, or condition. When he failed to check in, the climber’s friends reported him missing to the Siskiyou County Sheriff’s Office. Mount Shasta is one of California’s most popular peaks for mountaineers. Seven year-round glaciers cover its flanks, making it a perfect testing ground for budding mountaineers hoping to learn to use crampons, ice axes, and other mountaineering gear. The climber was in the Avalanche Gulch area, the classic mountaineering route to the mountain’s peak. It’s not an overly technical route, but it requires a 7,000-foot vertical ascent, with exposure to steep snow, ice, rockfall, and extreme weather, the Mount Shasta Avalanche Center (MSAC) wrote on its website. “The climb to the summit is steep and rigorous, requiring crampons, a mountain axe, helmet, and basic snow travel skills,” MSAC wrote. “Don’t consider this route a cakewalk.” According to MSAC, the best time to climb Avalanche Gulch is April through June, sometimes in July, and rarely August through November. In late summer, lower portions of the trail lose their snow cover, exposing climbers to loose scree, talus, and difficult hiking conditions. “Later season climbing will expose you to dramatically increased rock fall and is not advised,” MSAC writes. Mount Shasta Climbing Rangers, Siskiyou County Sheriff’s Search and Rescue, and the California Highway Patrol (CHP) began searching for the climber at 2 P.M. on September 11. Two hours into the search, responders said a hiker called them from Horse Camp, a historic base camp and alpine refuge located at about 7,900 feet. The hiker had found the missing climber—the latter of whom was barefoot. During his fall, the climber sustained significant lacerations and injuries to his feet. When trauma occurs at a high altitude, tissue can swell rapidly, making rigid mountaineering boots exceptionally painful. “The climber removed his boots due to painful swelling and crawled through the night, down the remainder of Avalanche Gulch to the Horse Camp Cabin,” the Forest Service wrote. “After evaluating the climber’s injuries, he was airlifted from Horse Camp to a nearby hospital for treatment.” The Forest Service notes there are several lessons to be learned from this incident. For starters, don’t begin such an ambitious hike so late in the evening. In mid-September, the sun sets around 7 P.M. in the area. “When climbing Mount Shasta or a similar objective, give yourself plenty of daylight to hike out,” a STFS spokesperson wrote. “This makes the descent safer, and if you or another member of your party needs help, it is easier for rescuers to find and assist you. Experts recommend climbers set a noon turnaround time when attempting Mount Shasta, even if that means they’re short of the summit. Always share your itinerary with at least one person, and give your friends a plan on what to do if you don’t check in. “The climber wisely notified his friends of his plan to climb Mount Shasta and made a point to check in and provide progress updates,” the STFS spokesperson wrote. When he lost contact, his friends contacted law enforcement to report him overdue and traveled to help with the search effort. When using electronic navigation, have a backup and be ready for rescue. Never rely solely on a GPS or phone to navigate—if the devices stop working, hikers need to use their own navigational skills to get home safely. “The Shasta-Trinity National Forest thanks the Siskiyou County Sheriff’s Office, SAR volunteers, CHP helicopter team, and the hiker who found the climber at Horse Camp Cabin for their assistance in this mission,” the spokesperson wrote.

item.title: “You Could See the Grimace on His Face.” A Climber Fell 200 Feet Off California’s Power Dome. His Friends Used a Shirt to Stop the Bleeding.
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine Score: 4.62
On September 11, a climber fell 200 feet while ascending on a 700-foot-tall rock face known as Power Dome in California’s Sierra Nevada mountains. He was bleeding heavily, and his friends used a shirt as a bandage while they awaited a helicopter rescue. A California Highway Patrol (CHP) helicopter flew within 15 feet of the sheer granite cliff and rescued the climber with a hoist evacuation system, officials said in a statement. Authorities have not released the climber’s name, age, or condition. “He was completely coherent and alert, despite a lot of blood loss,” flight officer and paramedic Scott Clays, who operated the helicopter’s hoist during the rescue, told Outside. “He just seemed very tough.” Power Dome is a 700-foot granite formation located near Courtright Reservoir, a popular climbing and camping area about two hours from Fresno, California. Authorities did not say which route the climber was on, but Power Dome has around 40 trad, sport, and toprope routes of varying difficulty. Around 12:45 P.M., CHP’s Coastal Division Air Operations said that it received an evacuation request for the fallen climber. During the climber’s ascent, he fell and hit the cliff face, Clays said. The climber lost a significant amount of blood from his injuries. His climbing partners removed his shirt and used it as a bandage to control the bleeding. Still connected to his ropes, the victim’s climbing partners lowered the man to a narrow ledge for rescuers to evacuate him from. “The ledge seemed to be shoulder-width,” Clays said, adding that it was about 200 feet off the ground. The Fresno County Sheriff’s Office, which assisted in the rescue, first sent in a drone to provide images of the climber’s condition and location. The CHP helicopter crew flew within 15 feet of sheer granite—the limit of their safety clearance—to execute a high-risk short-haul hoist rescue. Any closer, Clays said, and a “catastrophic” collision may have occurred. Responders used what’s known as a big-wall rescue to save the injured climber. The technique is often used in climbing-related accidents in Yosemite National Park and other parts of the Sierra Nevada. Here’s how it works: From the helicopter, a rescue technician dangles by a rope as the chopper inches closer to the wall—but not too close; any impact would be catastrophic, Clays said. During this time, the pilot hovers in place for 30 to 40 seconds in what Clays said is a constant battle with the wind to keep the chopper a safe distance from the wall. Once on the ledge, the rescuer disconnected his rope to stabilize and secure the injured climber for transport, and both were hoisted separately back into the helicopter. The climber was conscious and coherent when rescuers arrived, Clays said, and remained alert and helped keep himself steady while hanging from the helicopter. Once the helicopter delivered the victim to a waiting ambulance, Clays said he could see how much pain the injured man was in. “You could see the grimace in his face,” Clays said. “You know he was hurting.” In nearby Yosemite, where CHP crews train for similar big-wall rescues, records more than 100 climbing accidents each year.

item.title: Weighted Vests Aren’t New. They’re Just Humanity’s Oldest Workout, Rebranded.
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine Score: 3.73
(Photo: Ayana Underwood/Canva) This article has been medically reviewed by Rachel MacPherson, a certified strength and conditioning specialist and ACE-certified personal trainer. One day at 3 A.M., a few weeks postpartum, I had my baby latched to my chest while scrolling social media in the dark. The algorithm had decided it knew what I needed: new moms in weighted vests walking through neighborhoods after dinner. The comments claiming they were “life-changing” were a good enough endorsement for me. I ordered one on Amazon at 3:17 A.M. My partner saw the box when it arrived, looked at the baby, and said, with the patience of someone who has learned to choose their battles: “Why would you need a weighted vest when you can just strap the baby to your body?” He had a point. But unfortunately, a weighted vest and a baby harness aren’t interchangeable. A weighted vest distributes weight evenly across the body, but my baby harness keeps my daughter’s weight concentrated at the front of my body where she sits. A front load shifts my center of mass forward. So, while my baby might feel great, my back doesn’t. Because using my baby harness as a substitute weighted vest was out, I grabbed the real thing instead. But I found myself asking two questions: Why and how did weighted vests and load-bearing exercise become a thing? And what were the benefits? I dug into the history of the weighted vest and interviewed a physical therapist and a former military specialist to get some answers. Here’s what I found out. Load-bearing training didn’t start with TikTok, or even the U.S. military. The Spartans called it the agoge. The agoge was a mandatory state-run program that peaked between the 5th and 4th centuries BCE and required boys, as early as age seven, to learn the art of battle. By the age of 20, they were considered members of the army, according to a 1983 historical paper about life in ancient Sparta. Some were hoplites, a type of Greek soldier who had to wear heavy armor and carry bulky weaponry for many miles. Their shields could weigh around 15 pounds and were about three feet wide. Armies have long assumed that a soldier who can carry weight over distance is more valuable than one who can’t. Cal Coblentz, a former survival, evasion, resistance, and escape specialist in the United States Air Force, said that, in his world, carrying an extra 50 pounds was a baseline. “In my survival training and missions, it wasn’t uncommon to have a pack that weighed over 100 pounds,” he told Outside. He also said carrying a heavy load built an invaluable sense of mental fortitude. To be clear: most commercial weighted vests do not go this high in weight. But wearing a weighted vest that adds a few more pounds offers several benefits. People in the military weren’t the only ones who figured out the benefits of carrying more weight. For years, before weighted vests became a fitness accessory, physical therapists used lighter versions to help people recover from injury and boost their cardiovascular endurance. Peter Mason, a Wyoming-based physical therapist who works with athletes, describes the clinical logic: an evenly distributed load challenges the body without isolating vulnerable joints. In older adults with osteoporosis, a vest introduces progressive loading during functional tasks without requiring grip strength or external implements, he said. For someone rebuilding after injury or managing bone loss, that distinction matters. When you add load to a walk with a weighted vest, the weight distributes the load across your body evenly rather than, say, carrying a set of dumbbells (or my 15-pound baby). Because the load sits close to your trunk rather than hanging from one hand, your postural muscles work harder to keep you upright, and no single joint takes the whole load. Moreover, wearing a weighted vest helps activate core muscles and improves lower-body strength. A vest also gives your cardiovascular system a workout. A 2026 study published in the journal Physiological Reports examined the cardiovascular effects of wearing a weighted vest in people with obesity. Some of the 51 participants wore a heavy weighted vest (15 percent of their body weight), and others wore a light vest (one percent of their body weight). Participants in the heavy-vest group showed increased heart rate and cardiovascular workload. There is an important caveat. Mason said that vests are a good option for general conditioning, but “they are not a substitute for high-load resistance training in athletes who need meaningful improvements in force capacity and resilience.” In other words, for an athlete who wants significant strength gains in their sport, weighted vest training won’t be as beneficial as resistance training with heavy weights. But for a new mom like me, a weighted vest is ideal because I can do bodyweight movements like lunges, squats, and push-ups while wearing it and boost my heart rate without putting too much strain on my body. Eventually, weighted vests were no longer limited to physical therapy practices. They gained popularity through many mediums and went mainstream. According to a 2025 Forbes article, the global weighted vest market is projected to reach $350 million by 2033. Professor and bestselling author Michael Easter wrote in his Substack, Two Percent—where he writes about the latest in fitness and health—that the New York Times credited his 2021 book The Comfort Crisis with kickstarting the weighted-vest craze. In May 2025, when Peloton added weighted-vest streaming classes to their workout library, instructor Rebecca Kennedy said in a Time article that members responded with something close to relief and that the “appetite for weighted vests has been really wild.” If you want to try weighted vests, Mason suggests starting with a vest that’s five percent of your body weight and doing one to two non-consecutive weighted-vest walking sessions per week. If you weigh 160 pounds, that means you’d start with a vest that’s about eight pounds. A reasonable upper target for most people is ten to 15 percent of their body weight, he said. (That would be a max of a 16- or 24-pound vest for a person who weighs 160 pounds.) The best way to gauge when you can take on heavier weight, he said, is to pay attention to how your body responds over time. If you’re using an eight-pound vest and your movement is solid, aren’t experiencing pain, and have minimal fatigue, you can increase the vest weight, he said. “Fit matters: the vest should be snug enough to minimize movement and friction, but not so tight that it restricts respiration, trunk motion, or natural gait mechanics,” Mason said. One other important callout is that a weighted vest might not be for everyone. Skip the vest, or talk to a clinician first, if you’re pregnant, recently postpartum, or managing pelvic floor symptoms like leaking or heaviness. The same goes for anyone with a known vertebral fracture, uncontrolled balance problems, or a spine condition. If you feel pain, dizziness, or pelvic pressure, take the vest off. Overall, weighted vests are trendy for a reason; they are a legitimate tool for boosting the cardiovascular benefits of a walk. But they are not a substitute for strength training. As for me, I’ll still strap my baby to my chest for a walk just to get her outside, then throw on my weighted vest when I need some extra oomph for my daily walk or bodyweight routine. About the medical reviewer: Rachel MacPherson is a certified strength and conditioning specialist, an ACE-certified personal trainer, and a PN1-certified nutrition coach. MacPherson has spent over a decade helping lifters trade bro science for actual results. She’s happily turned an obsession with evidence-based health into a full-time writing and strategy career, helping publications, wellness brands, and supplement companies tell smarter stories that people trust. She’s a stickler for science-backed training advice that respects the reader’s intelligence, with the ultimate goal of getting you under the bar with total confidence (or moving in whatever way feels best). Want more Outside health stories? Sign up for the Bodywork newsletter. And for tips on how to train, fuel, and recover better, sign up for the Sweat Science 101 newsletter.

item.title: He Fell 120 Feet on Oregon’s Tom, Dick, and Harry Mountain. A Bystanding Doctor Came to His Rescue.
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine Score: 3.51
Tom, Dick, and Harry Mountain is a roughly two-mile-long volcanic ridge southwest of Government Camp (Photo: Ahorica) Just before 3 P.M. on September 15, a 33-year-old man fell 100 feet off a ledge on the second peak of Tom, Dick, and Harry Mountain—a jagged, multi-summit ridge above Government Camp in Oregon’s Mount Hood National Forest. The man tumbled while filming a movie, according to the Clackamas County Sheriff’s Office (CCSO). After his initial free fall, he slid 15 to 20 feet down the steep slope. Authorities have not released the man’s name or extent of injuries. “It’s hard to tell exactly what caused it, but at some point he lost his footing and fell from the top of the cliff band,” Sergeant Adam Peterson, a supervisor with the CCSO search-and-rescue team who responded to the incident, told Outside. Peterson added that the man had rigged ropes to capture a shot. “They were filming with a drone, just a couple of guys, making some sort of an indie film.” After the accident, witnesses told CCSO that the man was lying on his side with visible injuries, breathing but not moving. Tom, Dick, and Harry Mountain is a roughly two-mile-long volcanic ridge located 55 miles southeast of Portland, with three peaks rising to around 5,070 feet. Internet lore holds that early guides named the range after the idiom “every Tom, Dick, and Harry,” loosely meaning a random assortment of ordinary people. For decades, the peak was known simply as Tom Dick Mountain. In 1969, the U.S. Board on Geographic Names—a government agency not usually known for its sense of humor—added “Harry” to the mountain’s official name. Don’t confuse it with Georgia’s Big John Dick Mountain, Bloody Dick Peak in Montana, or Maine’s double-whammy: Tumbledown Dick Mountain and Tumbledown Dick Head. The name may be a punchline, but the mountain itself is no joke. Trails in the lower Mirror Lake area are popular with casual day hikers, but the upper ridgelines are steep, exposed, and loose near the summits, according to the U.S. Forest Service. Roughly half an hour after the incident, two people helped the man—one of whom was a medical doctor. The duo worked to keep him from rolling further down the hillside and applied direct pressure and tourniquets to control his bleeding, according to the CCSO report. During this time, they relayed details of his condition to rescuers, helping them prepare the appropriate response measures. “[The doctor] was able to control bleeding and handle essentially shock symptoms on the scene,” Peterson said. “That was very helpful due to the level of trauma.” Search-and-rescue coordinators activated a full rescue operation, with an Oregon National Guard helicopter crew and a paramedic reaching the man by 5 P.M. Within 30 minutes, responders strapped the man to a backboard, airlifted him into a helicopter, and flew him to a nearby hospital. Tom, Dick, and Harry Mountain keep rescuers busy, Peterson said. It sits directly above the popular Mirror Lake trail and next to a ski area, drawing countless hikers and an ongoing stream of minor-injury reports. “Usually it’s a lot more of your ankle sprains, things like that, for hikers over there,” he said. Just across the highway, though, is the south face of Mount Hood itself, where serious falls are far more common.

item.title: The iPhone 18 Pro’s Camera is Old School. We Couldn’t Be Happier.
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine Score: 2.55
The new iPhone 18 Pro has the widest aperture ever on an iPhone, letting in more light when needed. (Photo: Jakob Schiller) All traditional cameras, except for the simplest point-and-shoot, have always come with a mechanical aperture to control the amount of light that reaches the film or sensor. Phone cameras, on the other hand, have never incorporated one because of size restraints. That changes with the new iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max. Both come with a physical iris on the main 48-megapixel, 24-millimeter lens that can be manually controlled to let in more or less light. The shutter is still digital, but it can also be manually controlled for the first time. It feels odd to be celebrating something as basic as an adjustable aperture and manual camera options—like we’re going backwards in time. But, having tested it, I’m excited to have more control over how I make photos. After opening the iPhone 18 Pro’s camera app and choosing the main lens, you can peg the aperture and shutter controls to the top of the screen. Tapping these controls brings up a menu that lets you dial in your preferences. For aperture, you can choose from f/1.48, f/1.8, f/2.8, and f/4. That’s a limited range, but there’s a reason. The sensor inside the iPhone is much smaller and closer to the lens than what you’d find in a DSLR or full-frame mirrorless, so at f/4 you actually get a near-infinite field of focus and there’s little need to go higher. On the other end, Apple stopped at f/1.48 because anything wider would have necessitated a larger lens and compromised how it fits in your pocket. Note: The f-stop control on recent iPhones makes it seem like you can select f/1.4 to f/16, but the aperture is actually fixed. The illusion of changing the aperture and depth of field is created by the software digitally blurring or sharpening the background. Until now, you could not actually change the amount of light the lens let in. Using the iPhone 18 Pro’s f/1.48 aperture, the widest ever on an iPhone, you can now let in a lot more light. Anyone who’s shot a full-frame mirrorless camera knows that f/1.48 creates a razor-thin depth of field and helps you practically see in the dark. On the iPhone 18 Pro, the depth of field and light-gathering ability aren’t quite as powerful but are still significantly better than what you get with the fixed f/1.78 aperture on the main lens of the iPhone 17. I found the manual aperture control super useful. When I wanted to capture a scene with multiple people but emphasize just one, for example, I opened the aperture control, dialed down the depth of field, and was able to send the viewer’s eye to a specific part of the frame. In darker situations, I widened the aperture to allow light into the sensor, rather than having the phone compensate by dialing up the ISO, which can cause the photo to fall apart digitally (Note: the camera will still adjust the ISO whenever the light is too low for the widest aperture). Whenever I selected the aperture manually, the phone adjusted the shutter speed to ensure the correct exposure, just like the aperture-priority mode on traditional cameras. When I wanted a fast shutter speed to freeze fast-moving subjects, I selected the manual shutter control and the phone adjusted the aperture to create the correct exposure. In this setting, the phone acts like the shutter-priority mode on DSLRs and mirrorless cameras. In a lower-light panning situation, where I followed moving vehicles to keep them in focus but blurred the background, I selected manual control for both aperture and shutter. I was able to tell the iPhone to set the aperture at f/4 to allow in less light, which enabled me to slow down the shutter speed. I soon, however, discovered the limitations of the small aperture range, as even using the narrowest setting of f/4, the image got blown out with light whenever I slowed the shutter past 1/30th of a second. I still, however, was able to shoot better motion shots than on any previous iPhone. The 18 Pro is the first iPhone to get subject tracking, a feature photographers love on DSLRs and mirrorless cameras. It works by tapping a subject in the frame, which tells the camera to lock onto that person no matter where they move. This took some getting used to, but was helpful while photographing my son during a soccer game. Also new is a manual focus setting in which sliding one way on a digital dial tells the camera to focus whatever is closest to the lens, and sliding the other way focuses on the background. I found it a bit difficult to quickly identify where the focal plane was, but luckily there’s focus peaking, where whatever is in focus gets outlined in white as a visual cue. I found it nearly impossible to access any of these manual controls one-handed while holding the phone vertically, so I usually shot horizontally. Two hands made it much easier to tap the aperture or shutter speed feature, swipe to the setting I wanted, and click the shutter. The process was much slower than what I could do on a mirrorless camera, but with practice I had a well-organized workflow. I’ve long recommended the iPhone to Outside readers because it has a powerful camera that fits in your pocket and is great for adventuring. Thanks to upgrades like larger sensors and smart software, all the recent iPhones take damn nice photos. The inclusion of an adjustable aperture and more manual controls on the 18 Pro make it significantly more useful than the 17 Pro. Whether you should buy comes down to how you plan to use the camera and what other gear you already have in the closet. If you own a DSLR or mirrorless camera and don’t mind hauling it in your backpack, that’s still a better option. If you have an iPhone 16 or 17 Pro and don’t care that much about manual controls, don’t upgrade because your photo quality will be similar. If, however, you’re a photo geek like me and adventure a lot but don’t want to haul along a bigger camera, the iPhone 18 Pro is an attractive option.

item.title: 10 Best Down Jackets for Backpacking | 2026 Recomendations
item.description:
Source: Sectionhiker.com Score: 3.15
A down jacket has multiple uses on a hiking or backpacking gear list. It can be used as an insulating midlayer on its own or under a shell, as a warm outer jacket when you're less active in camp, or as an adjunct to your sleeping bag/quilt at night. For hiking or backpacking, some down jackets better meet hikers' needs than others in terms of warmth-to-weight ratio, hood design, durability, and cost. With these factors in mind, here are the best three-season down jackets that we recommend across a variety of price points. Be sure to check out our feature recommendations below, so you can choose the right jacket for your needs. | Make / Model | Gender | Weight | Fill Power | |---|---|---|---| | Patagonia Down Sweater Hoodie | M \| F | 14.8 oz/420g | 800 | | Feathered Friends EOS Jacket | M \| F | 11.8 oz/335g | 900 | | Arcteryx Cerium Down Hoodie | M \| F | 11.9 oz/335g | 850 | | Katabatic Gear Tarn Jacket | M \| F | 10.6 oz/303g | 850 | | REI Magma 850 Down Hoodie | M \| F | 13.1 oz/354g | 850 | | Mtn Hardware Ghost Whisperer | M \| F | 8.8 oz/249g | 800 | | Outdoor Research Helium Down Hoodie | M \| F | 15.4 oz/459g | 800 | | Montbell Ex Light Down Anorak | Unisex | 7.6 oz/215g | 900 | | LL Bean UL 850 Down Jacket | M \| F | 16 oz/450g | 850 | | Cotopaxi Fuego Hooded Down Jacket | M \| F | 13 oz/367g | 800 | 1. Patagonia Down Sweater Hoodie 2. Feathered Friends EOS Jacket 3. Arc’teryx Cerium Down Hoodie 4. Katabatic Gear Tarn Jacket 5. REI Magma 850 Down Hoodie 6. Mountain Hardwear Ghost Whisperer Down Hoody 7. Outdoor Research Helium Down Hoodie 8. Montbell Ex Light Down Anorak 9. LL Bean UL 850 Down Jacket 10. Cotopaxi Fuego Hooded Down Jacket Down Hoodie and Jacket Buying Guide Down Hoodies, Jackets, Sweaters, Anoraks, and Parkas Manufacturer product names are applied inconsistently to lighter-weight down hoodies and jackets. In general, hoodies, sweaters, and anoraks weigh under one pound. Look for ones with hoods, as they provide the most head and neck insulation. When it comes to jackets, some are lightweight and some are heavier, designed for winter use in harsh conditions. You really have to look at the overall jacket weight to determine which is which. Anything up to or slightly over 16 oz will be good for transitional weather in spring or autumn down to freezing by itself or layered under a shell, while heavier jackets will be more appropriate for winter use. Parkas are almost always intended for very cold winter conditions and are too warm for active use when hiking. Sewn Thru vs Baffled Construction With very few exceptions, lightweight down jackets and hoodies use sewn-through construction rather than box-baffled construction because it is less expensive and labor-intensive to manufacture. With sewn-through construction, the front and back of the jacket are sewn together, creating a pocket that prevents the down insulation from shifting. However, warm air can leak through the needle holes, making the jacket slightly cooler. This is not the case with a box-baffled design, which is more prevalent on premium down parkas intended for colder temperatures. Hood Adjustment The hoods on many lightweight or ultralight down hoodies and jackets are quite rudimentary, with elasticized hood openings that may be too large to prevent cold drafts from entering around your ears. It depends on your head size and the specific jacket. Hoods that are 1-way adjustable have volume controls in the back that let you shrink the size of the hood to provide a better fit. Hoods with 2-way adjustability go a step further and add neck cords that let you size the opening to fit your face and block out drafts. Two-way adjustability is pretty rare on lightweight down jackets and hoodies, but it's a premium feature worth looking for. Down Fill Power Down fill powers, such as 700, 800, 850, or 900, measure the effectiveness and compressibility of down insulation – the higher the better. Now, 900- or 950-fill-power down is primo stuff and can add a lot of cost to a jacket while keeping it very lightweight, since it takes less down by weight to keep you warm. You can get the same warmth with a lower grade of down, like 800 or 850, but it takes more of it to keep you warm and adds a bit of weight to the jacket. However, don't dismiss 700 fill-power down jackets, especially if they include synthetic insulation in moisture-prone areas. The warmth difference isn't that significant, and while they'll be a bit heavier, they're ideal in wet climates. Down Fill Weight The fill weight of a down jacket or hoodie measures the amount of down it has, by weight. While this can be informative, a jacket's actual warmth depends on both the amount of insulation and its design, which makes it hard to compare jackets with different styles. Most lightweight jacket manufacturers don't document the amount of down in their jackets, which can make it hard to tell which will be warmer in active use. Waterproof Down Some manufacturers use down in their jackets that has been coated with a chemical formulation, called DownTek or Nikwax, to make it more moisture-resistant and help it dry faster when it gets damp or wet. Honestly, the jury is still out on whether these treatments make any difference to the insulation performance of the down. Some manufacturers believe it degrades insulation value, and others use it because it's considered a desirable feature by prospective customers. I wish it were a bit warmer sitting around at camp when it gets down to 20-30F. Is there a jacket you think would perform better for those situations? I think the REI magma 850, the Katabatic gear Tarn of FF Eos will get you down to 20. Thanks, Philip. Those are ones that seemed like they might fit the bill from warmth standpoint to me. item.title: Wild Thing Canister Stove Windscreen
item.description:
Source: Sectionhiker.com Score: 2.58
The Wild Thing Canister Stove Windscreen works with most small backpacking stoves and small cook pots. This simple folding screen has a magnet that attaches to your gas canister and holds the screen in place. It provides plenty of ventilation to prevent your gas canister from overheating (and exploding), while improving stove efficiency and reducing boil times. - Weight: 2.65 oz - Material: Aluminum - Folded Dimensions: 3.75″ x 3.25″ x 1″ - Open Dimensions: 6.75″ x 3″ x 3.75″ What I like about this windscreen is that it works with all my canister stoves. Like most backpackers, I own a couple of canister stoves which I use in different circumstances or when the mood strikes me. Cook Pot Packability While a stove-independent canister stove windscreen is great, it's hard to know whether you can pack it, along with all your stove system components, into your cookpot for easy transport. I happen to place a very high value on this level of packability, as do most backpackers. Just because I can pack the Wild Thing Windscreen, a small gas canister, an MSR Pocket Rocket, and a plastic folding canister stand into an Evernew Ultralight Titanium Cookpot doesn't mean you can replicate my success with your cook system components. The problem is the shape of the Wild Thing Windscreen, which isn't very space-optimal, either folded or unfolded. While I could pack it into my cook pot above, I had to swap a larger canister for a smaller one to fit everything. Flat Cat Gear, which also makes canister stove windscreens, addresses this issue by emphasizing packability and fuel savings, but it limits the number of stoves and, in some cases, the stove-and-pot combinations it supports. Of course, you can opt to just use a Jetboil or a Wind Burner stove system, which hardwires the stove and pot combination, but those stove systems tend to be comparatively heavier. Assessement The Wild Thing Canister Stove Windscreen is a good choice for backpackers who want one windscreen that works with several small canister stoves. Its low weight, simple magnetic attachment, and broad compatibility are its main advantages. It can improve stove performance in windy conditions without committing the user to a stove-specific system. Its main limitation is packability. Backpackers who want to fit every cooking component into a single pot may prefer a more compact, stove-specific design. For users who value flexibility more than maximum space efficiency, however, the Wild Thing is a useful and well-conceived accessory. Overall assessment: Recommended for multi-stove users; less suitable for those who prioritize the smallest possible cook system. Disclosure: Wild Things donated a stove screen for review. Thanks for this post, I’ve been looking for something like this for awhile!

item.title: A taste of home: discovering Sweden’s local food heroes
item.description:
Source: The Guardian Travel Score: 4.79
‘It’s a magical place, and not just because of the hotel.” Standing outside the greenhouses at Högbo Brukshotell, two hours north of Stockholm, Stefan Johansson is talking about far more than hospitality. The former head chef, now responsible for sustainability at Högbo, has spent much of the past decade helping reshape the way this corner of Sweden grows, cooks and thinks about food. The catalyst was disarmingly simple. Years ago, a journalist asked Johansson why he was cooking the food he was cooking. Like many ambitious Swedish chefs, Stefan trained in Stockholm’s top restaurants, where ingredients from around the world were only a phone call away. The question lingered long after the interview ended. “Before, I wanted food to be spectacular; I didn’t really care where it came from,” he says. “Then I closed the window of where we source from down to the region. It was the best thing I’ve ever done.” Instead of looking farther afield for inspiration, he began looking closer to home. Högbo Brukshotell sits in the former Högbo ironworks, a quiet pocket of forest, waterways and historic buildings north of Sandviken. The area’s industrial past is still visible in its old manor houses, smithies and mill buildings, but since the factories fell silent in the mid-19th century, the woods have reclaimed their place. Walking, cycling and cross-country ski trails now lead into the forest, while the old bruk buildings house cafes, workshops and small businesses. Ingredients that once arrived at Högbo from far away are now grown here. The Made in Högbo project began with lamb, with animal rearing and butchery brought in-house. Vegetable production followed. Now greenhouses sit alongside kitchen gardens, producing ingredients for the restaurant and creating opportunities for people who might otherwise struggle to find work. Refugees from Myanmar helped establish some of the early growing projects. New arrivals from the Democratic Republic of the Congo have joined the initiative, splitting their time between Swedish language classes and work placements, their influence visible in the rows of papaya, bananas and other plants rarely associated with Sweden. There are plans for an aquaponics system that will combine greenhouse cultivation with tilapia fish farming. In farm buildings there are now also a bakery making sourdough and cakes, a microbrewery run by one of the chefs, a dairy making fresh cheeses, and an excellent deli. Högbo isn’t the only place asking these questions about food provenance. Over several days travelling through Gästrikland and neighbouring Hälsingland in eastern Sweden, I discover a network of millers, fishers, distillers, cheese makers and chefs connected by a shared idea: that food should reflect the place it comes from. At Gammelstilla, an old ironworks has become a small whisky distillery. In the village of Gästrike-Hammarby, The Old Mill is now an award-winning restaurant run by Bogdan Ioan Gheorghe and Ellinor Andersson, with a tasting menu that features a roll-call of local producers alongside surprising ingredients such as the invasive species Japanese knotweed. At Bergmans Fisk, in Norrsundet, low islands scatter across the bay and the Baltic stretches east towards Finland beyond the wooden smokehouses. The business is run by a seventh-generation fishing family whose connection to these waters stretches back more than a century. Inside the smokehouses, salmon hangs in neat rows, a slow process, refined over generations. But for traditions – and the business – to survive, they have to evolve and diversify, Dennis Bergman explains. In 2020, the family opened a waterfront restaurant overlooking the bay where much of their fish is caught. We enjoy a smorgasbord of smoked salmon and böckling (hot smoked herring) piled on dark rye crispbreads. The family also operates a travelling fish van serving coastal communities and is planning a small hotel: new ventures that will help secure the future of old skills. Driving north through the deep pine forests and lush fields of Hälsingland, I keep spotting hand-painted signs for potatoes, eggs and strawberries. Outside red-painted farm buildings, honesty boxes sit beside stacks of produce. At Teve Kvarn, a mill south of Järvsö, I meet Anna Larsson, a seventh-generation miller. She sources grain from roughly a 150km (93-mile) radius, selling seed to farmers and then buying back the grain to ensure high-quality flour production. Only a handful of mills of this type remain in Sweden. Anna points out her newest machine – it was installed in 1930. Beside the traditional wooden mill, shiny stills are visible in a tall glass building. This is the Tevsjö distillery run by Anna’s husband, Jonas, producing vodka, gin and aquavit using grain from the mill. The distillery runs on hydroelectric power generated from the nearby stream, and has already increased its production capacity more than 10 times on the strength of the products’ popularity – while creating 10 new local jobs. At nearby Järvsö Lanthandel, I meet chef Tobias Annerhult who runs the general store and restaurant. For Annerhult, local sourcing isn’t just desirable, it’s his entire food philosophy. “I only buy salt, pepper, sugar and oil,” he tells me. “I don’t use stabilisers. Nothing gets thrown away; that feeds the creative process. Our philosophy is to grow through limitations.” In a climate where vegetables arrive in abundance for only part of the year, preserving is essential. Annerhult pickles, cures and ferments local produce, including meat for charcuterie. Tonight, we too have to work for our dinner, taking a cooking class that Tobias offers for private group bookings. We have brought produce collected across the region: flour from the centuries-old mill; cheese and potatoes from honesty boxes; fish from a family that has worked the same waters for generations; and vegetables from local greenhouses. Together, we make fermented pea pancakes with sweet preserved apple and salty local goat’s cheese; bouncy fresh pasta using Anna’s wheat and eggs from Tobias’s chickens, served simply with burrata-style cheese, brown butter and garden herbs; and warm cake with the first of the season’s rhubarb. It’s a meal that tastes all the better for knowing the stories and people behind it. Combining preserved and fermented ingredients with the season’s freshest produce harks back to traditional approaches to cooking and eating. Today’s chefs are reclaiming that philosophy, and the results are delicious. It perhaps helps answer the question that changed Stefan’s career all those years ago. Why cook this food, in this place? Because when food truly belongs somewhere, it becomes a way of understanding that place too. The trip was provided by Visit Sweden. For more information visit gastrikland.se and destinationhalsingland.se. Högbo Brukshotell has doubles from 1,995 Swedish kronor (£155) B&B Comments (…) Sign in or create your Guardian account to join the discussion

item.title: The other side of Croatia: ‘a landscape that could out-Tuscany Tuscany’
item.description:
Source: The Guardian Travel Score: 2.96
‘You’re going to Samobor? You must try kremšnita,” my Dubrovnik friends told me before I set off on my trip north. “But I’ve already had kremšnita in Zagreb,” I told them. They do it better in Samobor, they insisted. I wasn’t about to get embroiled in a battle of the cream cakes in a region where Croatians, Slovenes and Austrians all like to celebrate their own versions of this decadently thick, fat custard slice topped with puff pastry and icing sugar. But I was more than willing – happy, even – to follow everyone’s suggestions to try kremšnita in Hotel Livadić’s Kavana Livadić, in Samobor’s main King Tomislav Square, a mere half-hour drive west of Zagreb. It lived up to the hype – delicately rich, creamy and with a light touch. After spending a few weeks in sun-bleached Venetian Dalmatia, amid the scrubby, limestone Dinaric Alps, I had swapped empires and was firmly in Habsburg Croatia. Here, in Zagreb County’s prettiest town, handsome baroque houses in pastel shades of buttery yellow, apricot and pistachio, festooned with stucco, line narrow King Tomislav Square, whose umbrella-shaded cafe terraces were filled with Croatians getting their morning fix of coffee and chatter. The lush green Samobor Hills overlook the medieval town, through which the Gradna – part river, part stream – flows and ripples under wooden bridges adorned with flowers. One of these bridges led to the onion-domed church of Saint Anastasia; another, with a fairytale wooden roof, took me to one of Samobor’s many green spaces, dotted with free red deckchairs, which had the slogan “Volim Samobor” (“I love Samobor”) written in white. In front of them, the stately former home (now the town’s museum) of one of Croatia’s foremost 19th-century composers, Ferdo Livadić, added to the air of gentle refinement, of culture worn lightly. It was easy to visualise Livadić entertaining his artistic friends, including Franz Liszt, in this august setting. As well as the graceful architectural legacy of the Austro-Hungarian monarchy, this rolling green landscape is crisscrossed with forested trails, particularly within the Žumberak nature park, about 16 miles (26km) west of Samobor, where weekenders from Zagreb come to hike and bike in woods of hornbeam, oak and beech with bubbling waterfalls. Not having time for a full-on hike, I could still drive to Potočna dolina Slapnica, near the Vranjak waterfalls, and scramble up the path beside a series of cascades each more impressive than the last. Closer to Samobor, the hilltop ruins of Okić castle rose to nearly 500m above sea level, one of the best-preserved romanesque fortifications in the country. The Mongols couldn’t defeat it, nor could the Ottoman Turks. Sadly, it defeated me when I attempted to hike to the top. Not realising there was a newer, easier path, I ended up on one that was little else but vertical tree roots. With a newly healed ankle and no phone signal, I thought it unwise to continue. But it’s on my list for next time. A much easier path to take was along the Plešivica wine road, where more than three dozen wineries were scattered on a heart-shaped route between the village of Plešivica (10 miles south-west of Samobor) and the town of Jastrebarsko. In a harmonious landscape that could out-Tuscany Tuscany, vineyards clung to steep slopes between forested hills, many producing the sparkling wine Plešivica is renowned for. I met Martina and Krešimir Ivančić, whose ancestors were given a noble title and coat of arms by the Austrian empress Maria Theresa in 1759. The griffin on the family crest inspired the name of the Griffin Winery, which came about when a Hungarian count gave them a licence to plant a vineyard in 1773. Martina took me to the covered patio of a wooden hut above the vineyards, a suitably bucolic place to taste an elegant and lightly fruity sparkling rose made from red portugieser grapes. We carried on in the extremely stylish tasting room, where plates of cured meats and cheeses accompanied glasses of full-bodied chardonnay. I was also offered copanjek, a thin savoury pastry pie of cheese and greens. “They’re very portable, so workers would take them to the vineyard,” Martina told me. This looked like the winemaker’s version of rudarska greblica, which I had tasted that morning in the village of Rude, about a 10-minute drive west of Samobor, and liked so much I had to have two. Filled with cheese and walnuts, carrots or greens, these used to be made by the wives of Rude’s long-gone miners. They’re such an integral part of the region that they have their own festival every July and have been given EU protected status. At Pekarnica Nikl, in Rude, I met Jelena and Andrejas Nikl, the only authorised bakers of this much adored speciality. Jelena acknowledged the responsibility of keeping up this tradition of rudarska greblica, especially with the paperwork that came with legal protection – but, she said, it was worth it. All around the Samobor Hills, people were holding fast to their heritage and infusing it with life. The Korak family is one of the most illustrious, with its Michelin-starred Korak winery and restaurant in Plešivica. Not a whiff of Michelin stuffiness or pretentiousness here, just the fourth and fifth generations of a family producing superb wine and making beautiful food in a serene setting facing the vineyards. Brother Bernard is chef (and has worked with Massimo Bottura of Italy’s Osteria Francescana and Ana Roš of Slovenia’s Hiša Franko); sister Vera is front of house; and parents Velimir and Mirjana tend the vines – even the siblings’ grandparents are still making cheese and pršut (prosciutto) for the restaurant. Bernard grows as much as he can – the rest comes from local producers, including the farmer whose pigs are fed on scraps from Bernard’s kitchen. And if it’s not in season, it’s not on the plate. My June visit rewarded me with a truffle tagliatelle, and clams and green beans in a caviar sauce, among other delicious dishes in a five-course tasting menu at €118 (a very reasonable price, and in keeping with the region’s overall lower prices). I could only imagine what delights autumn will bring, especially during the annual Wine Days festival in Jastrebarsko from 25-27 September. The Samobor Hills will be teeming with autumn truffles and mushrooms, and welcoming the change in season the best way they know – on the plate. item.title: Solo autumn walks for women in the UK and Europe: ‘it should be fun, not daunting’
item.description:
Source: The Guardian Travel Score: 2.02
I did my first solo hike during a sunny September, seven years ago. After a summer of feeding and ferrying four noisy teenagers (and their friends) around, I was exhausted. But despite being bone tired, I had barely moved. I yearned, above all, for time on my own, for the chance to walk without interruption (and at the pace I chose), and for the silence of some empty wilderness. But I was nervous. Not of being on my own, but of what might happen to me with no one around to help (breaking a bone, encountering a psychopath, being chased by a bull, getting fatally lost). I could have found a companion or joined a group, but my need for silence and solitude outweighed my fears. It seems that many women feel the same: in the UK, the proportion of women solo hiking surged by 27% between 2020 and 2022. In America, 41 % of female hikers report regularly walking alone. And yet many women, although keen to do something similar, feel intimidated. According to researchers at the Munich University of Applied Sciences who are studying solo female walkers, 30% of women interviewed said they would like to hike solo but are hesitant. In truth, women have long enjoyed a tradition of solo walking. From religious pilgrims to goat herders to 19th-century adventurers, there have always been women wandering, radically alone, through wild landscapes. But for those new to it, I’d say the best way to overcome your fear is to do it – and I’ve learned some simple ways to make the experience fun, not daunting. That first solo hike followed a French canal. It was beautiful but sometimes felt a little too abandoned. It was also bereft of facilities, and frequently involved a long, complicated walk to my accommodation. So here are some of the things I now look for in a route: no discomfort-inducing stretches of urban wasteland; wide open landscapes (ridgeways, cliffs and hilltops are favourites); excellently waymarked, well-maintained paths (like national trails); navigation-lite routes that follow rivers, (lively) canals or coastlines; and countries/regions with a tradition of hiking. I do my research with care, and I’ve always returned home exhilarated, revitalised and high on my own bravado. I’ve learned to avoid the trails where I might feel uncomfortable. I know now which landscapes calm me, and which trails are (almost) impossible to lose my way on. For the last seven years, I’ve walked solo every autumn. Indeed, autumn is the perfect time for a liberating, empowering and restorative (solo) hike. Falling leaves improve visibility, temperatures are pleasant, and the days are still long enough to ensure I can reach my destination before dark. Importantly, there are lots of other walkers around – but without summer’s hordes – and the landscape is autumnally crisp and colourful. If you’re new to solo walking, start with a single day. If you want to try walking for multiple days, consider paying for your luggage to be transported (or use a specialist tour operator who will plot your route, arrange accommodation and move bags). Otherwise pack as lightly as possible. Take a non-digital map and a stick/walking poles, and let someone know your arrival time. Study every aspect of your route – including transport options and the weather – before you set off. FOUR GREAT ROUTES FOR SOLO HIKERS The Bernese Oberland, Switzerland The Swiss Alps are one of my favourite places to walk alone. Swiss women are keen solo hikers (so no one bats an eyelid at yet another single woman), the waymarking is superb and the scenery is jaw-dropping. Because this is a nation of farmers and hikers, there are always people (and a phone signal) around. And yet – because of the mountainous terrain – there’s often a genuine sense of wilderness and solitude. The Bernese Oberland is overrun with tourists in summer, but come to this Unesco world heritage site in autumn and you’ll be walking, calmly, in the footsteps of dozens of 19th-century women who once came here specifically to hike alone. Base yourself in the car-free villages of Wengen or Mürren, and expect to find farm-cafes with homemade cakes and honesty boxes in the remotest of spots. The South Downs Way From Eastbourne To Kingston, near Lewes Time 2 days Distance 19 miles The UK has plenty of well-kept trails, but top of my list is the (expansive, clearly signposted) South Downs Way. In summer the Eastbourne to Alfriston clifftop stretch heaves with tourists, but in autumn you’ll share the panoramic views – dazzling sea, dramatic chalk cliffs – with a handful of dogwalkers. Just a few steps off the trail are cultural hotspots like the pretty village of Alfriston, Charleston Farmhouse (museum home of the Bloomsbury set), and Rodmell, where you can visit Virginia Woolf’s house. So you’ll never feel completely disconnected. The Cleveland Way From Saltburn To Filey Time 4 days Distance 52 miles The Cleveland Way was the UK’s second official national trail, meaning the route is well maintained, the signage is excellent and the scenery is glorious, covering coastline and windblown moors. The moors can feel bleakly exposed in the wrong weather, so opt for the four-day coastal section, Saltburn to Filey, with its quirky towns and villages. This is Yorkshire so expect plenty of conversation with passing walkers and the chance to feel romantically windswept – an intoxicating blend for the solo hiker who wants to feel alone in nature, but not too alone. The Fishermen’s Trail, southern Portugal From Praia da Luz To Sagres Time 3 days Distance 27 miles The Fishermen’s Trail is far too hot in summer, but when I went (November) the temperature was just right, the sea was warm enough to swim in, and there were enough solo female hikers to feel pleasantly companioned. With some rocky scrambling to make one feel suitably youthful, and sufficient sandy coves to squeeze in a siesta, this route (a chain of old fishing villages) also has abundant, inexpensive accommodation and fresh seafood galore. Like other sea-hugging routes it’s (mostly) impossible to get lost – just follow the coastline. I’ll leave the last word to writer Mathilde Blind, who (aged 19) walked alone through the Bernese Oberland in 1860 (no phone, no GPS, no bra, no waterproof trousers): “For once I felt truly free.” Annabel Abbs is the author of The Walking Cure and Windswept: Why Women Walk. She was a guest of InnTravel on its Coastal Algarve and Fishermen’s Trail route, and of MACS Adventures on its Highlights of the Bernese Oberland route. item.title: Chase Sapphire Reserve turns 10 with massive point giveaway, new credits and bigger DoorDash perk
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy Score: 5.82
Chase Sapphire Reserve turns 10 with massive point giveaway, new credits and bigger DoorDash perk The Chase Sapphire Reserve® (see rates and fees) is celebrating its 10th birthday — and it's doing so by handing out presents to cardholders. Those include a grand prize of a staggering 5.5 million Chase Ultimate Rewards points for one lucky cardholder, a bundle of limited-time travel offers and an increased monthly DoorDash credit that begins Oct. 1. Here's what Sapphire Reserve cardholders need to know about the increased DoorDash credit, new limited-time travel credits and the massive points giveaway. Increased monthly DoorDash credit on the Sapphire Reserve Currently, the Sapphire Reserve provides complimentary DoorDash DashPass* ($120 annual value), two $10 monthly DoorDash promos that can be used on grocery or retail DoorDash orders (but not traditional restaurant orders) and a $5 monthly DoorDash credit that can be used on eligible restaurant orders. Beginning Oct. 1, the Sapphire Reserve will increase the current $5 monthly credit to a $15 monthly credit that is eligible for use on all DoorDash orders, including restaurant orders. That will be offered in addition to the existing DoorDash-related benefits. That means eligible Sapphire Reserve DoorDash DashPass members can receive up to $35 in DoorDash value each month. *Must activate membership by Dec. 31, 2027 The more flexible $15 monthly DoorDash credit on the Sapphire Reserve is now quite similar to the up to $15 monthly (up to $35 in December) Uber Cash benefit on the American Express Platinum Card®, valid on Uber rides and Uber Eats orders in the U.S. (Note: Uber Cash will only be deposited into one Uber account when you add the Amex Platinum as a payment method and redeem with any Amex card.) Assuming you are as likely to use the increased credit as I am, this increases the value of the credits on this card by a full $120 a year, which is not insignificant. New one-time travel credits on the Sapphire Reserve In addition to the increased DoorDash credit, Chase is rolling out five limited-time travel offers to celebrate the Sapphire Reserve's 10th anniversary. Activation is required, and cardholders must complete payment by the applicable deadline to receive the offer. | Brand | Spending requirement | Offer | Deadline | |---|---|---|---| | IHG Hotels & Resorts stay | At least $500 | $125 credit back | Oct. 16 | | Miraval and Alila stay | At least $1,000 | $250 credit back | Dec. 14 | | JSX semiprivate flight | At least $200 | $200 credit back | Dec. 14 | | Sixt car rental | At least $500 | $125 credit back | Dec. 14 | | Wander vacation home rental | At least $1,500 | $350 credit back | Dec. 14 | The IHG offer applies to eligible U.S. stays, while the Miraval and Alila offer applies to eligible U.S. stays at participating World of Hyatt properties. You must have been a cardmember prior to Aug. 25, 2026 for the Sixt car rental offer. The terms also indicate that each of these requires payment directly with the retailer and isn't valid with bookings made via Chase Travel℠. That distinction is especially important with IHG. Sapphire Reserve cardholders already have access to a separate one-time $250 hotel statement credit through the end of 2026 for eligible prepaid hotel stays with select brands, including IHG, booked through Chase Travel. Since the new 10th-anniversary IHG offer requires booking directly with IHG, it appears you wouldn't be able to stack the two credits for the same stay under the terms. Related: Chase Sapphire Reserve statement credits: What they are and how to use them Enter to win up to 5.5 million Ultimate Rewards points Last but not least — especially if you win — is a contest that will award nine finalists 500,000 Chase points and one grand-prize winner 5.5 million Chase Ultimate Rewards points. To enter, cardmembers can post about their favorite trip since 2016 (the year the Sapphire Reserve launched) for a chance to recreate it with the Chase Sapphire Reserve. Ten finalists will advance to a public voting phase, with the grand-prize winner taking home 5.5 million points. Based on TPG's September 2026 valuations, 5.5 million Ultimate Rewards points would be worth an impressive $112,750, while 500,000 points would be worth a still-outstanding $10,250. The full contest rules and details can be found here. Bottom line The Sapphire Reserve was an absolute game changer when it sprang onto the rewards scene in 2016, and Chase is marking its 10th anniversary with several new ways for cardholders to get additional value. The limited-time travel offers could provide meaningful savings for cardholders who already have eligible purchases planned, while the winners of 500,000 to 5.5 million points are obviously sure to be thrilled. But the expansion of the DoorDash credit is especially good news, as that perk will stick around even after the card's birthday candles are blown out. To learn more, read our full review of the Chase Sapphire Reserve. Apply here: Chase Sapphire Reserve

item.title: Wyndham Rewards guide: How to earn and redeem points, elite status and more
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy Score: 5.74
Wyndham Rewards guide: How to earn and redeem points, elite status and more Wyndham Rewards is one of the lesser-known hotel loyalty programs, especially when compared to major players like Marriott Bonvoy and Hilton Honors. But Wyndham Rewards has been making some major changes in 2026, including refreshing its cobranded cards and launching a premium card in June and switching to a four-tier award chart on Sept. 15. Plus, Chase Ultimate Rewards added Wyndham as a transfer partner in February, and Wells Fargo Rewards added it in April. With all these changes, here's what you need to know about the Wyndham Rewards loyalty program. What is Wyndham Rewards? Wyndham Rewards is the loyalty program for Wyndham Hotels & Resorts, which has around 8,400 hotels across 25 brands in about 100 countries. Wyndham includes budget-friendly brands like Howard Johnson, Super 8, Days Inn and Travelodge, as well as higher-end brands like Wyndham Grand, Esplendor Boutique Hotels and Registry Collection Hotels. But, despite the name, Echo Suites Extended Stay by Wyndham hotels don't participate in Wyndham Rewards. Although it has a sizable worldwide footprint, Wyndham Rewards doesn't offer as many elite benefits as other programs. However, earning Wyndham points is easy, and the program maintains a four-tier award chart. Many of the ways to earn and redeem Wyndham Rewards points vary by country of residence. For simplicity, this guide assumes you reside in the U.S. Also, for simplicity, this guide discusses cardholder benefits for accounts opened on or after June 17; if you opened your Wyndham card earlier, your benefits may differ. Wyndham Rewards elite status Wyndham Rewards offers four standard member tiers, plus an invite-only Titanium status that's primarily for hotel owners. You'll progress to higher standard elite tiers as you complete qualifying nights at Wyndham Hotels & Resorts properties each calendar year. | | Annual requirements | Incremental perks | Cards and subscriptions that offer this status as a perk | |---|---|---|---| | Blue | None | Free Wi-Fi and rollover elite nights | None | | Gold | Five nights | Preferred room choice, 10% bonus points on stays and late checkout | | | Platinum | 15 nights | Early check-in and 15% bonus points on stays | | | Diamond | 40 nights | Suite upgrades, a welcome amenity and 20% bonus points on stays | | The information for the Wyndham Rewards Earner Card, the Wyndham Rewards Debit Card, the Wyndham Rewards Earner Plus Card, the Wyndham Rewards Earner Premier Card and the Wyndham Rewards Earner Business Card has been collected independently by The Points Guy. The card details on this page have not been reviewed or provided by the card issuer. Once you earn Wyndham status through qualifying nights, you'll keep it through the end of the calendar year after you earned it. You'll usually need to book directly with Wyndham to get elite earnings and benefits. However, some stays booked through independent travel agents can qualify if booked at loyalty-eligible rates. Wyndham Blue status All Wyndham Rewards members start at the Blue membership tier, and there aren't any requirements you must meet to maintain this tier. Blue members can get free Wi-Fi, earn points on stays, roll over qualifying nights to the next calendar year and access member rates. Wyndham Gold status Wyndham Rewards members earn Gold status after completing five qualifying nights in a calendar year. Additionally, cardholders of the Wyndham Rewards Earner Card and the Wyndham Rewards Debit Card get Wyndham Gold status automatically, as do Wyndham Rewards Insider members. In addition to the perks offered to Blue members, Gold members get their preferred room choice within the category they've booked, 10% bonus points on stays and late checkout up to two hours past the standard checkout time (upon request and subject to availability). Wyndham Platinum status Earning Wyndham Platinum status requires just 15 qualifying nights per calendar year. Additionally, cardholders of the Wyndham Rewards Earner Plus Card receive Wyndham Platinum status as a cardholder perk after their first year (but Diamond status for their first year). In addition to the perks offered to Gold members, Platinum members receive a 15% bonus on points for stays and early check-in up to two hours before the standard check-in time (upon request and subject to availability). Platinum members can also enjoy rental car upgrades through Alamo, National and Enterprise at participating locations in the U.S. and Canada, and status match to Caesars Rewards each year (only if your Wyndham status is earned through stays). Wyndham Diamond status After staying 40 nights per calendar year, Wyndham members earn Diamond elite status. Additionally, cardholders of the Wyndham Rewards Earner Premier Card and the Wyndham Rewards Earner Business Card get Wyndham Diamond status automatically. Plus, cardholders of the Wyndham Rewards Earner Plus Card receive Diamond status for their first year. In addition to the perks offered to Platinum members, Wyndham Diamond members get 20% bonus points on stays, suite upgrades (upon request and subject to availability), a complimentary snack or beverage when staying at select hotel brands and the ability to give Gold status to a family member or friend once per calendar year (only if you earn your Wyndham status through stays). Wyndham Rewards Insider subscription You can buy an annual Wyndham Rewards Insider subscription for $95 per year. In return, the perks of the subscription include: - At least 10% off the standard rate at Hotels by Wyndham when you book directly - Wyndham Gold status - Discounts on travel bundle bookings - Discounted cruise rates and theme park tickets - A one-time 7,500-point welcome bonus Status match to Wyndham You can match select elite status tiers with other hotel loyalty programs to Wyndham Rewards once per calendar year. Specifically, here's which hotel elite status tiers match which Wyndham Rewards tiers: | | Match to Wyndham Gold | Match to Wyndham Platinum | Match to Wyndham Diamond | |---|---|---|---| | Best Western Rewards | Blue | Gold, Platinum and Diamond | Diamond Select | | Choice Privileges | Member | Gold and Platinum | Diamond | | Hilton Honors | Member | Silver | Gold and higher | | IHG One Rewards | Member | Silver Elite and Gold Elite | Platinum Elite and higher | | Marriott Bonvoy | Member | Silver Elite | Gold Elite and higher | | Omni Select Guest | Insider | Champion | Ikon | | Radisson Rewards | Club | Premium | VIP | | World of Hyatt | Member | Discoverist and Explorist | Globalist | To request a status match, go to this page, sign into your Wyndham Rewards account and complete the status match request form (including submitting proof of your elite status in another program). Then you should be awarded Wyndham status within five to seven days of submitting the form. Once you have the matched status, you'll keep the status for 90 days. But if you complete a specific number of qualifying nights within 90 days, you'll keep the status through Dec. 31 of the next calendar year. Specifically, if you matched to Gold, one qualifying night within 90 days will let you keep Gold through the end of the next calendar year. Likewise, four qualifying nights will let you keep a matched Platinum status, and 10 qualifying nights will let you keep a matched Diamond status. Related: Complete guide to current hotel elite status match and challenge offers Is Wyndham status worth it? Wyndham Rewards elite status can be useful, but it's usually not worth striving to earn it through hotel stays. Even Diamond status, which requires 40 qualifying nights per calendar year, only provides a 20% bonus on points earned from stays, along with perks like space-available suite upgrades and a welcome amenity. By comparison, Hilton Honors Silver members get a 20% points bonus after just 10 nights, while World of Hyatt Explorist members get a 20% bonus after 30 nights. Marriott Bonvoy members earn Gold Elite status after 25 nights and receive a 25% points bonus. Higher tiers with Hilton, Marriott and Hyatt also tend to offer more valuable on-property perks, such as breakfast or lounge access. That said, Wyndham status is relatively easy to get without staying dozens of nights. Several Wyndham cards provide elite status as a perk, and Wyndham also offers a status match from many competing hotel loyalty programs. So, while you likely shouldn't book stays just to earn Wyndham status, it's certainly worth using the benefits if you can get status through a card, status match or stays you'd complete anyway. How to earn Wyndham points There are a few different ways you can earn Wyndham points. Here's an overview of your options. Earn Wyndham points on stays On qualifying stays, Wyndham Rewards members earn as follows: - 10 points per dollar of room rate paid to the participating property: AmericInn, Baymont, Days Inn, Dazzler, Esplendor, Hawthorn Extended Stay, Howard Johnson, La Quinta, Microtel, Ramada, Registry Collection, Super 8, Trademark Collection, Travelodge, TRYP by Wyndham, Vienna House by Wyndham, Wingate by Wyndham, Wyndham Alltra, participating Caesars Rewards properties and participating destinations - 10 points per dollar of total folio paid to the participating hotel: Applicable Dolce Hotels and Resorts, Wyndham Grand, Wyndham Hotels and Resorts (including Viva Wyndham properties) and Wyndham Garden properties - 5 points per dollar of room rate paid to the participating hotel: WaterWalk Extended Stay by Wyndham (only qualified stays in furnished suites) When staying at most Wyndham Hotels & Resorts or participating vacation club resorts, your earnings are rounded up to 1,000 points per qualifying stay if you would otherwise have earned less based on your room rate or total folio. You can earn points for up to three rooms or condos per night by associating your member number with each one. Gold, Platinum and Diamond members earn a percentage bonus on their base earnings from qualifying Wyndham stays. Specifically, Gold members get a 10% bonus, Platinum members get a 15% bonus and Diamond members get a 20% bonus. Wyndham Rewards also occasionally offers promotions that let you earn bonus points on stays. So keep an eye out for Wyndham promotions and register even if you aren't sure you'll have any qualifying stays during the promotion period. Finally, remember that bookings through third-party online travel agencies usually aren't qualifying. So, book your Wyndham stays on the Wyndham website or app to ensure you'll earn points and enjoy elite status benefits. Related: How I earned 24,500 points from $180 in hotel stays Earn points with cobranded Wyndham cards Wyndham Rewards offers several cobranded credit cards and a cobranded debit card. To earn Wyndham points on everyday purchases, review the Wyndham cards and determine which best fits your spending habits. - Wyndham Rewards Debit Card: 1 point per dollar spent on eligible purchases made at participating Hotels by Wyndham and qualifying gas and grocery purchases, and 1 point per $2 spent on all other qualifying purchases (earnings capped at 7,500 bonus points each anniversary year) - Wyndham Rewards Earner Card: 5 points per dollar spent on eligible purchases made at Hotels by Wyndham (including hotels through Wyndham travel bundles); 3 points per dollar spent on eligible vacation club, dining and grocery store purchases (excluding Target and Walmart), as well as eligible gas and electric vehicle charging purchases; and 1 point per dollar spent on all other purchases (excluding Vacation Club down payments) - Wyndham Rewards Earner Plus Card: 6 points per dollar spent on eligible purchases made at Hotels by Wyndham (including hotels through Wyndham travel bundles); 4 points per dollar spent on eligible vacation club, travel, dining and grocery store purchases (excluding Target and Walmart); and 1 point per dollar spent on all other purchases (excluding vacation club down payments) - Wyndham Rewards Earner Premier Card: 8 points per dollar spent on eligible purchases made at Hotels by Wyndham (including hotels through Wyndham travel bundles); 4 points per dollar spent on eligible vacation club, travel, dining and grocery store purchases (excluding Target and Walmart); and 1 point per dollar spent on all other purchases (excluding vacation club down payments) - Wyndham Rewards Earner Business Card: 8 points per dollar spent on eligible purchases made at Hotels by Wyndham (including Wyndham travel bundles); 5 points per dollar spent on eligible vacation club, gas, EV charging, marketing, advertising, office supply store and shipping purchases; and 1 point per dollar spent on all other purchases (excluding vacation club down payments) These cards are great for earning Wyndham points, especially if you spend a lot at participating Hotels by Wyndham or on Wyndham travel bundles. Plus, some of these cards give cardholders bonus points each anniversary year after payment of the annual fee. These bonus points could get you a few free nights and can partially — and, in some cases, fully — offset the card's annual fee. | Card | Annual fee | Anniversary bonus points | Value of bonus points based on TPG's September 2026 valuation | |---|---|---|---| | Wyndham Rewards Earner Plus Card | $95 | 15,000 | $105 | | Wyndham Rewards Earner Premier Card | $395 | 30,000 | $210 | | Wyndham Rewards Earner Business Card | $149 | 15,000 | $105 | Related: Which of the 4 Wyndham Rewards credit cards is right for you? Transfer rewards to Wyndham You can transfer several types of transferable rewards currencies to Wyndham Rewards at the following ratios: - Bilt: 1:1 - Capital One miles: 1:1 - Chase Ultimate Rewards: 1:1 - Citi ThankYou Rewards: 1:1 for ThankYou cards with annual fees and 1:0.7 for ThankYou cards with no annual fee - Wells Fargo Rewards: 1:2 The most favorable transfer ratio is offered by Wells Fargo Rewards. But in each case, other transfer partners may give you more value for your rewards.
