You shouldn't value these credits at face value unless they fit your existing spending, but frequent AA flyers who can use several of them naturally may offset a meaningful portion of the card's $695 annual fee. To learn more, read our full review of the Citi / AAdvantage Executive. Apply here: Citi / AAdvantage Executive World Legend Mastercard

item.title: Air France to open one of New York JFK's biggest lounges at new Terminal One
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy Score: 3.95
Air France to open one of New York JFK's biggest lounges at new Terminal One New York's newest airport terminal is months away from opening at John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK). And we just learned who scored the biggest lounge space. Air France plans to open a sprawling, 29,000 square foot club at JFK's new Terminal One, the airline announced Tuesday. It will be the French flag carrier's biggest lounge outside of Paris — and roughly triple the size of its current outpost in the airport's existing Terminal 1. Air France's new JFK lounge The new Air France Lounge will be one of the largest in any terminal at JFK — though the massive Delta One Lounge in Terminal 4 still reigns supreme at the airport. A sneak peek rendering of the club shared with TPG Tuesday shows a white and navy blue color palette that's been a staple in the newest lounges that Air France has opened (or renovated) in recent years. The facility is expected to span two levels inside the new terminal building, with space for more than 400 flyers. It will feature dining, working and relaxation areas — including a space Air France said it's reserving for "beauty treatments." Plus, the facility will include an exclusive dining area for meals whipped up by a "renowned French chef." How to access the Air France lounge at JFK Access will be limited to Air France and KLM passengers who book a seat in business class — or fly to Charles de Gaulle Airport (CDG) in Air France's luxe La Premier cabin on the Boeing 777-300ER. The new facility should certainly be a more worthy complement to the airline's most luxe premium seat in New York, which features on multiple daily flights from JFK. SkyTeam elites, too Plus, members who reach SkyTeam alliance Elite Plus status can enter when flying on an eligible itinerary. (For Delta SkyMiles members, that's Gold Medallion status and above). A brand-new Terminal One This new Air France lounge comes as part of the larger multibillion-dollar Terminal One that's currently in the final stages of construction. The new Terminal One is slated to replace the airport's existing Terminal 1 facility. And Air France is expected to be largest airline at the new terminal, thanks to its half-dozen daily roundtrips between JFK and Paris. "Air France's investment in our terminal's biggest lounge represents a strong vote of confidence in the seamless and modern travel experience we are building," new Terminal One CEO Jennifer Aument said in a statement Tuesday. The new building will also be home to a handful of other major global carriers, including Etihad, SAS, EVA and Turkish Airlines. Once the new facility opens, Qatar also plans to make the jump to the Terminal One from its current home in Terminal 8, the airport's main Oneworld alliance hub. Qatar is planning its own luxe club for the new JFK building — though it will be about half the size of Air France's new digs. In all, the new Terminal One is expected to house at least six lounges, including an arrivals lounge. How to book Air France flights with points and miles Travelers hoping to book Air France flights with miles have a wide range of options. Most major transferable credit card and rewards programs offer direct transfers to Flying Blue, the loyalty program it shares with sister carrier KLM. That includes 1:1 transfers from programs like American Express, Bilt Rewards and Chase. Plus, you can also book Air France flights using Delta SkyMiles, since the two carriers are partners. Bottom line Despite Tuesday's lounge news, the opening date for the new terminal itself has slipped a bit. A spokesperson for the new terminal tells TPG the facility is now on track to open during the first quarter of 2027. That's a delay from the previous 2026 timeline. "We want to ensure that all systems and processes are well-tested and prepared to deliver on our commitment to set a new standard in customer experience, from day one," the company said in a statement. Related reading:

item.title: The highest-ever Chase-to-Marriott transfer bonus is back: Get 70% more Marriott Bonvoy points
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy Score: 3.75
The highest-ever Chase-to-Marriott transfer bonus is back: Get 70% more Marriott Bonvoy points Good news: The highest Marriott Bonvoy transfer bonus we've ever seen is officially back. From now through Oct. 15, you can get a 70% bonus when transferring Chase Ultimate Rewards points to Marriott Bonvoy. This means if you transferred 100,000 Chase points from cards such as the Chase Sapphire Preferred® Card (see rates and fees) to Marriott, you'd get 170,000 Marriott points instead of the 100,000 points you'd usually get with the normal 1:1 ratio. This is the most generous Marriott transfer bonus we've seen this year, and it ties the highest transfer bonus we've ever seen. Here's how to make the most of this limited-time Chase-to-Marriott transfer bonus and how to decide if it is a good deal for you. Related: Current credit card transfer bonuses Deals available with the 70% Marriott transfer bonus To get you thinking about what is possible, here are a few award stays you could book with this 70% Chase-to-Marriott transfer bonus. Stay within walking distance of Walt Disney World for as low as 36,000 transferred Chase points per night On nights when it is just 60,000 Marriott Bonvoy points per night to stay at the Walt Disney World Swan Reserve, a Marriott hotel that's within walking distance of (or a free boat ride away from) Disney's Hollywood Studios and Epcot, it would cost you just 36,000 transferred Chase points with the 70% bonus. Note that, like at all other Marriott properties, you are still responsible for any resort or destination fees, even when you are staying on points at this and other Marriott properties — we'll circle back to that point shortly. Enjoy an overwater bungalow in Bora Bora from 50,000 transferred Chase points per night Award prices at The Westin Bora Bora Resort & Spa currently start around 84,000 Marriott points per night for a variety of room types, including its iconic overwater bungalows. With the 70% transfer bonus, these bungalows are bookable starting from 50,000 transferred Chase points per night, a solid rate for a stay in absolute paradise. Head to Hawaii for as low as 34,000 transferred Chase points per night You can stay at the fun, colorful Laylow Waikiki, Autograph Collection in Honolulu from just 34,000 transferred Chase points per night, as this 70% transfer bonus will get you the needed 57,000 points to cover a night at the property. If that's not the hotel for you, though, there are plenty of other Marriott properties in the Waikiki area, including the iconic 125-year-old Moana Surfrider, A Westin Resort & Spa, Waikiki Beach, which would also start at 34,000 transferred Chase points per night since it also has some nights that are bookable for 57,000 Marriott points. Have a luxe stay in New York from 63,000 transferred Chase points per night There are plenty of fancy Marriott properties in the Big Apple, but if you want one of the newest and swankiest, you might want to check out The Ritz-Carlton New York, NoMad. For a stay that's more elegant and classic, choose the timeless St. Regis New York. No matter how you slice it, both are pricey hotels, but with the 70% transfer bonus, rooms start at 60,000 transferred Chase points per night at the former and 63,000 transferred Chase points per night at the latter to get you the needed 102,000 and 106,000 points, respectively. Remember, though, that some nights will cost more. How to tell if you should transfer Chase points to Marriott with this bonus Booking a beloved theme park hotel for 36,000 transferred points a night or a bucket list-worthy stay in an overwater bungalow for 50,000 transferred points per night sounds pretty great — and it absolutely can be a tremendous deal. But even with a historically high 70% transfer bonus, moving Chase Ultimate Rewards points to Marriott Bonvoy won't always be your best option. Since point transfers are one way, you'll want to do a little math before hitting that transfer button. TPG currently values Chase points at 2.05 cents each based on our September 2026 valuations because of all the valuable transfer partners you can use them with, while Marriott Bonvoy points are worth 0.75 cents each based on TPG's September 2026 valuations. So, even with a 70% bonus, you are turning 1 Chase point worth 2.05 cents into 1.7 Marriott points worth about 1.3 cents. Average valuations are not the same thing as individual use cases, though. What really matters is how many Chase points — or even how much cash — it will cost to book the specific hotel you want. Before deciding to transfer points, make sure you: - Check the cash rate. You may not want to transfer a large number of valuable Chase points for a hotel that's relatively inexpensive to book with cash. - Check the hotel's price through Chase Travel℠. Depending on the Chase card you have and the hotel you're eyeing, your Chase points may be worth 1 cent each or closer to 2 cents each if the stay is eligible to book via Chase's Points Boost feature. - Check the Marriott award price directly on Marriott's site and divide it by 1.7. That's approximately how many Chase points you'll need to transfer during this 70% bonus. For example, if a hotel costs 60,000 Marriott points, divide 60,000 by 1.7 to get roughly 36,000 transferred Chase points. Then, compare your options. If Marriott wants 60,000 points for a room that would cost 50,000 Chase points through Chase Travel, transferring roughly 36,000 Chase points during this bonus could be the better option. But if Chase Travel only requires 30,000 points for the same room, transferring wouldn't make as much sense. There are a couple of other factors to consider, too. Marriott Bonvoy members get the lowest-priced night free when redeeming points for five consecutive nights, which can make transferring an even better option for longer stays. However, Marriott award stays can still come with resort or destination fees, so be sure to factor them into your comparison. And remember: An elevated transfer bonus like this one can be especially useful if you already have most of the Marriott points required for a specific redemption and just need to top off your account. I wouldn't recommend transferring points to Marriott speculatively without a specific redemption in mind, though, since Marriott award prices fluctuate. Related: 30 of the best Marriott hotels in the world that you can book with points How to earn more Chase points I like to have some of each major loyalty currency available for moments like this when high transfer bonuses come around. If you don't currently have Chase points available, you can be ready for potential future transfer bonuses if you start earning valuable Chase Ultimate Rewards points now via one of these cards: - Chase Sapphire Preferred Card: Earn 75,000 bonus points after spending $5,000 on purchases in the first three months from account opening. - Chase Sapphire Reserve® (see rates and fees): Earn 100,000 bonus points after spending $6,000 on purchases in the first three months from account opening. - Chase Sapphire Reserve for Business℠ (see rates and fees): Earn 200,000 bonus points after spending $30,000 on purchases in the first six months from account opening. Related: Best Chase credit cards Bottom line If you are planning Marriott stays on points, then it absolutely makes sense to run some award searches and see if this limited-time, highest-ever transfer bonus from Chase Ultimate Rewards to Marriott Bonvoy might help you unlock your travel goals. Even though the transfer bonus is the highest we have seen for Marriott, it won't always be the best deal for any specific trip, given how valuable Chase points are. That said, there are absolutely times when the math will be on your side to hit that transfer button, so crunch some numbers to see if you can book the stay you've been dreaming of for fewer points than you thought. Related reading:

item.title: Qantas’ A380 isn’t the newest way to fly — but kangaroo pajamas and an onboard lounge make it a treat
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy Score: 3.63
Qantas’ A380 isn’t the newest way to fly — but kangaroo pajamas and an onboard lounge make it a treat Quick take: Qantas continues to offer a solid business-class experience for long flights across the Pacific, but inflight Wi-Fi can't come soon enough. Pros - Seats are comfortable and have decent privacy. - Extensive menus offer diverse choices. - There's a fun onboard lounge space for passengers to enjoy. Cons - Award availability is very limited. - There's currently no Wi-Fi, so prepare to be offline. - The large cabin means meal service can take a while. The first Airbus A380 I ever flew was a Qantas aircraft way back in 2009, shortly after the airline started taking delivery of these double-decker jumbo jets. Since then, I've seen these planes evolve from newfangled novelties into long-haul workhorses not just for Qantas, but with several other carriers, too, including Emirates and Singapore Airlines. I have tracked its shifts from a time when it was hailed as the future of long-haul aviation, thanks to its enormous passenger capacity and flight range, to an uneconomic boondoggle that many thought was doomed to the fossil heap during the COVID-19 pandemic. The A380 endures, though, and Qantas currently has 10 of them in service, so it still holds a special place in my heart. I've been able to fly it dozens of times on many trips between the U.S. and Australia. My most recent flight was actually from Los Angeles to Melbourne at the kickoff of my honeymoon, when I got to experience Qantas business class for the first time in a few years. Here's how I booked my ticket and how the experience rates these days. How much does it cost to book Qantas business class? The cost of a Qantas long-haul, business-class ticket depends on the route, dates and whether you're flying round-trip or one-way. My one-way flight from Los Angeles International Airport (LAX) to Melbourne Airport (MEL) would have cost between $4,600 and $5,800 the week I flew. I was able to book an award ticket, though, with the option to use Alaska Airlines Atmos Rewards points or American Airlines AAdvantage miles. Here's a quick look at how my award ticket was priced across the two programs and Qantas' own Frequent Flyer program. | Frequent-flyer program | Miles and taxes | |---|---| | Alaska Airlines Atmos Rewards | 85,000 plus $36 | | American Airlines AAdvantage | 80,000 plus $24 | | Qantas Frequent Flyer | 151,800 plus $364 | Given the cost savings, I normally would have booked my ticket using American AAdvantage miles. However, I actually had many more Alaska Atmos Rewards points at the time, so I used those instead. Alaska Airlines is a 1:1 transfer partner of Bilt. You can also transfer Marriott Bonvoy points to Alaska at a 3:1 ratio. The best way to stock up on Alaska Airlines Atmos Rewards points quickly, however, is to apply for one of the following cobranded credit cards: - Atmos™ Rewards Ascent Visa Signature® credit card - Atmos™ Rewards Summit Visa Infinite® credit card - Atmos™ Rewards Visa Signature® Business Card If you do want to use American Airlines miles, the following cobranded credit cards are a great way to accrue miles quickly: The information for the AAdvantage Platinum Select has been collected independently by The Points Guy. The card details on this page have not been reviewed or provided by the card issuer. While the Qantas Frequent Flyer redemption rates were not a great option, I did consider it since Capital One was running a 20% transfer bonus to the program at the time; so, I would have only needed 121,440 Capital One miles. That said, although Capital One transfers to Qantas tend to be nearly instantaneous in my experience, I didn't want to chance the transfer taking too long and losing out on the award seat. That's because Qantas business-class award tickets available to book using partner miles are extremely rare. The airline seems to release a handful each month, typically in tranches (meaning a few award tickets become available on the same day for multiple dates over the following month or so). So if you find a seat, book it fast. I use tools like Seats.aero to monitor award tickets over multiple months at a time and get notifications when they become available, so I can book them quickly. Just one quick note on aircraft and routes: Qantas deploys both the A380 and the 787-9 on its Los Angeles-Melbourne route, and the airline will switch to solely 787-9s in October 2026. Checking into and boarding Qantas business class Qantas long-haul business-class passengers can enjoy the following priority services at the airport. | Priority check-in | Yes | |---|---| | Luggage allowance | Two checked bags up to 70 pounds (32 kg) each | | Lounge access | Yes | | Does the airline participate in TSA PreCheck? | Yes | | Priority boarding | Yes | My Qantas flight was scheduled to depart at 9:50 p.m. from LAX's Tom Bradley International Terminal. I arrived at the airport at 7 p.m., when the departure hall was pretty quiet, and there were only a few passengers in the dedicated business- and first-class lines. There were no lines at security, and thanks to TSA PreCheck, I was airside within just a few minutes of arriving at the airport. Qantas business-class passengers can use the Oneworld lounge on the fifth floor — a massive space with a capacity of nearly 600 guests and open to premium passengers from various airlines, including British Airways and Cathay Pacific. When I flew, the lounge had also converted a space near the bar by the entrance into a makeshift first-class dining room since the airline's permanent first-class lounge was under renovation. My flight departed from the 200 gates in the terminal's western concourse, which is a brisk 15-minute walk from the lounge, so I gave myself plenty of time to get over there. Boarding was right on time at 9:05 p.m. How comfortable is Qantas business class? Qantas' long-haul fleet consists of Airbus A330s, A380s and Boeing 787-9 Dreamliners. Its first A350-1000 was recently delivered and will be equipped with all-new seating options for the ultra-long-haul "Project Sunrise" flights the jet will operate. On the other three aircraft types, however, the business-class seats are all based on the popular Thompson Aero Vantage XL model, which are forward-facing in a staggered 1-2-1 pattern. The 15-year-old A380 operating my flight had the tail number VH-OQK and was named after Australian aviation pioneers (and brothers) John and Reginald Duigan. Here's a snapshot of its business-class layout and dimensions. | Number of seats | 70 | |---|---| | Cabin layout | 1-2-1 | | Seat recline | 80 inches fully flat | | Seat width | 21 inches (24 in lie-flat mode) | | Screen size | 15.5 inches | The business-class section on Qantas' A380s took up nearly the entire upper deck, with a smaller cabin of just 20 seats up front and a larger cabin with 50 more seats behind the galley and lavatory. The seats were in a staggered 1-2-1 configuration, so every passenger had direct aisle access. The single seats on the sides were alternately closer or farther from the window due to the placement of a wide armrest. Those in the middle had a wide armrest between them as well as a raisable shield, so there was a fair amount of privacy; however, there were no sliding doors, which are becoming more popular (and which you'll see on Qantas' forthcoming A350s). The gap between the armrest and the preceding seat shell — in other words, the exit from the seat — was 10 inches. This doesn't sound like a lot, but it is still more than you find in some other similar fixtures. | Best seats for solo travelers | Odd-numbered A and K seats in the forward cabin, even ones in the back cabin | |---|---| | Best seats for couples | Any E and F seats | The airline's A380s underwent a refurbishment starting in 2019 that was extended due to the coronavirus pandemic, so these pods were the latest versions from the airline's industrial design partner, David Caon. The seats had a sharp aesthetic with charcoal-gray leather accents and upholstery with silvery dotted patterning, brushed metal shells and dark faux-wood paneling. The seat cushions were 18 inches wide at the shoulders, but I measured the distance between armrests at the hips to be 24 inches, so they feel very roomy. The wider armrest had some shelving for small items, plus a hook for headphones, a water bottle holder and a small reading light. This was also where I found a universal power plug and a USB-A port (no USB-C, I'm afraid). There was a panel with seat controls that included preset positions for takeoff and landing, lounging and lie-flat mode, as well as buttons to control the individual parts of the seat; I found this handy for getting into a just-right position. I could also control the ambient seat lighting and the small reading light using buttons on the panel, and I could illuminate a "Do Not Disturb" indicator if I wanted the crew to leave me be while I rested. There wasn't much other storage to speak of since I didn't have one of the single side seats; those seats actually had large bins set against the window for storing amenity kits, bedding and other belongings. The seat's tray table popped out horizontally from the wide armrest and measured about 11 inches by 19 inches — plenty of room for my laptop. In lie-flat mode, the seat stretched to an 80-inch bed, and I found it comfortable to sleep in various positions. The foot cubby was 14 inches wide at its mouth and 11 inches tall, so folks with bigger feet might find it a bit cramped. Each seat had two individual overhead air nozzles, which made it easy to control the temperature in my area, though the crew kept the cabin pleasantly cool throughout the flight. There were two lavatories in the center galley section between the two business-class cabins and two more behind the larger business-class cabin. Although the restroom-to-passenger ratio was pretty good, there were lines after meals. The crew kept them very clean throughout the flight, though. One of the things I like best about flying Qantas business and first class aboard the A380 is the swanky little lounge at the front of the upper deck for premium passengers. It features a long banquette with seat belts and a self-serve area to one side of the staircase leading down to the lower deck, and two tables with plugs and seat belts to the other, so you can gather with your travel companions for a quick hang. Amenities in Qantas business class Each business-class seat was provisioned with a bed set that included a lightweight duvet, a seat cover and a medium-size pillow. I found the inclusion of a seat cover especially nice, as it meant I didn't have to sleep directly on a surface countless other passengers had sat on. I also found a little amenity kit from Australian clothing and leather brand R.M. Williams, which was a nice Aussie touch. Inside, it included: - A bamboo toothbrush - Toothpaste - Eye mask - Warm socks - Ear plugs - Grown Alchemist vanilla-orange peel hand cream - Grown Alchemist vanilla-watermelon lip balm - Grown Alchemist geranium and camellia day cream Shortly after boarding, flight attendants came through offering passengers pajamas, and though a small-medium would have fit me (I'm 5 feet, 8 inches), I asked for a large-extra large because I like them roomy. The seat's entertainment screen was 15 1/2 inches across diagonally and had dozens of new movies and TV shows, including "The Devil Wears Prada 2," "Hoppers," and "The Super Mario Galaxy Movie." The screen tilted up and down to make viewing easier, whether sitting upright or reclined. The airline provided basic headphones that plugged into a jack near the USB port, but there was no way to connect my own headphones to the system via Bluetooth. Unfortunately, Qantas does not have Wi-Fi on its A380s, but the airline is starting to equip them with the service, with rollout across all 10 expected to be completed by mid-2027. How was the food in Qantas business class? When I boarded, I found both the main menu and breakfast menu waiting at my seat. Unlike some other airlines, Qantas does not offer a preorder option for its regular menus, though those with special dietary needs can order ahead. As folks got settled in, flight attendants passed through the cabin with trays of Jacquart Mosaique Brut Champagne and water. About 30 minutes into the flight, meal service started with a choice of beverages and an "aperitivo" of mixed nuts served in a little Noritake porcelain bowl. The main meal was served between all on one tray — probably due to the late hour of the flight and the fact that most passengers wanted to get to bed. Flight attendants were quick, but given the size of the cabin, meal service started about an hour into the flight and lasted about 90 minutes. It included a small green salad with vinaigrette and a choice of the following from the menu designed by the airline's chef partner, Neil Perry: - Brassica and pea soup with mint and pea tendrils - Gnocchi with roasted pumpkin, asparagus, sage, hazelnut and ricotta - Seared halibut with braised beans, kale, calamari, capers, olives and almond salsa - Spicy kaffir lime chicken curry with stir-fried green beans, red chili and jasmine rice - Braised beef cheek with slow-roasted baby sweet potatoes, creamed silverbeet and black pepper sour cream I ordered the chicken curry, and it was fantastic. The portion was hearty, and the sauce was flavorful but light, while the meat turned out juicy and tender. To finish, folks could choose from a selection of cheeses, including Manchego and Fourme d'Ambert, tiramisu, ice cream, or seasonal fruit. I ordered the latter for a light finish to my meal. Throughout the rest of the flight, folks could order a few small dishes on demand, including crudites with hummus, a chicken-cheese sandwich with roasted peppers and zucchini, cookies, chocolate bars, mixed nuts, potato chips and fruit. The wines on offer were not listed on the menu, but included a chardonnay from Victoria and a sauvignon blanc-semillon blend from Western Australia, plus a Shiraz from the Barossa and a pinot noir. There were also various drinks and spirits on hand, including Four Pillars gin and Bundaberg dark rum, as well as a selection of Australian beers. Flight attendants often came through during and after meal service to see if passengers wanted refills. About two hours before landing, the cabin lighting gradually got brighter, and flight attendants began serving breakfast to passengers who were awake. I slept a little longer and was offered breakfast when I got up, about 75 minutes before landing. The crew could offer this slightly staggered service because passengers fill out their menu cards earlier in the flight, making it easier to assemble trays. Passengers could choose from a selection of juices, coffee and tea, along with food items like yogurt, fruit salad, muesli, toast, croissants and mains that included: - Buttermilk pancakes with raspberry compote, yogurt and hazelnut praline - Poached eggs with mixed mushrooms, asparagus and Manchego cheese on toast - Scrambled eggs with grilled applewood bacon, balsamic roasted tomatoes and sauteed kale and spinach I got a coffee with milk and sugar, which came out hot and strong, plus a healthy green juice and the scrambled eggs. The portion was substantial, and the eggs came out well — firm and slightly fluffy. We were landing in Melbourne at around 6 a.m., so I only ate sparingly since I had the whole day ahead of me to explore the city's food scene. All told, the meals were well executed, nicely presented and served efficiently, so passengers could maximize their rest and relaxation. Would you recommend Qantas business class? The main drawback to flying Qantas across the Pacific is the lack of Wi-Fi. So if you're traveling for business and need to stay online, that's a real consideration. Hopefully, that will resolve over the coming months as the airline installs Wi-Fi across its A380 fleet. Other than that, the airline remains one of my favorite ways to fly long-haul. The crew is friendly and polished, and the seats look sleek and provide enough privacy that the lack of a closing door doesn't feel significant. Plus, the meal service and entertainment options are plentiful. I do wish the airline would release more saver-level award availability to partner programs like American Airlines AAdvantage and Alaska Airlines Atmos Rewards. But if you have some flexibility in your schedule, you should be able to find a few seats each month, and tools like Seats.aero come in handy for doing so. As for me, you'll find me hanging out in my kangaroo-emblazoned Qantas pajamas plotting my next flight aboard the Australian carrier. Related reading:

item.title: Amex Platinum vs. Delta Reserve: Which card is best for Delta loyalists?
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy Score: 3.26
Amex Platinum vs. Delta Reserve: Which card is best for Delta loyalists? Editor's Note If you ask a Delta loyalist what credit card they have, they'll more than likely respond with either the American Express Platinum Card® or the Delta SkyMiles® Reserve American Express Card. Either of these cards makes a great case for a spot in a Delta fan's wallet; despite that, they have enough differences to make it important to carefully consider your traveling style before committing to one or the other. Committed Delta flyers will likely find the Delta Reserve more appealing, but travelers who place a high value on flexibility and lounge access may get more out of the Amex Platinum. Here's a full comparison of the key similarities and differences between these two cards, so you can choose the right premium card for your Delta flights. Amex Platinum vs. Delta Reserve: At a glance | Card features | Amex Platinum | Delta Reserve | |---|---|---| | Annual fee | | | | Welcome offer | Find out your offer and see if you're eligible for as high as 175,000 bonus points after spending $12,000 on purchases in the first six months of card membership. (Welcome offers vary, and you may not be eligible for an offer.) | Earn two domestic round-trip Delta Comfort flight certificates and 50,000 bonus miles after spending $10,000 on purchases in the first six months of card membership. (A 21-plus day advance purchase is required; up to $80 per person in taxes and fees apply. Other restrictions apply.) Offer ends Nov. 4. | | Authorized user fee | | | Quick picks by traveler type | Best for | Card | |---|---| | Travelers who don't exclusively fly with Delta | Amex Platinum | | Travelers who frequently redeem points for hotel stays, in addition to flights | Amex Platinum | | Travelers who exclusively or almost exclusively fly with Delta | Delta Reserve | | Travelers who often fly on Delta with a companion | Delta Reserve | Amex Platinum vs. Delta Reserve: Welcome offer Currently, new Amex Platinum cardmembers can find out their offer and see if they're eligible for as high as 175,000 bonus points after spending $12,000 on purchases in the first six months of card membership. (Welcome offers vary, and you may not be eligible for an offer.) According to TPG's September 2026 valuations, this welcome offer is worth up to $3,500. Meanwhile, new Delta Reserve cardmembers can earn two domestic round-trip Delta Comfort flight certificates and 50,000 bonus miles after spending $10,000 on purchases in the first six months of card membership. (A 21-plus day advance purchase is required; up to $80 per person in taxes and fees apply. Other restrictions apply.) Offer ends Nov. 4. According to TPG's September 2026 valuations, the miles in this welcome offer are worth $600. Amex restricts cardmembers to earning one welcome bonus per card per lifetime, so it's important to get the best offer you can. If you frequently fly with a companion or travel often domestically on Delta, the current Delta Reserve offer may be one of the strongest we've seen on the card for you. If you're able to get at least 150,000 points on the Amex Platinum, that's a stellar offer and worth applying for. Winner: Amex Platinum. The value of the Delta Reserve's welcome bonus is contingent on you flying frequently with the airline within the U.S., while the Amex Platinum's is both more valuable and more flexible. Amex Platinum vs. Delta Reserve: Benefits Statement credits | | Amex Platinum | Delta Reserve | |---|---|---| | Standout statement credits | Enrollment is required for select benefits. | Enrollment is required for select benefits. | The Delta Reserve differs some from other premium airline cards in that many of its key statement credits are not explicitly tied to flying. This makes it a closer competitor to the Amex Platinum, known for its array of merchant-linked statement credits. It's harder to justify the Delta Reserve's annual fee with statement credits alone compared to the Amex Platinum. Provided you maximize the Platinum's hotel* and Resy statement credits, you'll already be ahead of the card's $895 annual fee. *For use on Fine Hotels + Resorts and The Hotel Collection bookings; THC bookings require a minimum two-night stay. Conversely, even if you use the full amount of the Delta Reserve's Resy, Delta Stays and ride-hailing statement credits, you'll still be around $90 short of breaking even on the card's $650 annual fee. If you're not comfortable with a card's value hinging on booking at least a couple of flights with Delta each year in addition to maximizing its statement credits, the Amex Platinum is the safer bet. Lounge access | | Amex Platinum | Delta Reserve | |---|---|---| | Lounge access | Access to the American Express Global Lounge Collection for eligible cardmembers, including: Enrollment is required for select benefits. **When traveling on same-day Delta flights; 10 visits per calendar year; resets Feb. 1; unlimited visits after $75,000 in spending in a calendar year. | Enrollment is required for select benefits. ***15 visits per year when traveling on a same-day Delta flight; resets Feb. 1; earn unlimited visits by spending $75,000 in a calendar year on your card. | The Amex Platinum is always my recommendation for anyone looking for a premium card with great lounge access. Eligible cardmembers have access to Centurion Lounges, Delta Sky Clubs, Priority Pass lounges and more. It's hard to beat what the Amex Platinum gives you here, but the Delta Reserve offers solid lounge access for an airline card. Typically, airline cards offer lounge access only to their associated airline's lounge network, but the Delta Reserve also includes access to the Centurion Lounge. Of course, you must have a same-day flight with Delta to access a Centurion Lounge, but you're likely flying Delta often anyway if you're thinking of opening its top-tier card. Given that the Amex Platinum offers Sky Club and Centurion Lounge access for eligible cardmembers, along with a roster of other lounge options, I view it as the winner here. The only exception is if you plan to visit Sky Clubs more than 10 times per year, since the Delta Reserve offers up to 15 visits per year. Delta-specific benefits | | Amex Platinum | Delta Reserve | |---|---|---| | Delta-specific benefits | None, unless you select Delta as your qualifying airline for your up to $200 per calendar year airline incidentals statement credit | | Here's where the Delta Reserve really pulls ahead of the Amex Platinum. With perks like free checked bags, priority boarding and a companion certificate for round-trip travel on Delta to select destinations each account year, the Delta Reserve offers a lot more by default than the Amex Platinum for Delta fans. You can select Delta as your qualifying airline of choice for the Amex Platinum's up to $200 per calendar year airline incidentals statement credit and use that amount to cover charges like checked bag fees and seat upgrades. That's what I did this year, using the full amount of this statement credit to cover checked bag fees and Sky Club guest passes for a trip to Mexico. Even so, there's a good chance Delta loyalists spend more than $200 with the airline in a year. Plus, the Amex Platinum's airline statement credit won't grant priority boarding or a companion certificate. Winner: When comparing the benefits of both cards as a whole, the Delta Reserve is the better choice for frequent Delta flyers. Its annual companion certificate, higher number of Sky Club visits in a year and day-of-travel perks are a better fit for Delta fans than what the Platinum offers. That said, if you care more about statement credits and lounge access, the Amex Platinum makes a more compelling case. How to earn and redeem rewards with the Amex Platinum vs. Delta Reserve Despite what you may think, the Amex Platinum makes a more compelling case with its earning rates than the Delta Reserve, with a couple of exceptions. Earning rewards | | Amex Platinum | Delta Reserve | |---|---|---| | Earning rates | | | This comparison highlights what is, in my opinion, one of the Delta Reserve's biggest shortcomings: A low earning rate on Delta flights. Earning only 3 miles per dollar spent on Delta flights isn't the best rate, given the card's $650 annual fee. I can think of just a couple of circumstances where I'd suggest someone go with the Delta Reserve over the Amex Platinum if maximizing earnings on Delta purchases is the key goal. Since you can transfer Amex Membership Rewards points to Delta SkyMiles, it's not like you're locking yourself out of Delta's loyalty program by going with the Amex Platinum. One exception is if you're anticipating spending more than $500,000 in a calendar year on Delta flights, but I expect the grand majority of cardmembers will not hit this spending cap. Another is if you're chasing Delta status and want to earn bonus MQDs on your purchases. Neither card is a great choice for everyday spending. If you want to maximize your earnings on everyday purchases and use those rewards for Delta flights, another Amex card like the American Express® Gold Card is likely a better choice than either of these cards. Redeeming rewards You can redeem Membership Rewards points in a variety of ways, including for statement credits, travel, gift cards and to pay for purchases through PayPal and at Amazon.com checkout. Delta SkyMiles can be used to book flights with Delta and partner airlines, such as Air France-KLM, Virgin Atlantic and Korean Air. In addition, you can use SkyMiles for upgrades, premium purchases in Sky Clubs and more. As I mentioned earlier, Membership Rewards points can be transferred to Delta SkyMiles. They can also be sent to 19 other airline and hotel partners, including Delta's airline partners, such as Air France-KLM and Aeromexico. This is where you'll get the most value for your Membership Rewards, and why TPG values Membership Rewards significantly higher than Delta SkyMiles (as per our September 2026 valuations). I always recommend redeeming SkyMiles for flights, since that will give you the greatest value. I transferred 84,000 Membership Rewards points to Delta SkyMiles earlier this year to book three one-way tickets from Seattle-Tacoma International Airport (SEA) to Cancun International Airport (CUN). Winner: Amex Platinum. You can transfer your rewards to Delta SkyMiles, plus over a dozen other programs in the event your travel plans involve flights or hotel stays outside of Delta's booking system. Its earning rates are also more compelling. Can I have both the Amex Platinum and the Delta Reserve? If you're prepared to pay over $1,500 in annual fees for both cards, then yes. Having both the Amex Platinum and Delta Reserve makes a lot of sense for Delta fans, since you'll receive the flexibility of the Amex Platinum alongside the Delta Reserve's Delta-linked perks. You'll also be able to earn two welcome bonuses, provided you haven't held either card before. That's a huge stash of rewards for your future Delta flights. That said, neither of these cards will make sense for you if you aren't traveling at least a few times each year. While you may be able to make the Amex Platinum's annual fee work with its statement credits, you'll likely get just as much value from a mid-tier credit card. Should I get the Amex Platinum or Delta Reserve? If you're almost always or always flying with Delta, the Delta Reserve more than likely makes the most sense for you. However, Delta loyalists can still benefit from the Amex Platinum's lounge access, superior earning rate on airlines booked directly or through Amex Travel (subject to a spending cap) and up to $200 per calendar year airline incidentals statement credit. Ultimately, the decision comes down to the value you place on flexibility. Bottom line The Amex Platinum and Delta Reserve are close competitors. There's a strong case to be made for either card having a spot in a Delta fan's wallet, but it also can make a lot of sense to have both at the same time. You can't really go wrong with either choice, but their high annual fees mean you'll want to pick the better of the two for your situation: - If you're a Delta loyalist chasing status, frequently visit Sky Clubs or often travel with a companion, choose the Delta Reserve. - If you want extensive lounge access, high earning rates on flights (subject to a spending cap) and points flexibility, go with the Amex Platinum. To learn more, read our full reviews of the Amex Platinum and Delta SkyMiles Reserve. Apply here: Amex Platinum Apply here: Delta Reserve For rates and fees of the Delta Reserve, click here. For rates and fees of the Amex Platinum, click here.

item.title: I make my own amenity kit for long flights — here’s what’s inside
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy Score: 3.17
I make my own amenity kit for long flights — here’s what’s inside I love a good inflight amenity kit. Seeing a colorful little pouch stocked with travel-size products waiting at my seat is one of my favorite parts of flying in the front of the plane. Airlines often partner with fancy brands familiar to premium flyers, such as Sisley or Kiehl's, to provide skincare goodies in addition to the standard kit-stuffers like earplugs and eye masks. The only thing is, I have a bizarre allergy. While ultra-soothing for most people, aloe vera makes me break out. I know certain brands are safe for me. For example, the Shiseido Men skincare line stocked in Japan Airlines first class and the L'Occitane products in Lufthansa Allegris business class don't make me itch. Unfortunately, many other skincare products contain this scurrilous succulent, so I have to be careful about which amenity kits I use... and which ones I tuck away to take home to my husband. After encountering aloe-laden skincare products in amenity kit after amenity kit (I know, it's like complaining they only pour one type of Champagne in first class), I finally decided to take matters into my own hands. I put together my very own DIY amenity kit for flights so I would know I had all the essentials. And unlike airline amenity kits, I don't have to be flying in a premium cabin in order to enjoy the inclusions. In fact, my little amenity kit comes in even handier on long economy flights since I can primp before I land. Here are the items that I stock my DIY inflight amenity kit with and why I pack each one. Keep in mind, these aren't products like Trtl travel pillows; they are just everyday essentials I like to have on hand. DIY flight amenity kit Short on time? Here's a quick hit list of the things I pack, with links so you can purchase them yourself: Now for the full list. Clear pouch First things first, you need a handy, reusable kit to actually carry everything. Because many of my amenity kit items are liquids and there are TSA rules and all, I tend to pack my kit in a clear pouch like these to save headaches at the airport. In a pinch, I just use a Ziploc bag. Sanitizing wipes I was doing this even before the pandemic. I read article after article about how germy planes are and which surfaces around your seat tend to be dirtiest ... and I just decided to be my own seat cleaner at a certain point. That's why I always carry a pouch of Lysol disinfecting wipes, which will kill just about anything. The only thing to keep in mind is to wash your hands after using them, since you don't want to touch your face with the disinfecting agent. If you don't have an aloe allergy like me, Wet Ones makes skin-friendlier wipes. Hand sanitizer I swear I'm not a germaphobe, but it never hurts to have an extra spurt of sanitizer just in case. Many sanitizing gels also contain aloe, so my go-to is the fancy but inexpensive lavender-scented spray from EO. Tissues You never know when a sneeze will come on ... or if you'll need to pass a tissue to a seatmate, so I always have a travel-size packet of tissues on hand. Toothbrush and toothpaste I don't need these when I'm traveling in business or first class, but if I'm on a long-haul economy flight, I pack an extra-compact folding travel toothbrush. And you'll find a drawer in my bathroom littered with travel-size toothpastes since I go through them at a ridiculous pace. You could consider dry toothpaste tablets to save space (and they won't count against your liquid limit). Earplugs I'm a light sleeper, so even if I'm flying at the pointy end of the plane and receive a kit with soft foam earplugs, I tend to bring my own silicone ones along anyway. I know, I know, the otolaryngologists among you will decry me for waxifying my ears; however, I make sure to clean my ears after flights, and I don't use these too often. The benefit of drowning out cabin noise even outweighs the auricular hazard (for me). If those are too heavy-duty for you, though, you can always switch to the foam pairs. Eye mask From the overheads to the screen of that one person who insists on watching all the episodes of "House of the Dragon" while everyone else is sleeping, there are tons of LED lights in airplane cabins. That's why I always have an eye mask on hand. Even up in business class, where an eye mask might be provided, they tend to be itchy and not breathable, so it never hurts to tote your own. Saline nasal spray One of the worst parts about flying for me is how dried out my nose, mouth and sinuses get. That also makes me prone to catching colds. To solve for that, I always bring a squeezable saline nasal spray. Using a spritz every few hours keeps me breathing comfortably, and I've noticed I get sick a lot less often since I started using it. Lubricating eye drops I try not to overuse this since it can actually make dry eyes worse over time. But my eye doctor said it was perfectly fine to use eye drops on longer flights from time to time and recommended Systane in particular. Chewing gum Like my nose and eyes, my mouth gets dried out on long flights, no matter how much water I drink, so you'll always find a pack of gum in my bag. I tend to chew it during takeoff and landing to help with the pressure changes, too. Hand cream As we have now established, airplane air is dry. That has a big impact on my skin, too, especially my hands (which you now know I've been sanitizing like a fiend). To counteract all that, I make sure to have Cerave hand lotion with me. I find it moisturizes super well, and even a small tube lasts me several months. Facial wipes I can't imagine much that's grosser than washing your face with airplane lavatory water. Except drinking it, I suppose. Don't do either. Instead, after an inflight snooze, use some gentle face wipes to freshen up before using the next DIY amenity kit inclusion. Face lotion I like to step off the plane glowing. Kidding. I just want to look like a human being and not a zombie. So I make sure to have some heavy-duty face cream with me. Cerave's inexpensive eye repair cream does the trick — it's great for the sensitive area under your eyes, and you also only need a small amount for the rest of your face. It's also unscented, so no one will know your secret to looking so fresh. If you really want to plump up your skin with that glowing, dewy look (and you lack the self-consciousness gene), you could always apply Summer Fridays jet lag hydrating eye patches, too. Lip balm Go as fancy or as frugal as you like. I'm a simple guy, so my lip balm of choice is Chapstick with SPF. I can apply it on the plane and know my skin will be well-protected even if I land in the middle of the day. Deodorant You've dashed to the airport on public transport or via Uber. You've hauled your checked bag to the desk, parkoured around oblivious travelers shuffling aimlessly through the airport terminal and then settled into a seat that's always too hot or too cold but never just right. You're going to need some deodorant after a long flight, so pack a small stick to use in a pinch. A pen I'm that guy. You know, the one who seems to be the only responsible adult on the plane with an actual pen. I'm the guy everyone else is asking to borrow his pen to fill out immigration and customs forms, or just to make a note on something. So you be that guy, too. It'll save me from losing all the pens I have to loan out! A pill pack Especially on the long-haul flights I'm used to taking, which can last up to 16 hours, I like to keep a stock of my daily vitamins and supplements, plus a few Ibuprofen and Tylenol just in case. I don't want to pack tons of pill bottles, though. Instead, I bring a travel pill pack with various compartments so I can bring what I need for the flight and leave the rest in my checked or carry-on bag.

item.title: This easy-to-miss Marriott site earned me 3,000 bonus points
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy Score: 2.57
This easy-to-miss Marriott site earned me 3,000 bonus points There are the big and mostly obvious ways to earn points and miles — such as through credit card bonuses and spending, and, of course, on actual travel. But there are plenty of other easy-to-miss ways to earn rewards, too. From dining programs to Lyft rides, Starbucks reloads and so much more, you can earn points and miles in places you might not expect. And recently, for me, one of those places was on a private boat excursion in the middle of a bioluminescent bay during a trip to Grand Cayman. Taking good photos of the bioluminescent bay in the dark turned out to be ... impossible. But earning a few thousand Marriott Bonvoy points on the boat ride was shockingly easy. Here's how I did it: Marriott has what it calls a Marriott Tours and Activities site where you can book excursions around the world and earn, or even use, Marriott points in the process. Marriott doesn't operate these attractions and tours itself; instead, it serves as a third-party broker or aggregator. Some of the types of activities I've seen available to book through the site include: - Snorkeling trips - Walking tours - Boat and fishing trips - Food tours - Historical tours If you want to redeem Marriott points to cover one of these tours or activities, based on my test searches, you can currently do so at a rate of 0.4 cents per point. That means it would take 25,000 Marriott points to pay for a $100 activity. TPG values Marriott points at 0.75 cents each when used for travel (based on September 2026 TPG valuations), so that's not mathematically the all-time best redemption value with your Marriott points, but it is an option. But you can also earn Marriott points, like I did, at a rate of 5 points per dollar spent. Booking a private boat to see the bioluminescent bay in Grand Cayman for my group of five didn't cost any more per person than a group tour, so we booked that for $600, earning 3,000 bonus Marriott points we otherwise would have left on the table. In fact, booking directly with the company we used would have cost the same as booking via Marriott, so these were really just points waiting to be earned. Unfortunately, while the charge appeared on my statement as Marriott Bonvoy Hallandale Beach, Florida, it did not post as a Marriott purchase to earn bonus points on my Marriott credit card. Instead, on my transaction, it coded as entertainment - general attractions. So, you may want to pay with a card that offers a strong return on everyday spending or one that earns bonus rewards on entertainment. Bottom line Earning 5 bonus Marriott points per dollar on tours and activities isn't going to change the trajectory of your points and miles earnings. But I'm of the mindset that every point counts, especially when it doesn't cost anything extra to earn them and doesn't add any real hassle to my life. Marriott Tours and Activities checked all of those boxes for me. I paid the same price I would have paid by booking directly and walked away with 3,000 extra Marriott points for a pretty memorable boat ride to see the bioluminescent bay that I was going to book anyway.
